[I saw birds] whose sounds were varied, the birds called leaf-chariots, awakened by their own cries; [I saw] lakes whose beauty was produced by wandering bees. Having gone beyond them, I saw a great forest. What was it like? It was dense and difficult with the stems of nala, bamboo, reed, kuśa grass, and kīcaka. The kīcakas are kinds of bamboo with large spaces within; they were terrible and hard to endure, of a fearful appearance, and a playground for serpents and the rest.

My senses and body were exhausted and I was overcome by thirst; I sipped water. “At the base of the pippala” means at the root of an aśvattha tree. “Taking shelter” means sitting down. “With the self” means with the intellect or the mind. “The self abiding in the self” means the Supreme Self abiding in the heart; “the self” means the Supreme Self.
His mind was conquered and brought under control by devotional feeling, and his eyes were filled with drops of tears born from eagerness.
His limbs were covered with horripilation from the overwhelming weight of love, in a great flood of bliss, the vast ocean of supreme joy. He saw both—himself and the Supreme [Lord].
“The beloved of the mind” means the desired object. “That which removes sorrow” means that which takes away grief. “I arose” means “I became upright.”
Having placed the mind in the heart and made it steady, I became unsatisfied and distressed, as though unable to bear the separation; this is supplied by the context.
“Beyond the range of speech” means Īśvara, who is the object of perception. A variant reading says “beyond the range of the Vedic words.”

“Alas” is a compassionate form of address. “Do not [show Yourself to] me” means “I am not fit to see You.” Why? Because the impurities, such as lust, of unsuccessful yogins—those whose yoga has not reached completion—have not been matured and burned.

“Where, then, were You seen?” He answers: “I showed it only once,” and did so in order to create attraction toward Me. What use is desire directed toward You? He answers: “the man whose desire is for Me”—the desires that lie in the heart.
Even through a short period of service to the good, and after abandoning what is blameworthy, he will leave this body and attain My people, the status of My attendants.
“In the creation of beings” means in their creation, and “in their restraint” means in their dissolution. Alternatively, it means the restraint of the creation of beings.

That well-known great wonder is the breath of the Great Being, as in the revelation “this is the Ṛg Veda,” and so forth. What is He like? Īśvara, the controller of all. “Whose sign is the sky” means whose form is the sky. Though present, He is not marked by anything; He is the signless one. To that unseen Bhagavān I offered my reverence, bowing down. Through this I became the recipient of His compassion.

While continually reciting the names of the Infinite, I became free of shame and free of envy; this is supplied by the context. An old manuscript does not contain the words from “of the Infinite” through “reciting.”

At the appointed time, death appeared suddenly, like lightning. “Like lightning” gives the example of sudden appearance. The adjective “sau­dāminī” makes the comparison vivid. It may refer to a garland named Sudāmā, meaning lightning born at its edge; alternatively, Sudāmā may be a crystal mountain, and lightning born near a mountain of crystal is especially clear. Or “lightning” may mean something near at hand, according to the etymological tradition. An old manuscript preserves the explanation beginning with “Sudāmā” through the etymological citation.

When the Lord applied that [form] to me—namely, the pure, sattva-made body of a Bhagavān’s attendant that had been promised when He said, “Having abandoned this blameworthy world, you will attain My people”—the karma that had begun to bear fruit came to an end, or the end of the begun karma was itself its result. My five-element body fell. This indicates that the bodies of the Lord’s attendants are not produced by karma, and are pure, eternal, and so forth.

After taking in and withdrawing the three worlds, I entered, together with the breath, into the middle of the all-pervading Brahmā, who wished to sleep upon the waters of the single ocean. A passage of the Kūrma Purāṇa says: “Then, descending, the Universal Self entered the body of the discus-holder and attained Vaiṣṇavī sleep, becoming one with Viṣṇu.” In the reading “in his own resting place, in the waters,” understand that “Brahmā” is spoken with the intention of expressing non-difference from Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
From the vital airs and senses, I and the sages headed by Marīci were born.

Those devoted to action do not go beyond; those who have reached Brahma-loka through austerity and the like do not go within. But, by the grace of Mahā-Viṣṇu, while maintaining an unbroken vow of celibacy, I wander both within and without. My movement is unobstructed everywhere. A variant reading says “those who have gone to the outer world.”

Why do you wander? He answers: by the command of the Lord, for the welfare of the world. “Given by the Lord” means given by Īśvara. The seven notes—niṣāda, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, ṣaḍja, madhyama, dhaivata, and pañcama—are Brahman because they reveal Brahman; he is adorned with them. This means that he possesses the naturally established seven notes. “Having formed a melody” means having made it rich with melodic elaboration.
He states his own purpose: “he sings forth.”

He states the purpose for others. “Measures” are the sense objects, and “contacts” are their enjoyments; their minds are distressed by desire for them. The recitation of Hari’s deeds alone is a boat in the ocean of becoming. This is not established merely by the authority of revelation; it is directly seen through agreement and difference—when it is present, and when it is absent.

He strengthens the certainty “this alone” through experience. What does not pacify the mind through restraints and the other disciplines pacifies it directly through service to Mukunda. If it is pacified somehow by service to Mukunda alone, how much more by describing His qualities? That is the meaning.
What pleases your mind has also been explained.
“Having addressed” means having requested and given permission. “Spontaneous” means free from any resolve directed toward his own personal purpose.
He praises the good fortune of Nārada, the singer of Hari’s topics: “Aho!” “Intoxicated” means transported with joy; he makes music with the strings of the vīṇā.

Now, in order to speak of the birth of Parīkṣit, the hearer of the Bhāgavata, the punishment of Drauṇi for the killing of sleeping children is called the seventh [chapter]. [Having] heard Nārada’s intended meaning.

Note: In some copies the reading is “janma-karma-parīkṣitaḥ.”
On the Brahma-river—one dedicated to Brahman and resorted to by brāhmaṇas. [The place is called so] because it increases the sattra, the ritual action; thus [it is so named].

On a grove of badarī trees, adorned by a whole group of them. He concentrated the mind; he made it steady. He performed the meditation instructed by Nārada: “Remember his deeds in samādhi” [Bhāgavata 1.5.13]—that is the meaning.

“Fixed” means unmoving. Here the cause is “by bhakti-yoga,” “stainless.” First he saw the Puruṣa, the Lord. The reading may also be “pūrṇam.” And he saw māyā having the Lord as her support, dependent on Him.

And he saw the saṃsāra of the jīvas made by the Lord’s māyā—he says this with “by which.” Deluded by it, distracted by the covering of his own nature, although distinct from the three guṇas, he nevertheless obtains the anartha—such as doership—produced by identification with the three guṇas made by it.

He also saw that direct bhakti-yoga to Adhokṣaja which pacifies anartha. Having seen all this himself, he composed the Sātvata-saṃhitā, called Śrī-Bhāgavata, for the sake of the people who do not know thus. Therefore, by these three ślokas, the meaning of the Bhāgavata has been shown in summary. This is said: The Lord, controller of māyā through the power of knowledge, whose nature of supreme bliss is eternally manifest, omniscient and omnipotent; the jīva, deluded by His māyā, with his nature hidden and with qualities opposite to that; and liberation for him through knowledge obtained by devotion to the Lord. This was said by Viṣṇusvāmin:

Īśvara, embraced by Hlādinī and Saṃvit, is Being-Consciousness-Bliss; the jīva, covered by his own ignorance, is a mine of heaps of suffering.

And also: He is Īśa, under whose control māyā is; he is the jīva, afflicted by it; [one] whose supreme bliss is manifest; [one] whose very great suffering is manifest; distressed by distinctions arising from the reversal born of [dual] vision; remaining as one who enjoys through my māyā—this Nṛhari we praise; and so forth.
He displays the capacity of the Saṃhitā to pacify anartha with “in which.” “In which, merely while it is being heard”—what then when it has been heard [fully]? That is the meaning.
Having enumerated and purified.
For what reason? Vast, expanded.

“Nirgranthas” means those who have gone out from books. This is said in the Gītā:

“When your intellect has crossed beyond the delusion of bewilderment, then you will become indifferent to what is to be heard and what has been heard.” [Gītā 2.52]

Or, the knot itself is “grantha”—the knot in the form of anger and ego has ceased for them; that is, they are free from the knots of the heart. Now, to remove every objection beginning with “What need have liberated persons of devotion?” he says “such qualities.”

Note: The portion enclosed in the parenthetical marks is present in an old manuscript.

“Granted, let them perform devotion; but what is the reason for Śuka’s study of this scripture?” In answer he says “of Hari.” “He studied” means “he learned.” [He did so] because the devotees of Viṣṇu are dear to him. The meaning is that he desired their association in the context of exposition and so forth. By this, the answer has been given to the question, “How did Śuka begin the exposition, with [the statement] ‘his son, a great yogī,’ and the rest?”

To state the answer to the other question—“How did Parīkṣit listen by fasting unto death?”—with “his birth is greatly astonishing” and so forth, he says [the word] “Parīkṣit.” “Vilāpana” means liberation or death. “Saṃsthā” means the great departure. [The account is] in such a way that the rise of the stories of Śrī Kṛṣṇa comes about through it.

Here, intending to explain the birth of Parīkṣit, first of all he begins the account in order to state that the embryo was protected by Kṛṣṇa from Aśvatthāma’s brahmāstra, with “when.” When Drauṇi, Aśvatthāma, carried away the heads of Kṛṣṇā’s sons, the sons of Draupadī, then their mother cried; and Arjuna, the wearer of a crown and garland, consoling her, spoke [thus]—this is the syntactic connection with the third [quarter]. Why did he bring the heads of the children? In response to this expectation he says “in the battle.” Although the Pāṇḍavas are also Kauravas, nevertheless Dhṛṣṭadyumna, born in the Sṛñjaya lineage, was the commander of the Pāṇḍavas’ army; therefore “of the Sṛñjayas” is stated. “The destination of the hero” means heaven. “Atho” means afterwards. When the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Duryodhana, was in such a condition that his two thigh-bones were broken by the impact of the mace thrown by Vṛkodara.

“Of the husband”—of Duryodhana. “Sma” is used in the sense of deliberation. Thinking, “thus it would be pleasing,” [he did it]. The other sentence [says] that it was indeed displeasing to him. The reason for its being displeasing is given by “heinous.”

“I wipe away” means “I remove the tears of sorrow.” The phrase “O brāhmaṇa’s lowest” identifies Droṇa’s son as an aggressor: tradition remembers six kinds of aggressor—one who sets fire, poisons, attacks with a weapon, steals wealth, seizes land, or takes another’s wife. Here “aggressor” indicates one armed with a weapon and, by implication, the killing of a son. “I shall bring [him] before You” means “I shall bring him near with arrows released from the bow Gāṇḍīva.” “Having placed his head upon the ground” means having made it a seat; though a son, he was still unshaven.

“Graceful” means beautiful and varied speech. “He” means Arjuna. Acyuta alone was his friend and charioteer. He was armored, carried a formidable bow, and had the monkey, Hanumān, on his banner. He pursued the Guru’s son in his chariot.

“Rushing upon” means running toward them; he is Droṇa’s son, the killer of a child. His mind was agitated and his heart trembled. He desired to preserve his life, not his fame, and fled across the earth as far as he could go. The comparison is to Brahmā fleeing in fear of Rudra after becoming an animal and attempting to obtain his daughter. A reading “like the sun” alludes to a story in the Vāmana Purāṇa: a demon named Vidyunmālī received a golden aerial vehicle from Rudra, flew behind the sun and darkened the night with its radiance; the sun drove it away and brought it down, and Rudra, angered on hearing this, fled in fear of the sun. The demon’s vehicle fell at Vārāṇasī and became known as Lolārka.

“Without refuge” means without protection. One might think that flight itself is his protection; no, for that too was brought to a halt. “With weary horses” means the chariot whose horses were exhausted. “The weapon of Brahma’s head” means the brahmāstra. “Son of a twice-born” indicates his lack of foresight.
That was the brahmāstra. “Collected” means having concentrated his awareness. Though he did not know how to withdraw the weapon, the reason he could launch it was that he was in mortal danger.
Seeing the radiance released from the weapon blazing in every direction, and then seeing the danger to his life.
Before presenting his request, he first praises Kṛṣṇa in four verses. For those being burned by saṁsāra, He is the liberation—the one who frees them from it. This is the meaning.

You are directly Īśvara. Why? Because You are the Person beyond prakṛti. Why is that so? Because You are the primal cause. Although He is the cause, he states His changelessness: having overcome māyā, He remains established in the Self whose nature is liberation.

You alone also give the three human aims, he says with “He.” You who remain having overcome māyā arrange the fruits of dharma and the rest for the person overcome by māyā. This is done through Your power.

By this incarnation too, Your favor toward the side of the good is revealed. Could the burden of the earth not be removed by Your mere will? He answers: [You appeared] for the contemplation and protection of Your own relatives, and also for Your one-pointed devotees.
Having praised Him, he presents his request: “What is this, what is its nature, and from where does it arise?” The word “perhaps” expresses uncertainty.

This is the weapon of Brahmā belonging to Droṇa’s son. When his life was threatened, it was merely displayed; he was not skilled in using it, because he did not know how to withdraw it. “You know this” means “You understand this matter.”

“Withdrawal” means making it thin and bringing it to an end. Therefore destroy the blazing, formidable power of that weapon with the power of the brahmāstra itself. Your weapon, once launched, will subside on its own after you withdraw it, since you are skilled in weapons.

“The enemies” are those very foes, and “the hero who kills them” is Phālguna, Arjuna. Having touched water and performed ācamana, he circumambulated Śrī Kṛṣṇa. He did this in order to withdraw the brahmāstra.

The powers of the two brahmāstras, enclosed by their arrows, met one another and grew. They covered heaven, earth, and the sky, just as at dissolution the fire from Saṅkarṣaṇa’s mouth and the sun, joining together, increase in force.
“The two” are Droṇa’s son and Phālguna. Those being burned by them thought the radiance to be the fire of universal dissolution.
“The disturbance of the worlds” means their overturning and destruction. Perceiving Vāsudeva’s intention, he withdrew both brahmāstras.

He was the son of Kṛpī, born in the line of Gautama. His eyes were copper-red from anger. The comparison for his lack of compassion is to an animal. The comparison for binding him as a matter of dharma is to a sacrificial animal; the rope is the cord with which he was bound.

To establish that Arjuna remained devoted to dharma even while overcome by grief and anger, Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s words are given in six verses. He desired to take [Droṇa’s son] to the camp, the royal residence, and appeared to be angry.

Just as the jīva’s birth and the rest are māyā, so also the birth and the rest of Īśvara are māyā—this is stated with “thus.” “The actions of the non-agent” means the deeds of one who is not an agent. “The births of the unborn” means the births of the Lord, the master of the heart and the inner controller.

Even the killing of an enemy who is asleep, and of a child, is not righteous. He demonstrates this through alternatives: one intoxicated by drink; one heedless; one insane through possession or madness; one dull and unable to act; one who has taken refuge; and one whose chariot has been broken.

His killing in the form of punishment is itself his welfare, the attainment of his human purpose. For without the fault being removed by punishment and atonement, that person would descend to a lower state. The tradition says: “People who have committed sins, when kings inflict the proper punishment, go to heaven purified of their stain, like the righteous.”
Although he had been instructed to do so, he did not wish to kill even the killer of a son, because he himself was a great and noble person.
“The beloved charioteer of Govinda” means the one whose charioteer was dear Govinda. He acted for the sake of the mother who was grieving for her sons.

He was brought in this way, with contempt, and made to face downward by the blameworthy act he had committed. Seeing the offender with compassion, she—whose disposition was gentle and beautiful—[spoke].
The two actions “he bowed” and “he spoke” indicate his agitation and bewilderment. He could not bear bringing him in bound.

“Together with the secret” means together with the concealed mantra. “Release” and “withdrawal” mean the use and retraction of the weapon; the group of weapons is included with both. Moreover, Kṛpī is the body, the very self, of Droṇa, and is his half. The revelation says that the wife is half of a man’s self, and the ritual texts show that husband and wife have one form through the fire rite. One may object: if her husband was dead, how did she live? He answers: she did not follow her husband, because she was the mother of heroes and had sons.
Therefore, O rulers acting in this matter, the venerable family of your teacher must not be made to undergo suffering. Rather, it must be honored and revered.
“One whose child has died” means one whose son is dead.

He states the opposite fault with “by whom.” The action of that royal family, together with its descendants, is afflicted and pervaded by grief; it burns the family of the brāhmaṇas, whose members are the agents [of the punishment].

The six qualities of the queen’s speech are to be seen in the six preceding verses: “righteous” means not contrary to dharma; “just” means not contrary to justice; “with the secret” and the rest are explained accordingly; “with compassion” is “he is half of her self”; “without deceit” is “O knower of dharma”; and “equally” is “do not let both [mothers] cry,” because their suffering is equal. “The great one who was angered” is a stern statement offered as beneficial instruction. O brāhmaṇas, the king approved and welcomed the queen’s words.
Nakula and the others also approved. Yuyudhāna is Sātyaki.
For Droṇa’s son, in that condition, killing alone was best; otherwise there would be the prospect of his falling into hell. “He killed” means “he slew.”

The meaning of the statement about four arms is this: when Bhīma began to kill him and Draupadī suddenly began to stop it, Kṛṣṇa manifested four arms in order to restrain both. Arjuna, His friend, was uncertain about what to do.

“Worthy of killing” means one who deserves death. “A brāhmaṇa must not be killed” is the rule established by the scripture I have made. Yet tradition also says: “Even an aggressor who is learned in Vedānta may be killed; by that one does not become a killer of a brāhmaṇa.” Uphold both instructions.

He says, “Fulfill your promise.” While consoling the beloved Draupadī, you promised his killing; make that promise true, and make it pleasing. In killing him, Bhīma’s wish is fulfilled; in not killing him, Draupadī’s wish is fulfilled; both wishes are Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s concern.

Understanding his inner intention, he knew that the two aims could not both be accomplished; therefore this was his intention. With a sword he cut what had grown on the head—the hair together with the hair-knot.
He was deprived of the jewel as well and was driven out.
By this, everything spoken by Śrī Kṛṣṇa was fulfilled. “Shaving” means cutting the hair.
“Removal” means taking him away for the purpose of burning [the body].

In the eighth [chapter], the protection of Parīkṣit from the weapon of the enraged Drauṇi, the praise of Śrī Kṛṣṇa by Kuntī, and the grief of the king are narrated.

The Pāṇḍavas, together with Kṛṣṇā [Draupadī] and accompanied by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, went to the Ganges to give water to their dead relatives. Having placed the women in front, making the women go before. Because in that action the prescription is that women precede.

Having led [them] and given [the water]. In the water of that river, the Ganges, which is purified by the dust of Hari’s lotus feet. From the mention of bathing again, it is understood that they bathed at the beginning also.

“The lord of the Kurus”—Yudhiṣṭhira. “With his younger brothers”—accompanied by Bhīma and the others; “afflicted by grief for sons” is an adjective of the three [women].

Note: The reading “afflicted by grief for sons” is not found in many places.

“Accompanied by the munis.”

“By the cheaters”—the deceitful, Duryodhana and the rest. Those whose lifespan was damaged, destroyed, by acts beginning with the seizing of Draupadī’s hair.

“Having caused [him] to perform” and the rest is a summary of the future account. Like that of Śatamanyu, the performer of a hundred sacrifices [Indra].

“Śaineya”—Sātyaki, the grandson of Śini, together with Uddhava.

Seated on the chariot, he perceived, saw, Uttarā, the mother of Parīkṣit, running toward [him], agitated and bewildered with fear.

Uttarā prays to Śrī Kṛṣṇa with “protect, protect,” in two [places]. He says that there is no other fit to be prayed to. “From You” means than You; “fearlessness” means freedom from fear; “I do not see.” “Where” means in the world in which there is death among one another, mutually.
Here she reports the fear at hand. It rushes forward; it comes facing [her]. He whose missile is heated iron, made of metal. He says with extreme humility: “kāma”—as desired, as one wishes.
He understood the brahmāstra of Drauṇi, who was extremely enraged through defeat, as having been set in motion to make this world without the Pāṇḍavas, empty of Pāṇḍavas.
Therefore it came with many faces; he says this with “then indeed.” “Then indeed” means just at that time.
Seeing that danger, difficult to ward off because the brahmāstra cannot be turned back by other weapons. “Those whose self has no other object”—that is, those exclusively fixed [in Him].

Being within Vairāṭī Uttarā, he covered the embryo. The reason there is: because [he is] the Self, the inner controller. “Lord of yoga” is stated in order to establish entry even though He is externally situated. “For the continuation of the Kurus,” for their progeny. It is said thus because the Pāṇḍavas too are born from the Kuru lineage.
“Amogha” and “apratikriya.” It became completely pacified; it was fully quieted.
Do not regard this subduing of the brahmāstra as an ordinary matter; do not think the Lord is merely human. “This universe” is [also included in the wonder being revealed].
[She offers this obeisance] together with Kṛṣṇā, Draupadī.

“I bow to You.” One might object: how can You bow to me, who am younger? He answers: You are the Primal Person. Why? You are beyond prakṛti. Why is that? You are Īśvara, the controller even of prakṛti. Therefore You are established as the fullness within and without all beings. Yet You remain unperceived.

Māyā itself is a curtain, a concealing power; by it You are covered. Therefore I, being ignorant and unacquainted with bhakti-yoga, merely bow to You. You are called Adhokṣaja because knowledge born from the senses does not reach You. You are imperishable and unlimited, and so You are not perceived by a deluded person identified with the body.
This is for the supreme swans—the paramahaṁsas—in their discrimination between the Self and the non-Self. Indeed, [even] women [may approach You in this way].
Having stated that You can be reached through the yoga of knowledge and devotion, she again simply offers obeisance, in the two verses beginning “to Kṛṣṇa.”
“Whose navel is a lotus”; “whose garland is made of lotuses”; “whose eyes are clear like lotuses”; and “to Him whose feet are marked with lotuses.”

She remembers the favors He has bestowed, saying this in two verses. The meaning is: Your affection for me is even greater than a mother’s. “O Hṛṣīkeśa, just as Devakī, imprisoned by Kaṁsa, was freed by You, have I likewise been freed?” The rhetorical question expresses a great difference. She was imprisoned for a long time and freed only once, and she was afflicted by grief; her sons were not protected, and she has another protector. I, however, together with my sons, was repeatedly and quickly protected from a multitude of dangers, and You alone were our protector.

He now enumerates the multitude of dangers: Bhīma’s poisoning through the giving of poisoned food; the great fire, the burning of the house of lac; the man-eating demons, such as Hiḍimba, through encountering them; and the wicked assembly, the place of gambling. We were protected from all sides.
In those very calamities, what kind of vision was there? A vision from which there is no return to worldly existence and no repeated seeing of You [as the indwelling Lord].

Prosperities, however, stand in the way of the highest good, she says. “Birth in a noble family”; “one whose pride grows through birth and the like”; and even the ability to utter “Śrī Kṛṣṇa Govinda”—You are an object within the reach only of those who possess nothing.

She bows again to fulfill her present wish. You are the entire wealth of devotees who possess nothing. From You the movements of the qualities concerned with dharma, artha, and kāma have withdrawn; therefore You are the Self-delighting One. Why? You are peaceful, free from attachment and the like. Moreover, You are the Lord of liberation, capable of granting it.

One might object: “Why do you praise Me in this way, when I am the son of Devakī?” She answers: “I consider You Time, not merely Devakī’s son.” The reasons are that You are the Lord, the controller; beginningless and endless; all-pervading; and moving equally everywhere. One might object: how can You be equal when You were Pārtha’s charioteer? She answers: conflict arises among beings because of You, who are its instrumental cause; there is no partiality or inequality in You Yourself.

One might object: partiality in the form of punishment and favor toward me is well known. He answers: there is no such partiality. It is only the imitation of human behavior by one who acts through You, in whom an apparently unequal attitude of favor and punishment is seen.

Those are the births of the Unborn and the actions of the Non-agent: among animals, birth in the form of Varāha and the like; among humans, in the form of Rāma and the like; among sages, in the form of Vāmana and the like; and among aquatic beings, in the form of Matsya and the like.

The imitation of a human being is exceedingly wondrous, she says with “the cowherd woman.” When You had broken the curd pot and Yaśodā took up a rope to bind You, that condition of Yours at that very moment bewilders me. Your face was lowered because You stood fearing that she would beat You; Your eyes were agitated, mixed with tears and collyrium. Even fear itself fears You—yet this was Your condition.

Because Your birth and the rest are difficult to understand, being bewildering to the world, they describe them in many ways, she says in four verses beginning “some.” Some speak for the fame of the righteous Yudhiṣṭhira; or, the phrase may mean “for the fame of the Yadu dynasty,” just as sandalwood is spoken of through the fame of the Malaya lineage.

In Devakī, the wife of Vasudeva, You, though unborn, appeared as a son; “to become a son” is supplied. The use of the first person is an archaic form. The reading “to become a child” is clearer. Earlier, in the forms of Sutapā and Pṛśni, You had been requested by those two for the welfare of this world.
This is said with the intention of giving prominence to Brahmā’s prayer.

An alternative interpretation is this: ignorance of the Self whose nature is supreme bliss gives rise to identification with the body; from that identification comes desire, and from desire come actions. For the cessation of the suffering caused by these, he will undertake actions such as hearing.

He now establishes this interpretation as the conclusion and states the fruit of hearing and the rest. Those people rejoice in the deeds recited by others; they see Your lotus feet themselves, and see them soon—the word “only” is understood throughout. What are those feet like? They are the feet in which the cessation of the stream of becoming, the succession of births, is present.

With the intention that Your abandonment of us today would be improper, she speaks in four verses beginning “also.” O Lord, do You perhaps even now wish to abandon us, Your exceedingly affectionate friends and dependents? We have no other refuge. Why? We are those upon whom suffering has been imposed by kings. “O You whose own action was expected” is a form of address to one from whom protection was expected; the reading ending with a visarga makes “You” an adjective.

One might object: “Your relatives, the Yadus, and your sons, the Pāṇḍavas, are heroic and capable; why do you speak so helplessly?” She answers: whenever You do not see us, then, despite the names and forms by which the Yadus and Pāṇḍavas are famous and prosperous, who are we? No one—we are utterly insignificant. Just as, when the soul who rules the senses is not seen, there is no meaningful name or form, so it is with us.
Moreover, just as this earth, which we protect, now shines because it is marked by the signs of Your feet—vajra, goad, and the like—so then, when You have departed, it will not shine.
Moreover, these settlements and lands are prosperous and well furnished with abundance.

If the Pāṇḍavas depart, it is harmful; if the Yadus depart, it is also harmful. Thus, with her mind agitated in both ways, she prays that Your affection for them not cease. The addresses beginning “Lord of the universe” show Your power to cut the bonds of affection. “Firm” means firmly established.

What follows from this? She says: “May my mind, being directed to You alone, bear uninterrupted love.” “Flood” means a full stream. Just as the Gaṅgā does not heed an obstruction, so may the mind not heed obstacles.

Having made this request, she bows again. She addresses Śrī Kṛṣṇa repeatedly while remembering His favors: friend of Arjuna, the friend of Kṛṣṇa; best of the Vṛṣṇis; destroyer of the royal lineages that oppose the earth; and One whose unconquered power is never diminished. “Govinda” means the Lord possessing the wealth of wish-fulfilling cows, and the One whose incarnation removes the distress of cows, brāhmaṇas, and the gods.

He whose entire glory has risen was praised with words containing graceful, sweet phrases. The verb means “to praise”; the long syllable is used in accordance with the meter. “Gently” means slightly. His smile itself is māyā; it will later be said that a smile can bewilder people.

Accepting the request “may my mind have no other object,” He came from the place of the chariot to Gajasāhvaya, Hastināpura. He took leave of Subhadrā and the other women, headed by her, intending to go to His own city. King Yudhiṣṭhira lovingly requested Him to remain there for some time, and so He was detained.

He introduces the account of Bhīṣma’s departure. Although Vyāsa and the others had awakened him, he remained covered by grief and did not attain discernment. Why? It was the Lord’s intention: the king had to go to Kurukṣetra with him for the great festival of the departure of the Lord’s devotee Bhīṣma, and Bhīṣma himself had to awaken him. Those who did not know the Lord’s intention, which ordained these two tasks, could not understand it. Even when Śrī Kṛṣṇa awakened him, he did not awaken. The reason was the Lord’s wondrous action: just as He went to reconcile the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas yet, while speaking appropriately, firmly established their conflict, so here, while awakening him, He firmly established his bewilderment.
He elaborates upon this lack of understanding in six verses. “With a material self” means with a mind covered by ordinary lack of discrimination. O brāhmaṇas.

“For the sake of another’s body” means for the body that is food for dogs, jackals, and the like. “By me” means by me [the killing was done]. An akṣauhiṇī is the number of troops called an akṣauhiṇī. Vyāsa gives its enumeration: 21,870 chariots and the same number of elephants, 109,350 soldiers, and 65,610 horses. Those who know the true principles of counting call this the proper numerical constitution of one akṣauhiṇī.
“Friends” means relatives; “companions” means close friends; “fathers” means uncles.

One might object: the instruction based on sacred memory says that killing enemies in a righteous war is not sinful. He answers that this rule is only for the protector of subjects. The meaning is: killing is permitted when one’s own subjects are threatened by another, but Duryodhana killed them while they were under my protection, solely from greed for the kingdom; therefore this is certainly sinful.

Even if the killing of men in war is accepted as righteous, I am not capable of removing the treachery toward the women whose relatives were killed by me, although that treachery was not explicitly commanded. It is the householder’s [duty and means] that is involved here.

One might object: the revelation says that one crosses all sin, even brahma-killing, by performing the aśvamedha and by knowing it in this way; therefore sin should indeed be destroyed by the aśvamedha. He rejects this argument, which has arisen from lack of discrimination, with an example. Just as muddy water is not cleansed by thick mud, and impurity caused by a little wine is not cleansed by a great quantity of wine, so one act of killing living beings, arising through negligence, cannot be cleansed by sacrifices whose chief feature is extensive killing.

In the ninth [chapter], the exposition of all dharmas by Bhīṣma for Yudhiṣṭhira, and his praise of Kṛṣṇa and liberation, are described. He shows that the lack of discrimination for whose purpose it was increased by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, with “thus” [and so forth]. [It is] with the desire to know all dharmas. “Vinaśana” is Kurukṣetra. “Devavrata” is Bhīṣma.
“Good”—the horses in which are excellent; with those chariots.
“Sānugāḥ” means accompanied by the retinue, together with the family.
“There”—then. “They were there” means they had arrived at that very moment. “The bull among the Bharatas” means Bhīṣma.
“Son of Reṇukā” means Paraśurāma. “Brahma-rāta” means Śuka. “Āṅgirasa” means Bṛhaspati.
“Vasu-uttama” means Bhīṣma. “Knower of the division of place and time”: because he was unable to rise, he honored [them] with mind and speech while lying down; that is the intention.
He worshiped Him who was situated in the heart and seated before [him].

“Those seated nearby” means seated close by. “Praśraya” is humility; “prema” is affection; [he addressed those] joined by these two. In another reading, [those] bowed by the two. “He addressed” means he spoke. [He was] marked by sight made blind by tears of affection.

Note: Another reading is “prema-sannatān.”

He speaks the address with eleven [verses], beginning with “aho.” “O sons of Dharma!” “You ought not to live in a condition that is painful”—this “ah, what hardship!” is despised [as terrible]. “Ah, this is unjust too.” Because you are those for whom the brāhmaṇas, Dharma, and Acyuta are the shelter.

Moreover, “saṃsthite” means dead. “Bāla-prajā” means one whose sons are children. “And the daughter-in-law”—by this helplessness is displayed. “Toka” means offspring; “possessing them” means [she is] endowed with them. The meaning is that she obtained afflictions together with the offspring.
He wards off grief by attributing it to Time, with two [verses] beginning “all.” “Of you” also. “Under whose control” means subject to whose control.

Ah, Time is skilled in accomplishing what is difficult to accomplish, he says with “where.” “Kṛṣṇa” [and] Arjuna, armed and bow-bearing. Then, even there, calamity. The meaning is: even when there was the wealth of piety, bodily strength, strength and skill in weapons, arms, and divine [aid].

One may ask: how could Time overtake Kṛṣṇa? He answers by pointing to Him: “Nothing is to be done by Him,” meaning that He has no desired action left to perform. “Of whom there is a desire to know” means that the question concerns the One whose intention is being sought.

Having determined that pleasure, pain, and the like are governed by fate and depend upon Īśvara, he became a follower of that Lord. O Master, Lord of the lineage passed down through generations, protect the helpless people.
He says that Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone is to be followed as the Supreme Lord. This alone is Bhagavān, the Lord of all. Why? He is the Primal Person. And why is that? Because He is Nārāyaṇa directly.
He establishes that point: “power” means influence and majesty.

Through ignorance you think Him to be a maternal cousin, the son of Devakī; dear, an object of affection; a friend, one who creates affection; the best of well-wishers, one who helps without expecting help in return; and, through your trust, you made Him your minister.

One might object: if He is Īśvara, how did He engage in such low work as driving a chariot? He answers: there is not even the slightest inequality in His judgment of what is suitable or unsuitable, what is high or low, because He is free from blame and from attachment and the like. Why is that so? He is without ego; beyond duality; of equal vision; and, above all, the Self of everyone. Alternatively, this is a chain of reasons, each explaining the preceding one.
Even though He is equal toward all, He has shown compassion toward me. O King, [this is the meaning].

He now prays that Śrī Kṛṣṇa remain until the giving up of his own body, in two verses. “As long as” indicates delay; “I leave” indicates independence. “This” is understood as non-Self. His lotus face is beautiful with a gentle smile and reddish eyes. He is the object of meditation; He whom others merely conceive in meditation stands before me and waits for me—that is the meaning.
Having heard those compassionate words.

He says that he described duties according to the ordinary human disposition. “According to the class” means the duties of one’s social class; “according to the stage of life” means the duties of one’s āśrama. The characteristics of both—the path of renunciation and the path of activity—are arranged according to the two conditioning factors, detachment and attachment.

He states the special teachings there with “giving.” “Duties of liberation” means restraint, control, and the like. “Duties of Bhagavān” means practices that please Hari, in the form of observances such as the Ekādaśī and Dvādaśī vows. Condensation and expansion are themselves the two methods, the two means; [he taught] by both of them.

He described dharma and the rest according to each person’s qualification, together with the specific means suited to that person; and he described the histories in the various narratives just as they are found there.
“Whose death was according to his will” means that death came according to his own intention.

“Leader of thousands” means Bhīṣma, who leads and protects a thousand chariot warriors stationed near him in battle. In the reading “possessing thousands,” it means one whose speech has the value of thousands. He fixed his mind upon Him whose two garments were yellow and shining, and whose eyes remained unclosed.

By this very pure concentration, he had destroyed all inauspiciousness. Through the merciful glance of that Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the exertion caused by weapons had departed from him. Therefore the wandering of all the senses had ceased; abandoning the body that had arisen from them, he praised Janārdana.

Before asking for love of Śrī Kṛṣṇa as the supreme fruit, he first offers the attainment produced by his own practice. The mental concentration produced by various dharmic means has been offered to Bhagavān, the best of the Sātvatas. He is without desire; alternatively, “not satisfied” means without being satiated by any lesser object. He is the One from whom all worldly greatness has departed, meaning that there is nothing greater than Him. He has attained His own bliss, the supreme bliss that is His own nature. Sometimes He accepts prakṛti, His yoga-māyā, in order to play; this does not mean that, like the jīva, He becomes dependent through concealing His true nature. The statement that He plays is expanded by saying that from Him the stream of creation proceeds.

He now describes Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s form and prays for love. “May my love be for the body that is the one supremely beautiful thing in the three worlds.” The body is dark in color like the tamāla tree; it is clothed in a pure yellow garment shining like the morning rays of the sun; its lotus face is covered above by masses of curls; and it belongs to the friend of Vijaya, Pārtha’s charioteer. May my love there be faultless, without a motive or expectation of reward.

He prays for love while further describing His friendship with Vijaya. In battle, the dust raised by the horses made His locks gray; the curls moved in every direction; scattered drops of sweat, produced by exertion, adorned His face and revealed His affection for His devotee. May my mind delight in that Śrī Kṛṣṇa. His skin was pierced by my sharp arrows, and His armor was torn and shining as it broke apart beneath them.

“Place my chariot between the two armies,” Arjuna had said. Hearing the words of His friend, He immediately placed the chariot between the armies of His own side and the opposing side. As He stood there as Pārtha’s friend, He acted in friendship: by the glance of His vision, He took away the lives of the opposing soldiers. Under the pretext of showing Arjuna “here is Bhīṣma, here is Droṇa, here is Karṇa,” He drew out the lives of all of them merely by His glance and secured Arjuna’s victory.

He brought about victory not only by taking away the lives of Arjuna’s enemies, but also by taking away ignorance. “The face of the distant army” means Bhīṣma and the others standing at the front of the army, as Arjuna looked upon them. Arjuna had withdrawn from killing his own relatives, as the Gītā says: “Having spoken thus, Arjuna sat down on the seat of his chariot, casting aside his bow with its arrows, his mind overcome by sorrow.” “Bad understanding” means the mistaken thought, “I shall kill them,” and the like.

He says in two verses that Kṛṣṇa showed him great favor. “His own vow” means His promise, “I shall not take up a weapon; I shall only assist.” Abandoning that promise, He suddenly leapt down from the chariot and ran toward Bhīṣma in order to make my promise true—my promise that I would make Śrī Kṛṣṇa take up a weapon. He ran like a lion to kill an elephant, holding a chariot wheel. In His intensity, forgetting the play of being human, the earth that bears the weight of all beings moved at each step. The garment that had fallen on the road lay behind Him. May that Mukunda be my refuge.

When He rushed forward, Bhīṣma, a smiling archer and aggressor, was struck by my sharp arrows; his armor was shattered, and he was drenched in blood. He passed even Arjuna, who was forcibly trying to restrain Him, and advanced toward me to kill me. Thus, although He appeared to the world to favor Arjuna, in truth He showed me His own favor: He made the words spoken by His devotee, “May they not become false,” come true. May that Bhagavān be my refuge.

Even while acting in ways that appeared unjust, Kṛṣṇa was intent on protecting His devotee, and Bhīṣma longs for love of Him. “Vijaya” is Arjuna; his chariot itself was a family to be protected, even at the cost of hundreds of acts of apparent injustice. Kṛṣṇa held the goad and the reins of the horses, and the splendor of that charioteer’s service made Him beautiful. “The one wishing to die” is Bhīṣma. One might object: why ask for love of One who acted unjustly? He answers: He is Bhagavān, possessed of inconceivable majesty. Seeing His own form, all those killed in this battle attained a form equal to His.

It is not surprising that those who fought according to the duty of warriors attained a form equal to His. He says that even women who were blinded by pride attained it. The cowherd women, whose minds were fixed solely on Him, imitated His acts, such as lifting Govardhana, and attained His nature. The elision of the letter m is an archaic usage. The connection is with the earlier prayer, “May my love be in Him.”

Remembering His being honored by the world, he says: in the assembly of Yudhiṣṭhira’s Rājasūya, filled with sages and kings, He received worship while being looked upon with wonder—“Ah, what a form! Ah, what greatness!” The Self of all is now manifest as the object of my sight. “How fortunate I am”—that is the feeling.

He says, “I am fulfilled.” I have properly attained that Unborn One, with delusion regarding difference removed. To explain why the differences are only conditioned appearances, he says that He is established in the heart of each embodied being, appearing manifold because the supporting bodies differ. The example is the sun, which appears separately in each person’s sight.
The movements of mind, speech, and sight have dissolved within Him, Śrī Kṛṣṇa. “Whose breath is entirely within” means one whose breath has become wholly internal.
He saw the self merging into the partless, unconditioned Supreme Self, like birds [coming together at their final resting place].
“Played by gods and humans” means [His deeds were] performed and celebrated by gods and human beings. Among kings, there were saintly and non-envious ones.
“Removal” and the rest mean the cremation rites and related ceremonies, properly performed for the departed—even for one who is liberated.
“With His secret names” means with the names taught in the Veda. Those whose heart is Kṛṣṇa are “Kṛṣṇa-hearted.”
“Father” means Dhṛtarāṣṭra. “The ascetic woman” means the woman afflicted by suffering.
“The king” is Yudhiṣṭhira. “Permitted” means given leave.

In the tenth [chapter], the arrival at Hastināpura of Hari, whose work is accomplished, and the arrival at Dvārakā of Him being praised by the women are described. “He made the kingdom”—thus the question is asked with “having killed.” Those who used to compete for their own inheritance, their wealth; or those for whom there was a battle over their own inheritance, who were aggressors because they sought to take wealth and so forth—having killed them. “Whose food was obstructed” means whose enjoyment was contracted by the grief of killing relatives, or whose enjoyment was obtained through gaining the kingdom. “How did he engage in the kingdom?” Or, “what did he do thereafter?”

Having caused the lineage of Kuru to sprout, by protecting Parīkṣit and making it germinate. What kind? “Burned by the forest fire of the lineage”: the lineage itself is a forest; the fire born from it, in the form of anger, burned it. And having installed [Yudhiṣṭhira] in his own kingdom.

Having stated the reason for his engagement, what did he do? He answers this. [His] knowledge arose: the world is dependent on the Supreme Lord and is not independent; by it his delusion, consisting of ego and the rest, was destroyed. Followed by his younger brothers, serving [him]. “The Unconquered”—Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone—is whose refuge. He ruled the earth up to the boundary, the ocean.

He describes his kingdom with three [verses] beginning with “everything desired.” The earth became a giver of all desires. “Vrajas” means cow-pastures. “With swollen udders”—[cows] with swollen udders; an udder is a receptacle of milk, meaning with large udders. “They sprinkled” means they moistened.
“Anu-ṛtu” means in each season.

“Ādhis” means mental anguish. “Vyādhis” means diseases. “Kleśas” means those caused by heat and cold and so forth. Those whose causes are the divine, beings, and the self—the afflictions beginning with the divine—did not arise in the creatures.
Now, to explain the journey to Dvārakā, he says “having stayed.” “Of the sister”—of Subhadrā.
“Him”—Yudhiṣṭhira.
“Yuyutsu”—born of Dhṛtarāṣṭra by a Vaiśya [woman]. “Gautama”—Kṛpa. “The twins”—Nakula and Sahadeva.
“Daughter of Matsya”—Uttarā. The mention of her again is due to increased delusion from separation from Kṛṣṇa, who protected the embryo. Or, “daughter of Matsya” [means] Satyavatī.

He states their inability to tolerate separation from Kṛṣṇa by the rule of inference from the stronger case, with two [verses] beginning “from the association of the good.” “Freed from bad association by the association of the good”—one from whom attachment to sons and so forth, the bad association, has been freed. Having once even heard the fame of Hari, which is pleasing when sung by the good, he cannot give up good association. Those whose intellects have been placed on Him, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, through seeing and the rest.
Therefore, with unwinking eyes, they used to move here and there for bringing offerings and so forth. Because they were fully bound by affection. Therefore, those whose minds had run after Him.

“Having come out of the palace” means when they came out. Because of eagerness, the excess of attachment, they checked the flowing tears, the tears streaming out, holding them in the eyes only. The reason is: “May there be no inauspiciousness for us”—for this purpose.
“Mṛdaṅga and the rest”—ten kinds of instruments.
They were women whose glances were preceded by love, modesty, and a smile.
“Guḍākā’s Lord” means Arjuna, the lord who has conquered sleep.
They held the fly-whisk and the cāmara. Kṛṣṇa is the Lord of Madhu.

“Of Satyā” means that Kṛṣṇa never deviates from them. Yet the words “may you be happy” and the like are not fitting for the attributeless Supreme, whose nature is supreme bliss; they are fitting for the Lord appearing in a human līlā, whose nature is expressed through qualities. The sandhi follows an archaic usage.
He is charming to all the Upaniṣads. The Upaniṣads themselves, as though embodied, rejoiced in His conversation.

The other women tell their friends, who were astonished by His extraordinary radiance and beauty: there is no need for astonishment, since He is directly the Lord. They begin with four verses, “He alone.” “Indeed” signals remembered authority. The one nondual Person who existed was this Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Where did He exist? In His own Self, free of manifestation. When? Before the agitation of the qualities, and also during dissolution. His characteristic is that He is the Self of the worlds, when the living beings, their powers asleep, are dissolved in the Lord. The dissolution of the jīvas means the dissolution of the powers such as sattva that serve as their adjuncts.

Having stated the unmanifest condition at the beginning of creation and after dissolution, they describe the manifest condition between creation and dissolution. He alone, whose own nature never falls away, followed and presided over prakṛti again. This “again” is used because the stream of creation is beginningless. He presided over māyā, the deluding power of the living beings who are portions of Himself, impelled by His own power of time and wishing to create. Why did He do so? To give name and form through the creation of adjuncts to the living beings who are themselves without name or form, for their enjoyment. They also say that He made the scriptures in order to prescribe action.

They say that the vision of this Lord, which we have obtained, is exceedingly difficult to attain. Those alone whose vital air has been conquered see Him, by an immaculate mind made eager through devotion. The friend says: O friend, only this Lord is able to purify the mind; not yoga alone. Alternatively, the meaning is that this knowledge cannot be destroyed or made imperceptible by going far away; one must depart together with Him.

They speak of His holy fame. O friend, this is He whose true account is sung in the Vedas and in the secret scriptures by those who explain their mysteries. They describe the manner of the song with “the One Lord,” and the verses that follow.

They state the reason for His appearing in many incarnations: when kings whose understanding is covered by tamas live only by unrighteousness, sustaining their lives through it, He assumes forms from pure sattva for the welfare and preservation of the world, age after age. “Glory” means majesty; “truth” means truthfulness of promise; “ṛta” means teaching what is real; “compassion” means mercy toward devotees; and “fame” means wondrous deeds.

They describe the good fortune of the incarnation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa in particular. Because this Supreme Person, the Lord of Lakṣmī, sanctifies and honors the Yadu family by His birth, that family is most praiseworthy. By His walking He sanctifies the forest of Madhu, Mathurā; therefore it is most holy. The word “enough” expresses the extreme degree of the excellence, and “ah!” expresses their astonishment.

They praise Dvārakā. “Ah, indeed!” expresses wonder. What is it? Kuśasthalī, Dvārakā. Its fame surpasses the fame of heaven and makes the earth a producer of holy renown. There all the women continually saw Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of their own self, not merely a bodily husband such as a father or the like. The variant readings explain the same point through His compassionate residence and smiling glance. Such a vision is not found even in heaven.

O friend, this very Lord was surely worshiped by these wives, who now hold His hand, in previous births. They have been captivated by the nectar of His lower lip; this expresses His irresistible beauty.

This is elaborated in two verses. His power was the bride-price, and His strength made Him desirable. The sons Pradyumna, Sāmba, and others were born to Rukmiṇī, Jāmbavatī, Nāgnajitī, and the other wives beginning with Satyabhāmā. The next verse is connected with this one. These women make womanhood itself supremely beautiful. What kind of beauty? Their independence has been removed, their pleasant individual distinction has been set aside, and even their purity has been subordinated; yet it never leaves them. Through His words—or, alternatively, through the bringing of dear objects such as the pārijāta—He touches their hearts and gives them joy.
Having received and honored such varied, wondrous words with a smiling glance, Hari departed.
Even for the protection of the Gopīs, the Lord who conquered Madhu, fearing enemies because of His affection for them, deployed a fourfold army—elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
Because the Pāṇḍavas belonged to the Kuru lineage, they too were Kauravas. He traveled with dear companions such as Uddhava.

“Kuru” means the Kuru region itself; the order of the events is not intended here. “Maru” is a waterless land; “Dhanva” has little water; “Anarta” is the region of Dvārakā. He reached that place. “O descendant of Bhṛgu” is a form of address. The horses were only slightly tired.

At each place, gifts offered by the people of that place were presented to Him. In the evening He went toward the western direction. “The sun who is in the sky has entered the waters” means that it had set, as the revelation says: “He rises from the waters in the morning and enters the waters in the evening.” Alternatively, at evening He descended from His chariot, stood upon the earth, and worshiped the western water, the twilight.

Being praised by the Ānartas, having entered the city with relatives, the complete delight of the Lord of the Yadus is described in the eleventh [chapter]. With festivals, with the citizens rising, with flags and arches rising, with rows of shining jewel lamps, the Lord entered His own city. “Svṛddhān” means prosperous. “Dara-vara” means the Pāñcajanya conch. “He sounded” means he played [it].

“He” [means the conch]. The conch, being sounded and being filled by Bhagavān, shone, that is, became exceedingly beautiful—this is the syntactic connection. What kind of conch? One whose belly is white. Yet it has redness from the quality of the red lower lip of Kṛṣṇa, the Wide-Strider. Being present in the middle of the joined lotus-hand, that is, the lotus palms. How did it shine? Just as a royal swan in a mass of red lotuses [makes] a high sound, so.

“Of the world”: [the sound] which brings the fear of the world’s fear. “They went out to meet” means they went out to meet. “Those whose desire for seeing their lord” means those whose eagerness for seeing their protector [was present].

“There,” in that [place], [were] those by whom offerings, gifts, were presented to Śrī Kṛṣṇa. An example for the offering respectfully even to Him who is indifferent is “like a lamp to the sun.” “Like children [to] their father,” with the following [verse] connected: they spoke to Him, the friend of all and protector. “Protector” through friendship alone, not through desire. Here the reason is “self-delighting.” There too the reason is “fully satisfied” solely through attaining the own nature of supreme bliss.

What did they say? He says that with “we are bowed.” “Viriñca” is Brahmā. “Vairiñcyāḥ” are Sanaka and the others. In this saṃsāra, for those desiring the highest welfare, [Your lotus feet are] the supreme refuge. Why? Even Time, the lord of the superior ones such as Brahmā, is not powerful where [Your lotus feet] are.
Therefore, for our welfare, become [present] for us. O sustainer of the universe! We have become successful, fulfilled.

They state their fulfillment itself. “Oh, by You we are protected.” Because we may see Your form. That whose seeing is distant even for the residents of heaven; meaning, [Your form] difficult even for the gods to see. The face in which there is a glance made affectionate by a smile arising from love; that form in which such a face is present. That in which there is auspicious beauty in all the limbs.

They spoke compassionately, like children. “Whenever” means whenever. O lotus-eyed one! In the reading “no You,” “na” is a sixth-case [form] expressing disregard. “Having disregarded us,” having abandoned [us], He went away. “The Kurus” [means] Hastināpura; “the Madhus” [means] Mathurā, or [He went] to either. “There” means then. As, without the sun, because of blindness of the eyes, even one moment would be like millions of years, so too [it is] for us, Your people; that is the meaning.

“How” [means]: O Lord! The entire affliction of those who have surrendered, which is in the form of thirst, is dried up and destroyed by seeing You; because thirst arises in those who have surrendered [when they are without You].
“And thus”—hearing these and other words of this kind, granting favor with a glance of welcome, He entered the city of Dvārakā.
He praises that Dvārakā with five [verses]. [It is] protected by Madhu, Bhoja, and the rest, whose strength is equal to His own.

[He praises] that [city] whose beauty is [formed] by reservoirs surrounded by gardens and so forth, in which are sacred trees and creeper dwellings, creeper pavilions, possessing all opulences and flower wealth in every season. A garden is chiefly for fruits. A grove is chiefly for flowers. A pleasure-garden is a forest for play.

“Gopura” is the city gate. “Door” is the house door. [He praises] that [city] in which arches were made through festivity. Flags are marked with signs such as Garuḍa. Banners are marked with devices granting victory. [He praises] that [city] within which the sunshine was stopped by the ends of variegated flags and banners.

[He praises] that [city] in which the great roads and so forth were swept, their dust removed. Great roads are royal roads. “Rathyāḥ” are side roads. Marketplaces are streets of merchandise. “Catvarāṇi” are courtyards. [It was] strewn with fruits and so forth.
Having heard that the dearest inner Self was approaching, Vasudeva and the others went out to meet Him; this is the syntactical connection with the fourth [verse].
With the force of their joy they leapt up, crossing over beds and the like. The verbal root means “to leap.”

They placed the lord of elephants at the front for auspiciousness. They carried flowers and other auspicious objects in their hands. “The sound of Brahman” means the recitation of mantras. Those who came through affection had a respectful excitement and eagerness.

The leading courtesans, the dancers and others, also went out to meet Him. Their cheeks shone with earrings, and their faces possessed beauty. “Leading courtesans” means dancers, that is, women who perform in public.

The “wonders” are connected with the word “and” and with the panegyrists. The actors were skilled in portraying the nine sentiments; the dancers moved according to rhythm and the like; and the Gandharvas were singers. The tradition explains: “Sūtas are called reciters of Purāṇas, Māgadhas are proclaimers of lineages, and Vandins are clear-minded speakers whose words suit the occasion.” All of them sang the wondrous deeds of the Most Glorified Lord, such as His affection for devotees.
Having met each person according to the proper procedure and as appropriate to that person, He honored everyone. That is the meaning.
“Bowing” means bowing with the head; “greeting” means bowing with words. Having reassured them and granted fearlessness, He honored even the dog-eaters with gifts and desired objects.
He also honored the other panegyrists and bards.
O brāhmaṇa Śaunaka, those women for whom His glance itself became a great festival.
Even though they continually looked upon Acyuta, their eyes were never satisfied, and therefore they rose. He was the abode and source of beauty.

Lakṣmī’s residence is His chest; His face is a vessel from which all living beings drink the nectar of beauty; His arms are the dwelling of the guardians of the worlds. The devotees who sing the essence, and whose shelter is His lotus feet, are called sāraṅgas. The connection is: their eyes were fixed upon Him.

He was adorned with white umbrellas and fly-whisks. The sun, the moon, the stars, the rainbow, and lightning are compared with those objects: the sun with the umbrella, the stars with the shower of flowers, the moon with the circular movement of the fly-whisks, the rainbow with the forest garland, and lightning with His yellow garment. This is an extraordinary comparison. If a cloud had the sun’s disk above it, two moons on either side, stars all around, two fixed rainbows in its midst, and the radiance of lightning, then it would shine as Hari did.

The seven mothers beginning with Devakī bowed in order to show special respect for the beauty and status of the mothers. All eighteen wives of Vasudeva were also honored with obeisance because they were mother-like.
“Waters born from the eyes” means tears of joy.
He now describes His entrance into His own home. The phrase “sixteen thousand” together with “and” is understood as sixteen thousand plus one hundred and eight.

The wives who had remained abroad, seeing Him from a distance, experienced a great festival in their minds and rose from their seats. They rose even from the inner mind, because they could not tolerate any obstruction between themselves and their union with Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Their eyes were shy because they looked only from the corners, and their faces were shy because they were lowered. Alternatively, “together with their vows” means that they rose after giving up rules such as abstaining from play. Yājñavalkya states such vows: “A woman whose husband is away should give up play, bodily adornment, attending public festivals, laughter, and going to another’s house.”

Before seeing their husband who was approaching, they embraced Him inwardly with their minds, then with their eyes; when He came near, they embraced Him through their sons, holding them by the neck as though they themselves had embraced Him. Their feelings were profound. Although the water in their eyes was held back, it flowed out slightly through helplessness and loss of composure. Therefore their faces and eyes showed the loss of self-control. O best of the Bhṛgus, hear this wondrous account. An alternate reading understands the sons as lifting up the children and embracing the Lord’s neck.

He remained nearby, and even there he acted in seclusion. At every moment the experience was ever new. “Who could refrain?” is a rhetorical question. She was naturally fickle, yet even she could not withdraw.

He summarizes the deeds of Śrī Kṛṣṇa in two verses. He was born to remove the burden of the earth, and the brilliance of those born for that purpose was surrounded on every side by the eighteen akṣauhiṇīs. As wind rubbing two bamboos against each other produces fire and then the fire subsides, so their power was brought forth and then extinguished.
He stood among a cluster of the finest women.

One may object: how could Bhagavān have appeared despite such association with women and the like? He answers in two verses. The women’s intentions were profound; their beautiful smiles and shy glances, revealing those intentions, struck down even Mahādeva, the great god, who had conquered Kāma, and he became bewildered with shame and abandoned his bow. This much is intended: such was the power of these women. Alternatively, just as Maheśvara was bewildered by Bhagavān’s Mohinī form, so these women possessed similarly astonishing sports. By their deceptions and bewildering movements they could not agitate His mind or senses. Or, “struck” may mean that even Kāma, conqueror of the world, became bewildered and confused about his duties, and in shame abandoned his bow. The rest is understood as before: these were the finest women, conquerors of desire.

The ordinary world thinks that Kṛṣṇa is an attached human being, using its own likeness as the measure. The reason is that He appears to be engaged in human activities; the world is without true knowledge.

What is the characteristic of the Lord’s sovereignty? Even while standing in prakṛti, He is never joined to its qualities such as pleasure and pain. This is like the intellect, which, though supported by the Self, is not joined to the Self’s qualities such as bliss. Alternatively, the example is meant by contrast: the intellect is joined to existence, illumination, and so forth that are present in the Self. The body, which is unreal, is joined to the qualities present in it, and the jīva, whose adjunct is that body, appears joined to them; in the same way, the Lord, though standing in prakṛti, is not joined to its qualities. This non-joining is the sovereignty of the Lord.

He says that even His wives did not know His true nature. They considered Him a man controlled by women, devoted to them and following them in solitude. “Not knowing the measure of the husband” means not knowing His extent and greatness. Just as people think the indwelling Lord, the knower of the field, is subject to them and follows His own duty under their control, so they thought of Him. Alternatively, according to each wife’s own conception, they regarded that Lord as having the form of a woman-controlled husband and the like.

Having earlier stated in detail the punishment of Drauṇi and the rest for the purpose of the connection, in the twelfth [chapter] that very birth of Parīkṣit is described. Having made the promise, “Now I shall speak of the birth, deeds, departure of the royal sage Parīkṣit, and also the dissolution of the sons of Pāṇḍu; I shall speak the arising of Kṛṣṇa’s topics,” the standing of the Pāṇḍavas’ kingdom has been described, as a preface, beginning with Chapter Seven, along with the relevant context. Now he asks the introductory [question] after repeating what was stated: “by Aśvatthāmā.” “Released” means discharged. [The syntax is] connected with what follows: “tell [us] his birth and so forth.”
“He” is Parīkṣit. “After leaving” means after abandoning the body.
He says, “I request, not command,” with [the words] “if you think to narrate, then speak.” “To whom Śuka gave knowledge” is the reason for the desire to hear.

Although the king was without desire, such a grandson was born through Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s favor; to state this he speaks of the rise of his devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa with three [verses] beginning “he protected.” “Like his father,” he protected and ruled.

“Sacrifices” are those obtained by him; “worlds” are the future destinations. “Desirable to the gods” means wealth and the like desired by the gods; “objects of enjoyment”—did they produce any pleasure for the king? They did not produce [it], that is the meaning. Here the reason is that his mind is only in Mukunda. Just as garlands, sandalwood and so forth do not give pleasure to one who is hungry and whose mind is fixed only on food, so.
He states the subject at hand with “of the mother,” [the verse beginning] “situated in the mother’s womb.”

“Puraṭa” means gold. He who has a shining golden crown; [the suffix] -in is according to the rule beginning with rice and so forth. “Apīcya” means exceedingly beautiful to see; “darśana” is the form that is seen. By the words “dark” and “wearing lightning,” an analogy to a cloud accompanied by lightning is indicated. “Acyuta” means unchanging.

That which is heated and has passed beyond burning, namely gold, in earrings made of that is he whose [earrings]. “Eyes red with blood” means eyes exceedingly red from agitation. [The thought is] “Ah, the weapon-affliction even of my devotee in the womb!” Therefore [the redness] is from anger.

“Making the radiance of the weapon disappear” means destroying it. “The sun, lord of rays, [causes] snow to disappear.” The child situated in the womb saw such [a being] nearby. Having seen [him], he examined and thought, “Who is this?”

How did the immeasurable Self destroy it? Because His nature cannot be conceived. “Protector of dharma” means he who protects dharma. Or, “the protectors of dharma” are the kings; He is their Lord, because He is also their protector. There, where [the child] was seen by the one whose ten months could be counted, while he was looking, He disappeared then and there, not having gone elsewhere. Because the All-pervading One is everywhere.

“Udarka” means the later result. [This was] at an ascendant sign indicating the increasing excellence of all qualities, one greater than another. The reason is that in it was the rising of auspicious planets together with other favorable planets.
“Jātaka” means the birth-rite. “Maṅgala” means the auspicious day, puṇyāha.

“Varān” means excellent [gifts]. “Good food” means excellent food. “Knower of the tīrtha” means knower of the time for giving charity. [According to the statement:] “As long as the cord is not cut, the period of impurity does not arise; when the cord is cut, thereafter the period of impurity is prescribed.” Therefore he gave before that, or raw grain. “At the tīrtha of the people” means at the auspicious time of the birth of a son; “what is given at the birth of a son becomes imperishable,” according to the smṛti. [The text then says:] “The gods and fathers also come when a son is born to a twice-born,” and so forth.

O bull among the Pauravas! In this pure descending line of the Kurus, of the Kuru lineage. What kind of fate? Unopposed, hard to ward off. When [their] dissolution had occurred, [he] was given by Viṣṇu, who is capable of arising, for your benefit; because of this he will be named Viṣṇu-rāta in the world and will be a great devotee of Viṣṇu. He will also be great in qualities—there is no doubt. Thus the brāhmaṇas spoke to the king; this is the syntactic connection of the three [verses].
Delighted, he asks: “Could it be that he will become a great devotee?” “Will he be followed by noble praise and fame?” is supplied from the preceding statement and applies here as well.
O Pārtha, he will be a protector of living beings, a human, the son of Manu, beneficial to the brāhmaṇas, and true to his promise, like Śrī Rāma.

Śibi was the king of the land of Uśīnara; he protected a pigeon who had taken refuge by giving his own flesh to the hawk. The son of Duṣyanta, Bharata, expanded the fame of his relatives and of those who performed sacrifices.
“Arjuna” refers to Arjuna and to Kārtavīrya Arjuna.
He will be like the Himālaya, a resort for the good because he has no other refuge; like the earth, patient and forgiving; and like loving parents, tolerant out of affection.
“Grandfather” means Brahmā; he is equal to him in greatness. “The abode of Lakṣmī” is Hari.
His greatness is marked by all good qualities; he is equal to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
“With steadfastness” means with courage. “Firmly grasping the good” means having a firm and auspicious resolve; he is its doer. The next verse refers to the royal sages, beginning with Janamejaya.
Having heard his death from Takṣaka, who was impelled by the son of a brāhmaṇa, he became detached and will attain the feet of Hari.
He will inquire into the true nature of the Self and, having abandoned this body in the Gaṅgā, will attain a fearless state—certainly.
Those by whom he received worship [will be honored through him].

He explains the name Parīkṣit. Since he was capable, and since he remembered the Person seen in the womb, he examined every person among those visible, thinking, “Is this that same Person or not?” Therefore he became famous as Parīkṣit, “the examiner.” A variant reading says “the Person previously seen,” meaning the Person seen earlier in the mother’s womb.

In the bright fortnight, the well-known moon grows day by day as it is filled with its fifteen portions. In the same way, he grew as he was filled with the desires and blessings of Yudhiṣṭhira and the others and with the sixty-four portions of royal excellence.

He now describes in due form the aśvamedha sacrifices that had previously been postponed. Wishing to avoid betrayal of his relatives, he intended to perform them with wealth obtained by means other than taxes and punishments, and reflected on this. Wealth obtained from taxes and fines was exhausted merely in maintaining his attendants. A variant reading connects “he reflected” with “elsewhere,” meaning that he did not obtain the wealth.
The Marut sacrifice had been left [with its materials], and the gold vessels and other articles abandoned there by the brāhmaṇas were brought.
Having gathered the required materials, he was nevertheless afraid because of the betrayal of his relatives.

Vidura’s account concerning Dhṛtarāṣṭra by Vidura’s instruction is given in the thirteenth [chapter], with the consecration of the grandson, in order to speak of the king’s great path. Now, intending to narrate Parīkṣit’s deeds beginning with the subduing of Kali, it describes Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s departure through Vidura’s arrival; then, on hearing of Arjuna’s arrival and thereafter Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s disappearance, [it describes] the Pāṇḍavas’ departure, through three chapters. “Gati” is Hari. By that course of the self, he by whom everything desired to be known was attained.

That very [matter] he says. All the questions concerning karma-yoga, vows and so forth that he first asked, in the presence of Kauśārava, Maitreya. Afterwards, by mere knowledge of the meaning of three or four questions, having one-pointed devotion to Govinda, being fulfilled, he desisted from those questions. Thereafter he did not inquire further.

“Sūta” is Sañjaya. “Śāradvata” is Kṛpa. “Pṛthā” is Kuntī. “Kṛpī” is the wife of Droṇa. “Jāmayaḥ” are the wives of relatives. Other women also. “Like the returned life”—when life has failed because of a fault such as swoon, the limbs of the body—hands, feet and so forth—become motionless; when it manifests again they rise, so [did they].
[They were] helpless through the eagerness caused by separation.
“Him” means Vidura.

Birds indeed raise their young with great affection under the shade of their wings; similarly, do you remember us, raised under the shade of your partiality and protection? We were released from the multitude of calamities; he states the fact of our being raised thus.
“You” means by you. “By what livelihood was [it] maintained?” means [by what means] was the body maintained. And which holy places and so forth were served?

Your pilgrimage was not for your own benefit, but for the benefit of the holy places—thus he says with “those like you.” The holy places, which have become impure through contact with impure people, are again made holy places by the saints themselves. “Your inner self” is mind; “by Him situated there,” or by Him situated within your own heart.
“Is it well? Have you seen or heard [of them] anywhere?”
He gives the reason for not describing the destruction of the Yadu dynasty: “as a matter of fact.”
“Doing good” means instructing in the truth.

“Surely he is a śūdra—how could he instruct?” He is not a śūdra, but Yama was present in that form. What is the reason there? When Yama is present here, who is the bearer of punishment there? In response to this expectation he says “he administered.” It means he held [the office]. Because of the curse of Māṇḍavya. Indeed: the king’s men, once pursuing thieves, arrived near the sage Māṇḍavya who was practicing austerities; having bound and brought the thieves together with him, they reported to the king, and by his order they impaled all on stakes. Then the king, recognizing the sage, removed him from the stake and sought his forgiveness. Then the sage went to Yama and angrily said, “For what reason was I impaled?” He replied, “As a child you pierced a grasshopper with the tip of a blade of kuśa and played.” Having heard that, Māṇḍavya cursed him: “Because, when I was a child and did not know, you caused me a great punishment, therefore become a śūdra.”

He now concludes the account of the kingdom’s decline while stating its former prosperity, with “Yudhiṣṭhira.” “Bearer of the family” means protector of the dynasty. One traditional text adds a verse describing Acyuta taking leave of His relatives and Arjuna, Uddhava, and Śaineya departing for Dvārakā.
“By that activity” means by the affairs of the household, which had made them heedless. The time allotted for their lives passed beyond them; alternatively, it means that time overcame them.
Having understood the situation and recognized its meaning.
One might ask: “Let a remedy be performed; why leave?” He answers with “remedy.” “Of all” means including those who ought to respond to the situation.
