How could separation from wealth and the like be endured? He answers: he was seized and overwhelmed by it.
Showing that remaining there was extremely pitiable, he produces detachment in seven verses beginning “father and brother.” “The self” here means the body itself.
The son who was killed by him was given the rice-ball by Bhīma, and it was received like food by a household guardian. “Household guardian” means a dog.

“Cast away” means thrown out. “Poison” means the toxin; “dishonored” means insulted. What use is there in preserving one’s life with food and the like obtained from those people? None—that is the meaning.
Even your life, although you are experiencing such misery, is wasting away. Therefore [become detached] from worldly existence.

When asked, “What is the mark of a steadfast person?” he answers: one whose personal aims—fame, worldly duty, and the like—have gone; one who has broken the bonds of possessiveness; whose destination is unknown; that is, the steadfast person, through enduring the suffering that has come to him, attains liberation.
The excellent man, however, had already carried out the remedy before that. He did so either by his own initiative or through instruction from another.

But you were not such an excellent man; therefore now become steadfast, he says with “then.” “Earlier” means in the former time; “he is coming” is the meaning. Such a person draws away and cuts off qualities such as patience and compassion.

He was an Ajāmīḍha, a descendant of Ajāmīḍha, blind yet possessing the eye of wisdom. Having been instructed in this way, he possessed firmness of mind; his brother showed him the path of bondage and liberation.

Gāndhārī, the daughter of Subala and a virtuous, well-conducted woman, followed her husband as he went to the Himālaya. One may ask: how did this delicate woman go to the Himālaya, a place full of the sufferings of snow and the like? He answers: it was a place where renunciants who had laid down their staffs found joy. Even suffering becomes a cause of joy for some; the example is how a fierce battle is joyful for heroic, high-minded warriors. A variant reading says “a righteous battle.”
He performed the Maitra observance, the twilight worship dedicated to Mitra, and bowed respectfully to his parents, Vidura and Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
O son of Gavalgaṇa—O Sañjaya.
“Without understanding” means dull-minded. He feared that Dhṛtarāṣṭra might be anticipating some offense. He was together with his wife.
The two were protected—Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī—from this place.
Because he could not see Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of himself, who was overwhelmed by affection and compassion, Sañjaya, worn down by separation, did not answer.
He steadied his mind with his intellect and made it firm, for the sake of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, his master.
And [he did so] for Gāndhārī. “Resolved” means certain. “I have been robbed” means “I have been deceived and deprived.”

After grieving for some time, Nārada arrived. A variant reading says “honoring the sage.” Because of the force of grief, the king appeared to honor him, as though he were doing so, but did not truly honor him. Tradition says: “A person overcome by grief, possessed by compassion, and without faith does not properly worship teachers, gods, or the twice-born.”

“I do not know” means “I do not understand.” “The ascetic woman” means the woman afflicted by suffering. In the shoreless ocean of grief, Bhagavān alone is the one who can carry a person across; therefore the unfinished request is, “Please tell me.”

To keep Yudhiṣṭhira from fainting from grief when the whole account was told at once, he first quiets his grief: “Do not grieve for anyone.” Why? The world is under the control of Īśvara. He explains this: He joins and separates [beings].

Just as oxen, tied by ropes through their noses to a long cord, carry their master’s offering, so all beings, bound by the cord of speech—the Veda that prescribes what is to be done and not done, with names such as “celibate student”—carry the offering of the Supreme Lord, impelled by Him.
Having stated dependence in activity, he states dependence in union and separation as well. The example is the dependence of playthings, such as wooden sheep, upon the one who plays with them.

It has been said that one should not grieve because the world is under Īśvara’s control. He now says that, when the nature of grief is examined, it has no real object. A person is eternal in the form of the jīva and temporary in the form of the body; alternatively, he is neither eternal nor temporary, being indescribable as pure Brahman with conscious and inert aspects. In all four positions, the father and the others are not objects of grief, except through affection. Affection alone is the cause of grief, and affection is rooted in ignorance.
Therefore give up the agitation of your mind, thinking, “How will they live without me?”

Their livelihood cannot come from your body. Time agitates the qualities; action is the cause of birth; the qualities are the material cause; and the five-element body, being inert, is perishable when its elements separate. It is like a snake swallowed by a python, which cannot protect another.

He says that livelihood is easily available everywhere under Īśvara’s arrangement. “Without hands” means animals and the like; “food” means grass and the like. Even among those without hands, the food is meager. In this way every living being is the livelihood of every other living being. By this alone, the fact that all are food for death has also been stated.

To remove delusion, he states that duality has no independent reality. This world, in forms with hands and without hands, is Bhagavān alone, self-luminous, and not separate from Him. He too is one, not many. One might object that distinctions within the same class and between different classes are directly perceived. He answers: He is the Self, the essential nature, of all enjoyers; therefore there is no difference within the same class. He shines both within and without, as enjoyer and enjoyed; therefore there is no difference between classes either. One might ask how the One appears in this way. He answers: see Him as appearing manifold through māyā.
“Where is this great magician, such a Lord?” He answers: in Dvārakā, on this earth, for its destruction.

Do not remain here thinking, “Śrī Kṛṣṇa is still here.” The work of the gods has been completed by Him; only the destruction of the Yadu dynasty remains. Then He will go to His own abode, and you too should go. Although this event had already occurred, he did not describe it, just as he did not describe it to Vidura.
Having removed his grief and attachment, he tells the inquirer the actual course of events in six verses beginning “Dhṛtarāṣṭra.” “In the southern part of Himālaya” is the meaning.

“Where?” He answers with “streams.” The famous celestial Gaṅgā divided herself into seven streams there. Why? So that she might be recognized as flowing separately in seven streams for the seven sages. Therefore that sacred place is called the Seven-Stream [Gaṅgā].

He now describes the eight-limbed yoga practiced there, in four verses beginning “having bathed.” Bathing, offering oblations, and drinking water are the observances; “water-drinking” replaces “food-taking.” “Peaceful self” means one whose mind is quiet, and “one from whom the desires for sons and the like have departed” describes the restraints. “Having conquered the seat” and the following words describe posture, breath control, and withdrawal of the senses. “Through meditation on Hari” describes concentration. “Whose impurities in the forms of rajas, sattva, and tamas have been destroyed” describes meditation by its result.

He describes samādhi in two verses. Separating the self, which is the seat of mind and ego, from the gross body; joining and uniting it with the intellect, the self of knowledge; separating that knower-self from what is seen and dissolving it into the knower, the witness called the field-knower; then separating the field-knower from its witnessing aspect and dissolving it into Brahman, the support called the ground—this is like separating the space in a pot from the pot’s adjunct and dissolving it into the great space. He then describes the absence of rising from samādhi. There is no rising caused either by inner agitation of the qualities or by outward distraction of the senses. The residual tendency of māyā’s qualities has been destroyed; the instruments, the eyes and the rest, and the mind are restrained; and all taking of food, whether food itself or the senses’ taking of objects, has ceased. He remains motionless like a post.

To one who was preparing to bring him back even in that condition, he says: “May you not become an obstacle”—the augment is Vedic. To one who was preparing even to see him, he says: “Let me see him only as far as today,” meaning beyond the present day. “His own” means independent. To one thinking, “I will go there to burn his body,” he says, “And that too”—do not go.
He says that he will not go to bring Gāndhārī. She will enter the fire after her husband’s body, which is together with the leaf hut, is burned by the fire of yoga along with the household fires.

He says that he need not go to bring Vidura. On hearing and seeing his brother’s fortunate departure, Vidura, joyful because of that good fortune and sorrowful because of his death, will leave that place to serve the holy places.
“Sorrow” means grief.

In the fourteenth [chapter], the king, having seen the evil omens, became apprehensive; the disappearance of Kṛṣṇa, heard from Arjuna, is being narrated. “And of Kṛṣṇa”—by the word “and,” [he wished] also to know the intention. “A few”—seven. Even though time had passed, Arjuna did not come from Dvārakā. “Omens” means disturbances; “the foremost of the Kurus” means Yudhiṣṭhira.

“Fierce” means terrible. He says that very thing: of that in which the ordinances of the seasons are reversed. “Livelihood” means means of living. Those whose selves are joined with anger, greed and falsehood.

“Predominantly crooked” means abundant in deceit. “Conduct” means dealings. “Deceit” means cheating; that mixed with it, “friendship” means friendship. “Quarreling” of fathers and others with their respective counterparts means quarrel and so forth.
Having seen extremely inauspicious [omens], and having seen the nature of people—greed and so forth, irreligion—[he spoke] to his younger brother Bhīma.
“Or” is in the sense of conjecture. “For what reason has he not come?”—to this he says: “I do not know.”
“Api”—what? When he wishes to abandon the plaything of the self—the limb, the human drama, a means of play—that time has arrived.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the cause of our being [the object of] all human goals; therefore, with the intention that without separation from Him there would be no misfortune, he says [this]. “From whom”—from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, for that reason. Arjuna will make this clear later. “And the worlds”—those attainable according to the performance of sacrifice—by whose favor.
“Not far” means near. “Of us.” “Indicating” means [the omens] announcing disturbances.
Regarding the bodily [omens], he says “the thighs.” The left thighs and so forth are throbbing. Trembling and quivering are present in the heart. These will give me an undesirable thing that is near.

Regarding the earthly [omens], he speaks in three and a half verses. “Śivā,” a female jackal, cries at the rising sun—she cries facing the rising sun. “Fire-faced” means vomiting fire through the mouth. “O limb”—O Bhīma. Looking at me, this dog barks with a leap, fearlessly.
“Useful [animals]”—cows and so forth—make me [pass] on the left themselves. Others, asses and so forth, make [a] circumambulation on the right. “Carriers”—horses.
“This pigeon” is a messenger of death, a sign of death. “Ulūka” is an owl. “Pratyūlūka,” its opponent, is “dhūka,” or a crow. By shrieks—disagreeable sounds—they desire to make the world empty.

“Smoky” [are] the directions; the encircling boundaries cover the world, fire alone. Regarding the heavenly [omens], he speaks in two and a half verses. “Nirghāta” is a thunderbolt falling from a cloudless [sky]. “Thundering ones” here are roars, together with them.
He produced [the omen] especially through darkness; “blood” means red color.

“Marda” of the planets means a battle. “Beings” means the followers of Rudra; together with their hosts, mixed with various creatures. He sees the two worlds—heaven and earth—as though they were blazing and aflame.
Again he speaks of earthly omens with three and a half verses. “Rivers” [are mentioned], and the minds of living beings as well.
The form “they milk” is an archaic use of the agent in a transitive construction. The meaning is: they do not give milk.
“Deities” means images. “Agha” means suffering.
Who [else could be the cause]? Among other people there is no splendor marked by the signs of the thunderbolt, elephant-goad and so forth; therefore I think the earth is deprived of the Lord’s feet.
Thinking with an anxious mind about the omens seen by that king, [he continued].
“Fallen in an unusual way” means fallen unlike before. He explains this with “afflicted” and so forth: “drops of water” means tears, issuing from the two eyes.
He whose heart is disturbed and trembling; “without luster” means deprived of radiance.
“His own people” means his relatives.

Wondering what he will say, he asks in a displaced order, beginning with “Śūra.” “Māriṣa,” O noble one, is the Yādava named Śūra, the maternal grandfather and father of Kuntī. “Ānakadundubhi” is Vasudeva.

“Sisters” means the sisters of one another. Their welfare had already been asked indirectly by asking about Vasudeva’s welfare; nevertheless he asks about them separately, beginning with “themselves.”

“Āhuka” is Ugrasena. “Whose son” means [the one] whose son he was. Therefore the welfare of the living being alone is asked. Devaka is his younger brother. Hṛdīka’s son is Kṛtavarmā. Jayanta and the others are Kṛṣṇa’s brothers.
Among all the Vṛṣṇis he is a great chariot-warrior, with a deep course and great speed in battle. “He grows” means he rejoices or prospers.
Kṛṣṇa’s offspring are the Kārṣṇis; [the verse refers to] their foremost members.
“Those whose chiefs are Sunanda and Nanda” means those for whom Sunanda and Nanda are the principal leaders.
Fearing that it would be improper to ask whether Bhagavān is happy, he speaks beginning with “in the city” and so forth.

Because Bhagavān’s remaining there brings auspiciousness to the worlds, and not otherwise, he speaks in four verses. “For auspiciousness” means for blessing; “for welfare” means for protecting what has been gained; “for existence” means for origination. “Friend of Ananta” means accompanied by Balarāma.
“Worshipped by all” means honored by everyone, in such a way that supreme bliss arises. “The great Person” is Viṣṇu; His great-person attendants are like the attendants of the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha.

Service to His feet alone is the foremost duty, superior to austerity and the rest. Satyabhāmā and the others, in battle, conquered the gods by Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s strength. “Their blessings” means the Pārijāta and other objects of enjoyment belonging to the gods; they were suitable for Śacī, the beloved of the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Those who live by the power of His arm tread upon the Sudharmā assembly hall with their feet. This is connected with the preceding fifth verse: may that Govinda dwell happily.

He now asks about His welfare with six verses beginning “whether.” “Anāmaya” means health. Has He not received honor from His relatives? Or have they instead shown Him contempt and insulted Him, because He has remained there for a long time?

The division is “without affection,” meaning devoid of love. Has He not been struck by inauspicious men through words and the like? Or has He not said to those seeking charity, “I shall give you something”? Or, what was promised together with hope—“I shall give as you hope”—has that not been given?
Or have you not abandoned a living being who came for refuge? For formerly you were a giver of refuge, one who provided shelter.

The division is “not to be approached.” Have you not approached a woman who ought not to be approached, a disgraced woman, or one dishonored by dirty clothing and the like? Or, has an inferior opponent defeated you? “Not by excellent, unequal or equal [opponents]” is the meaning; alternatively, “not by unequal, inferior [opponents]” is the meaning.
Have you perhaps eaten while leaving aside elders and children who were fit to share the meal? Have you failed to do something that was impossible or improper to do?
Always separated in your heart from your dearest one, your own kinsman Śrī Kṛṣṇa, you think, “I am empty.” Otherwise, this mental pain of yours would not arise.

Having observed the entrance of Kali, and placing the burden on Parīkṣit, the king ascended to heaven—thus he says in the fifteenth [chapter]. “Kṛṣṇaḥ Arjunaḥ” is the division [of the expression]; having perceived a form that was the object of various doubts, “vikalpitaḥ” means [he was] perplexed. It is connected with the following “he was unable to speak” [1.15.2]. The reasons there are: “afflicted by separation from Kṛṣṇa”—made emaciated.
“By grief”—by that cause. “Mouth” and “heart”—those two are lotuses. He whose mouth and heart-lotuses dry up; he whose splendor is destroyed.

“Grief”—the tears of grief that arise. Having checked them in the eyes themselves and wiped away what had fallen with the hand, because Śrī Kṛṣṇa was out of sight, being distressed by the increased longing of love, he says to the king [as connected with verse 4].
“Friendship” means wishing well. “Maitrī” means beneficence. “Sauhṛda” means being a friend. And by “ca,” relationship also. “With tears” means with a choked throat, faltering [speech].
“By whom”—by whom I was deceived. “[My power] which astonishes the gods.”

The words beginning with “by separation for a moment from whom” are connected with the word “by Him I am now deprived,” occurring in the seventh verse. An example of even the dear becoming undesirable is “with life” [the life-breath]. “This” refers to father and so forth.

He recalls the favors of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—beginning with “by whose shelter” in ten [verses]. By whose shelter, by force; “by Smara”—by Kāma, desire—the power of the extremely proud was taken away as if by grasping the bow alone. Afterwards that bow was made ready too. By it the fish revolving atop the device was pierced. Then, having conquered them, Kṛṣṇā, Draupadī, was obtained.

“U” expresses astonishment. “Khāṇḍava” is Indra’s forest; “I gave [it] to Agni”—I gave it. The assembly hall made by Maya, who was saved in the burning of Khāṇḍava, was obtained; [it was] of wonderful architectural form. “In that sacrifice”—in the Rājasūya sacrifice.

The following verse is not recited [in some readings], nevertheless it is explained. Jarāsandha, whose feet were worshiped by the heads of kings, was killed by your younger brother Bhīma for the sake of the sacrifice; without his defeat the Rājasūya sacrifice would not be possible. He whose being, enthusiasm-power, prowess and strength were like those of ten thousand elephants. Having killed him, the kings whom Mahābhairava, lord of the Pramathas, had brought for his sacrifice, and whom he released, brought tribute to the sacrifice because they had been released.

By whom—the cheaters, Duḥśāsana and the others—your wife’s hair-lock, having been loosened and scattered, was touched and dragged; their wives became husbandless. Therefore, because of widowhood, [he] made [them] loose-haired. What sort of hair-lock? By the great consecration arranged in connection with the Rājasūya sacrifice, it was most praiseworthy; beautiful. At the remembrance of which, when remembering Śrī Kṛṣṇa—obtained at that very time by our mercy—the tears of the wife, which had fallen at His feet, [were] from her mouth. Although the word “fallen” depends on “feet,” it is compounded with “tears” because of their constant mutual dependence.

The one who eats before ten thousand disciples in their row—because of Durvāsā, and because of the unbearable hardship characterized by a curse, created by the enemy Duryodhana—having come to the forest, protected us from that danger. Having done what? Having eaten only the vegetable food, using up the remnant in that very vessel. Because of its being eaten, the assembly of sages, immersed in water, considered the three worlds satisfied.

Thus indeed there is a story in the Mahābhārata: Once Durvāsā was entertained as a guest by Duryodhana. When, being pleased, he said, “Choose a boon,” Duryodhana, having formed in his mind, “May the Pāṇḍavas be destroyed by Durvāsā’s curse,” said: “Yudhiṣṭhira is the chief of our family. Therefore you should also be his guest in exactly this way, accompanied by ten thousand disciples; but you should go to his house after Draupadī has eaten, so that she may not suffer from hunger.” Then, when Durvāsā arrived in just that way, Yudhiṣṭhira, with the highest honor, requested the assembly of sages, “After performing your midday rites, please come,” and the assembly plunged into the water for the Adhamarṣaṇa rite. There, merely remembered by the distressed Draupadī, Śrī Kṛṣṇa immediately came, leaving Rukmiṇī seated on His lap, out of affection for devotees. When she reported the event, the Lord said, “O Draupadī! I too am hungry. First feed Me.” She replied with great embarrassment: “Lord, the inexhaustible food in the vessel given by the sun was eaten by me, after feeding everyone, up to my own meal; therefore there is no food.” Even so, with great insistence, having brought the vessel, He tasted a little vegetable food clinging to it and said, “By this, may the Lord, the self of the universe, be pleased.” Then He sent Bhīma: “Now invite the assembly of sages to eat.” And they, by that much, were completely satisfied and fled out of fear of eating in vain.

Having been astonished, together with Girijā, [Lord Śiva] gave his own Pāśupata weapon. The other guardians of the worlds also gave their own weapons. He states another wonder: “By this”—the great [one], half of Indra’s seat.

“There itself”—in heaven. “While staying as a guest” [with] Gāṇḍīva as the mark; that [is, the arms] whose mark is Gāṇḍīva. “The enemies” are the demons called Nivātakavacas; [the gods] resorted to [my arms] for their killing. By whom [the arms] were made endowed with power. O Ājamīḍha, Yudhiṣṭhira. By Him I am now deprived, bereft. “By the Supreme”—by abiding in His own greatness.

The three verses beginning with “whose friend” are also connected with the preceding “I am deprived by Him” [verse 13]. Being alone, a friend of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, I crossed the ocean of the Kaurava army, whose end was absent in depth and whose far shore was distant, at the seizure of the northern cows. In it were beings difficult to cross, such as Timiṅgila, in the forms of Bhīṣma and the others. The cattle taken away by the enemies were brought back. And from the heads of the enemies, after bewildering them with the bewildering weapon, much wealth—the source of brilliance, in the form of turbans and jewel-studded crowns—was taken. [This was done] by me, as the friend of Kṛṣṇa.

The excellent kings, immense and without limit, whose armies were adorned with circles of chariots, in the armies of Bhīṣma and the others, while He remained beyond my sight in the form of a charioteer. O Lord! He who, by a mere glance, took away the life and so forth of the commanders of the chariot-hosts. “Minds” means power such as enthusiasm. “Saha” means strength. “Ojas” means skill in weapons and so forth.

In whose arms I was placed, the weapons applied by Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Bhūriśravā, Suśarmā, Śalya, Jayadratha, Bāhlika and the others—though prescribed and wielded by those very teachers and great warriors—did not touch me. “Guru” means Droṇa; “Trigarta” means Suśarmā, the ruler of the Trigarta country; “Śala” means Śalya; “Saindhava” means Jayadratha, ruler of Sindhu; “Bāhlika” means the brother of Śantanu. Their glory was thus truly invincible. Even according to the variant reading, the meaning is the same. The example of remaining untouched despite the failure to counteract the weapons is Prahlāda, the servant of Nṛsiṁha, just as the demons’ weapons did not touch him.

Recalling his own offense and suffering because of it, he speaks: I chose Him as my charioteer through poor judgment. “Atma-giver” and the following words indicate the result—liberation. “Excellent” means noble. “The horses were weary” means that the horses were exhausted. At the killing of Jayadratha they needed water; I descended from the chariot and, piercing the earth with arrows, produced water for them. Then, by His power, which destroyed the enemies’ minds, they did not strike me. Thus it was poor judgment to choose Him merely as a charioteer.

O king! The jokes made beautiful by His noble, profound and pleasing smile, and His sweet, heart-touching words spoken when discussing matters—“O Pārtha,” and so forth—now roll about and agitate my heart as I remember them. The absence of the causative suffix is an archaic usage.

“Boasting” means praise of one’s own qualities and so forth. Because of our inseparability even on beds and in other places, I called Him “friend.” Sometimes, although He saw my transgression, I reproached Him with the crooked words, “You are truthful.” According to another reading, “ṛbhumān” means one who has the gods as attendants. Though He was great, thinking Him a friend I treated Him with contempt. He bore my offense with greatness, like a friend bears a friend’s offense and like a father bears a son’s offense.

He says, “You suspected my defeat, and I also experienced defeat.” Without that friend I am empty in heart. “O limb” means “O king.” “The possession of Urukrama” means the sixteen thousand women who belonged to Him; among low people they are like powerless women.

Here he says that separation from Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone is the cause, and no other. From those kings, before whom the Lord caused [us] to bow, the earth became empty and incapable of producing a result, like an oblation cast into ashes even with the proper ritual formulas. What is obtained from deceitful, magical people, even when highly cherished, is useless, like a seed sown in barren land despite thorough cultivation.

Among our friends in the city, of the friends you asked about, only four or five remain. The cause is the brāhmaṇa’s curse and so forth. “Vāruṇī” means food-made [liquor]. They struck one another with handfuls of eraka grass as though they did not recognize one another.
By the word “left over” he indicates in three verses those who caused it: beginning with “for the most part.” “They nourish” means they protect.
Among aquatic creatures, such as fish, the large and gross ones eat the smaller and subtler ones.

Thus the powerful and proud Pāṇḍavas killed Duryodhana, Jarāsandha and the others; the Yadus killed the others, Śālva and the rest; the Yadus then killed one another; and Bhagavān destroyed those who had become the burden of the earth.

Indicating, “I cannot speak any further,” he says: As I remember Govinda’s words—words joined with meanings appropriate to place and time and capable of calming the pain of the mind—my heart is stolen and drawn away.
“Thus” is Sūta’s statement. Arjuna, thinking of the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa with very intense affection, became peaceful in mind, free from sorrow, pure and detached.

He states the result of the mind’s purification. By devotion whose force has been increased through meditation on Vāsudeva’s feet, all residual impurities such as lust were churned out and uprooted; thus he became one whose intellect was [purified]. “He again attained knowledge” is syntactically connected with the following verse.
That [knowledge] had been obstructed and covered by time, actions, darkness and attachment to enjoyment.

He states the result of knowledge with “free from sorrow,” and establishes it through the absence of sorrow’s cause. The cause of sorrow is the illusion of duality; its basis is the body, its subtle form is the liṅga, its qualities are the guṇas, and their root is ignorance. Through realization of Brahman—by hearing the Vedānta and knowing “I am Brahman”—prakṛti, here ignorance, is dissolved; this is freedom from the guṇas, not a mere remainder of ignorance as in deep sleep or cosmic dissolution. Thus the effects of the guṇas, including the subtle body, are destroyed. Because he is without that subtle body, repeated embodiment for experience is impossible. The doubt characterized by duality is cut off, and he becomes free from sorrow.
Having discerned Bhagavān’s course, heard of the destruction of the Yadu dynasty and recalled Nārada’s words, he went toward the path of heaven with a steady mind.

That course is difficult to know. He will say in the Eleventh Canto: “As the lightning moving through the sky leaves the mass of clouds, its course is not perceived by mortals; so the course of Kṛṣṇa is not perceived even by the gods.” “He stopped transmigration” means that he became liberated while living; alternatively, it means that he abandoned the body.

To dull-minded people who, not understanding Bhagavān’s distinction from the Yadus, declare Him equal to them, he clarifies the distinction with two verses. By the body in the form of a Yadu He removed the burden of the earth, like removing a thorn with another thorn. Both the Yadu body and the body that was the earth’s burden were alike in being subject to the Lord’s destruction.

He now states the special nature of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s form. Just as an actor, while remaining in his own form, assumes and puts away other forms, so He likewise took up and abandoned that body; “He entered it” means that He put it away. A traditional note records that these two verses were absent from some old readings.

To introduce Yudhiṣṭhira’s ascent to heaven, he speaks of Kali’s entrance. “He abandoned [the world] with His own body” means that He ascended to Vaikuṇṭha with His own body. His story is worthy of hearing. “On that very day” means on that day; the word “day” has an elided locative ending. “Those whose minds are unawakened” means the undiscerning; for the discerning, He is not their master in this way. “He followed” means that, having entered earlier in part, He continued in that form.
The wise Yudhiṣṭhira, seeing the spread of Kali, whose wheel is made of greed and irreligion, and whose nature is crookedness, put on the garment appropriate to it.

He installed [Parīkṣit], who was equal and exceedingly similar to himself in qualities, as the lord of the earth. The earth has the ocean water, spread all around it, as its special garment or girdle.
“Vajra” is Aniruddha’s son. “Having appointed” means having installed him. He absorbed him into himself. The Lord is capable.
All the bonds—meaning the limiting adjuncts—were severed by him.

He explains this with two verses. “Speech” stands by implication for all the senses: he dissolved all the senses into the mind, the mind into the vital air because activity depends upon it, and that vital air into apāna, the other [vital air], because apāna draws it in. The activity of apāna is excretion; together with apāna, he dissolved it into death, the presiding deity. The same association with their respective functions is to be understood for speech and the other senses. He dissolved death into the body, in the joining of the five elements. The meaning is that death belongs to the body, not to the self. “Ajohavīt” is an archaic form.

“Five-ness” means the body in the threefold form of the guṇas. That threefoldness was dissolved into oneness, ignorance; and all ignorance, the cause of every superimposition, into the self, the jīva. “Ajuhavīt” is an archaic form used where “ajohavīt” would be expected. Having thus purified the self, he placed it in imperishable, immutable Brahman; the meaning is that it does not dissolve anywhere else.
Having stated realization of the self, he now describes the external condition with two verses beginning “wearing bark.” He bound speech and mind in silence.

Not looking back and not waiting for his younger brothers and the others, he went toward the direction of hope. “Gone before” means having entered earlier; [he followed] the great souls, those who know discrimination, because they had gone in that direction.
“He whose friend is irreligion” means one accompanied by irreligion.
“Those by whom all aims, beginning with dharma, were properly accomplished.” Therefore, knowing the lotus feet of Vaikuṇṭha to be the ultimate refuge.

What kind of abode was it? A place that is the residence of those whose impurities have been removed. They attained that destination with a stainless self alone, not with the liṅga consisting of the sixteen elements. Alternatively, “stainless” qualifies the destination: those whose impurities were removed attained an existence in the form of that destination.
Having then understood that her husbands were not considering her, Draupadī attained Him, with her mind fixed exclusively upon Bhagavān Vāsudeva.
Thus is the departure. It is exceedingly auspicious and a source of well-being; it is also exceedingly purifying.

Then in the sixteenth [chapter], in the dialogue of Earth and Dharma, both afflicted by Kali, the attainment of the protector Parīkṣit is described. “By the instruction of the best of the twice-born”—by good instruction. “At the birth”—at his birth. “Expert in what is born”—knowers of the birth rites. O brāhmaṇa! “In whom are great qualities”—he in whom great qualities are.

“Janamejaya and others”—the excess of a syllable is metrical. In the reading “producing,” the present-participle suffix is used in the sense of cause. The construction of the sentence is: he married in order to beget sons.
“Performed”—that is the meaning of ājahāra. “Śāradvata”—Kṛpa. “In which”—in which Aśvamedha sacrifices—the gods became visible.
“Nijagrāha” means restrained or punished. He points out Kali himself: “the king.”
“For what reason?” This is the meaning: for what reason did he merely seize Kali, and not kill him? Because he is a śūdra, extremely contemptible. “Who struck the cow with his foot.”

“Of this Viṣṇu”—the nectar of the lotus feet of this Viṣṇu. Those who lick and taste it—of those good or great persons, “the support of the topics” is the remainder of the compound. Then let it be spoken.

If not, what [use is there] in other conversations with the untrue [topics], by which life is wasted in vain? Even our effort in this sacrifice is only for drinking the nectar of Hari’s narration—thus he says in one and a half verses. “Small” means short, whose lifespan is [short]; therefore, of mortals, those whose nature is death. Nevertheless, [we are] desirous of the true [and] liberation.

“He who is death”—he was invited in this sacrifice for the Śāmitra rite, the act of killing the animal, for the purpose of restraining death. What then? To this he says, “no one.” What further? To this he says, “Alas! In the human world, let the nectar of Hari’s pastimes—the words—be drunk,” for this purpose. “That in which there is only Hari’s pastime.”

In the absence of that, life is indeed in vain, he says. “Of the dull”—of the lazy. At night, whatever lifespan is ours is taken by sleep. And by day, whatever [time] is ours is taken away by useless actions.

Here then he speaks of the context of punishing Kali—beginning with “when.” When he heard that Kali had entered the country protected by his own army, he then heard that unpleasant news, and somewhat pleasant because it provided the opportunity for the delight of battle; thereafter he took up his bow for the purpose of punishing the wicked. “A śauṇḍa in battle” means skilled in war. In another reading, “śauri in battle” means Śauri, equal to Kṛṣṇa.
Then he departed for conquest of the directions.

“Bhadrāśva and the others” are regions joined to the ocean in the east, west, south and north. Ilāvṛta is on all sides of Mount Meru. Then to the north are Ramyaka and Hiraṇmaya; to the south are Hari-varṣa and Kimpuruṣa.
“The glory being sung.” Hearing the glories and so forth, he gave to them; this is connected with the third [line].

Moreover, hearing of Viṣṇu’s acts—charioteering and the rest—for the affectionate Pāṇḍavas, and hearing the praise offered to Viṣṇu by the world, King Parīkṣit developed devotion to Viṣṇu’s lotus feet. The reading “pārṣadam” is a metrical separation of the sounds; here it means presiding over the assembly. “Service” means following with the mind. “The hero’s posture” means standing watch at night with a sword in hand.
“Following the way of life” means while remaining engaged in his duty. “Not far away” means very soon.
“Dharma” is in the form of a bull. “Without luster” means deprived of radiance. “The cow” is Earth in the form of a cow. “Without a calf” means without offspring.

Although no external disease of your body is perceived, I see you as afflicted by an internal pain. Since you are without luster, your face—slightly faded and discolored—is the sign of it. He asks about the causes with five verses beginning “far from relatives.” “Far away” means a relative situated at a distance.

Being deficient by three feet, only one foot remains. “Me” means a person marked by me. “To be enjoyed by śūdras from now onward” is the meaning of “by the śūdras.” “Manhood” qualifies the self. “Those whose shares of the sacrifice have been taken away” means those deprived of sacrificial portions because sacrifices and the like are no longer performed.

O Earth, women who are not protected by their husbands and children who are not protected by their fathers are instead afflicted and tormented by them, as though by merciless man-eaters. Divine speech, Sarasvatī, is situated in evil conduct. The foremost members of the family are excellent brāhmaṇas, who have become servants.

“Afflicted” means overwhelmed. “Removed” means driven away. “Sexual union” means intercourse. Alternatively, “the world of living beings” means people everywhere, without regard for prohibitions, advancing toward eating and the other [forbidden activities].

O mother, remembering the deeds of Him who incarnated to remove your heavy burden, you grieve because He has now released you. “Nirvāṇa delayed” means liberation has been postponed for those in whom it is delayed. According to another reading, “nirvāṇa mocked” means mocked by them; the meaning is that His deeds are more blissful than liberation.
O mother, your good fortune has been taken away by time.

You know this already, yet I shall speak. By the Lord who is the cause, you stand on all four feet; in the world from which Śrī-Nivāsa is absent, where truth and the other great qualities no longer remain, I grieve. This is connected with the sixth verse.

“Truth” means speaking what is real. “Purity” means cleanliness. “Compassion” means inability to bear another’s suffering. “Forbearance” means restraining the mind when anger arises. “Generosity” means an open hand toward those who ask. “Contentment” means a mind that is satisfied. “Straightforwardness” means freedom from crookedness. “Tranquility” means stillness of mind. “Self-control” means stillness of the external senses. “Austerity” means one’s own prescribed duty. “Equality” means absence of distinctions such as enemy and friend. “Endurance” means bearing another’s offense. “Withdrawal” means indifference when gain is obtained. “Learning” means inquiry into scripture. “Knowledge” concerns the Self. “Dispassion” means freedom from thirst. “Sovereignty” means the power to control. “Heroism” means enthusiasm for battle. “Splendor” means influence. “Strength” means competence. “Memory” means keeping in view what should and should not be done. “Independence” means freedom from dependence. “Skill” means expertise in action. “Beauty” means loveliness. “Courage” means freedom from agitation. “Gentleness” means softness of heart. “Boldness” means exceptional insight. “Humility” means modesty. “Character” means a pleasant disposition. “Mind-power, sense-power and bodily strength” mean excellence of the mind, the knowing senses and the active senses. “Fortune” means being an abode of enjoyment. “Depth” means inability to be shaken. “Steadiness” means immovability. “Faith” means trust. “Fame” means renown. “Honor” means being worthy of worship. “Absence of ego” means absence of pride. These are thirty-nine qualities. Other great qualities, such as taking refuge in Brahman, are eternally innate in Him and never decline.
By that holder and abode of qualities; “sinful” means the cause of sin.

Who could endure separation from Him? He explains this in four verses. Brahmā and the others, desiring the release of Śrī’s sidelong glance, performed austerities properly for a long time. Even that Śrī, though sought by exalted devotees, serves Him whose foot-beauty she greatly loves.

“His glorious feet” are His feet of splendor. “A banner” means a flag; “lotus and the other banners” means those whose marks are the lotus and so forth. Alternatively, Earth, whose body was fully adorned by the supports of the lotus and other marks, says: Having obtained the Lord’s majesty, I surpassed the three worlds and became radiant. When the end of that majesty—its destruction—arrived, He abandoned me while I was becoming proud.

Moreover, He removed my great burden in the form of a hundred divisions of armies belonging to kings of demonic lineage. He also restored you, who were distressed because you had lost one foot, to a complete and secure state in Himself through His own manly effort. The present participle expresses the cause; “he bore” means he maintained.

Who could endure separation from Him? He took away the love-filled glance, pleasing smile and charming speech of the women proud of their sweetness—Satyabhāmā and the others—which together gave them their firmness. From the dust raised by His foot upon the ornamented earth there arises a festival of horripilation, appearing in the guise of crops and the like.
While the two were speaking, they were at Kurukṣetra, beside the Sarasvatī flowing eastward.

Then in the seventeenth [chapter], the punishment of Kali is spoken, and the extraordinary renunciation of the king, although he possessed such power, is spoken. “Being killed” means being struck or beaten.

“Lotus stalk” is the lotus root, therefore white. “From fear, urinating.” By “as if,” Dharma, remaining with one leg, is shown as if urinating from fear, trembling because his remaining portion is diminishing at every moment through inability to sustain it.

“Yielding dharma”—a giver of oblation. “Emaciated”—thin. “Grass”—herbage. Here, through the destruction of the production of crops and so forth, [she is] like one bereft of a calf. Through the absence of sacrifices and so forth [she is] emaciated. Therefore Earth is indicated as desiring her share of the sacrifice.
“Kārtasvara” is gold. “Whose equipment is made of that”—whose accessories are made of gold; that is the meaning, bound or embossed with gold. “With the bow made ready.”
“You kill” means you cause [them] to be killed. If [he says], “I am a king,” to that he says: by dress alone you are a man-god, like an actor; by conduct, however, you are a non-twice-born śūdra.
“Those not to be lamented”—the innocent ones whom you strike secretly. He is to be lamented; he is guilty; therefore he deserves to be killed.
He addresses the bull: “Who are you?” Or, “you”—he addresses you himself. Are you some god who, existing in the form of a bull, is causing us distress?
“Protected by arms” means protected as if embraced by arms. “Your tears”—without the tears of others, your tears do not fall; thus the cause of distress is shown.

Having said thus, he again addresses the lamenting bull: “O son of Surabhi, do not grieve”—do not lament; “may it go away”—may it depart. He addresses the cow: “O mother, while I, the ruler, am alive, your good alone [will be]; therefore do not cry.”

“I shall kill this one only for my welfare, not for your benefit”—thus he speaks in the two [verses] beginning with “whose.” “O chaste one”—the meaning is: all whatsoever [people]. “Are terrified by the wicked” means are afflicted by them. “Bhaga” is fortune. “Gati” is the next world.
Again he addresses the lamenting bull: “Who cut off”—who severed. “Like you”—those of your kind who are afflicted.
“May there be good for you.” The one who made deformity in your person by cutting off your legs, and thus disgraces the fame, is named.

“When he has been named, how can there be good?” To this he says: Since whoever inflicts harm and suffering on a blameless person, fear of me, such as I am, arises everywhere, therefore there will indeed be good for the virtuous.

Do not think, “I am unable to punish this one”; thus he says, “the offenseless ones.” “Āgaskṛt” is an offender. I shall take away the arm even of an immortal god. By “with the arm-ornament” it is shown that I shall uproot and take it from the root.
One might ask, “What purpose is there in favoring one person by restraining another?” He answers: for the sake of the king—to protect others by punishing those who are irreligious.
Your words, by which the afflicted obtain fearlessness, are indeed appropriate.
We do not know that person from whom causes of distress to living beings arise, because we have been bewildered by the differing arguments and words of disputants.

He explains the different arguments in the speech. Yogins who cover the Self with their own alternatives say that the Self alone is the lord of the self, giving happiness and sorrow. As it is said in the Gītā: “The self alone is the friend of oneself, and the self alone is one’s enemy.” Alternatively, atheists covered by sophistry say: the deities are not sovereign because they depend on karma; karma is not sovereign because it is not independent and is unconscious; therefore the self alone is sovereign and there is no other. Others—astrologers—say destiny, in the form of planets and other deities; the Mīmāṃsakas say karma; and the materialists say nature.

“Among some theists” indicates the rarity of this view. “Certainty” means a settled doctrine. Reflect with your own intelligence that everything arises from the Supreme Lord, who cannot be reasoned about because He is beyond the mind and cannot be described because He is beyond speech.
“Free from distress” means free from delusion. “He answered” means he spoke in reply, or understood.

You speak Dharma in this way: knowing the killer, yet not pointing him out, as though saying that the matter were undetermined. Therefore you are Dharma. One might ask, “What fault is there in pointing him out?” He answers: the destination would be hell and so forth.

Alternatively, failure to speak may arise even from ignorance. The course of God’s māyā—the activity marked by the relation of the slain and the killer—is beyond the grasp of beings, mind and speech, and cannot be easily understood; this is the conclusion.

Knowing, “This is Dharma,” he describes the arrangement by repeating the feet in two verses. Your three feet, the three portions belonging to irreligion, have been broken. “Astonishment” is the meaning of “smaya.”

Now, in the age of Kali, O Dharma, your fourth portion, truth, alone remains. Through truth you somehow maintain yourself; alternatively, a person may establish you. Kali, this irreligion nourished by falsehood, wishes to seize even that remaining foot. In the Kṛta age Dharma was complete with four feet. In Tretā, a quarter of each foot was lost: austerity through pride, purity through attachment, compassion through intoxication, and truth through falsehood. In Dvāpara half remained; in Kali one quarter remains, and even that will perish at the end.
The immense burden that belonged to Earth was brought down through one another’s agency; her auspicious undertaking was accomplished.
The fragment of tears is what sheds tears. Having been abandoned by him, she grieves, thinking, “The śūdras will enjoy me.”
“Sharpened” means made sharp. The meaning is: [he took the sword] to kill Kali, the cause of irreligion.
“Having determined” means having intended and understood.
“Worthy of refuge” means deserving to be approached for shelter. “Worthy of praise” means deserving of noble renown.
Gudākeśa is Arjuna. We are the bearers of his fame; toward him we hold our hands joined in reverence. But one must not associate with you in any way, because you are a friend of irreligion.

He explains this: you have spread everywhere throughout the bodies of kings. “Un-Aryan” means wickedness; “sin” means abandoning one’s own duty; “the eldest” means misfortune; and “māyā” means deceit.
Therefore one should live according to dharma and truth in Brahmāvarta, the land where the sacrificial canopy is spread and experts in sacrifice reside.

“Whose form is sacrifice” means He whose form is the sacrifice. “Śam” means welfare, and “desires” means desired objects. One might object that Indra and the other gods are worshiped in sacrifice, not Hari. He answers with “steadfast.” He is the Self of stationary beings and the rest; nevertheless, unlike an ordinary living being, He is not limited. Like air, which is within as the vital breath and also outside, the Supreme Lord, the inner controller of all, is within and without.
“With a raised sword” means with a drawn sword; “holding the rod” means Yama; “raised” means prepared and ready.
By your command, “Do not remain here,” I shall live wherever you direct. Yet wherever I live, I shall see you—holding arrows and a bow.
Therefore, because of that [command], I shall remain fixed and unmoving.

“Drinking” means drinking liquor. “Slaughterhouse” means the killing of living beings. “Dice” means falsehood. Intoxication through drinking destroys compassion; here intoxication is also understood as pride, which destroys austerity. Attachment to women and cruelty in violence destroy compassion. Although everything can occur everywhere, falsehood and the rest are to be understood chiefly in dice and the other places respectively. In the Twelfth Canto the feet are truth, compassion, austerity and charity; there “charity” means purity, because giving fearlessness to beings purifies the mind. The statement that in Tretā a quarter of each foot is gradually lost is consistent: “dissension” indicates attachment to women, and “lack of contentment” indicates its cause, pride.

Because all four [vices] were present in one place, when Kali again begged for a place, the king gave him gold. From gold came falsehood, intoxication, attachment to women in the form of lust, violence rooted in rajas, and then a fifth—enmity.
By Uttara’s son, Parīkṣit. The meaning is that he placed Kali in these places. He was acting under the command of that king.
“Then” means because of this, wishing to arise or become manifest. “Not using women and gold” means nonattachment to them.
Having thus restrained Kali, he restored the feet of the bull, meaning that he reestablished austerity and the other virtues.

Even the commencement of your sacrifice is due to his influence. At that time he occupies the seat offered and entrusted to him by Yudhiṣṭhira, who was preparing to enter the forest. The present tense “he sits” is used in the sense of something occurring very near the present; alternatively, “he remains and protects” is supplied.
Those who were initiated in order to perform the sacrifice had completed their initiation. Thus ends Śrīdhara Svāmī’s Bhāvārtha-dīpikā commentary on the First Canto, Seventeenth Chapter.

Then in the eighteenth [chapter], the brāhmaṇa’s curse of that king is described. And that curse itself became a blessing for him, producing detachment. In order to speak of Parīkṣit’s departure, and to establish that wonder, he recalls the wonder of his birth: “he who…” “Burned” means having been scorched.

From Takṣaka, arising from the anger of a brāhmaṇa, came the disturbance or destruction of life; from that, whatever great fear there was—because of that he was not bewildered. The reason is: his mind was offered to Bhagavān alone.
But “having abandoned” [means this]. Being a disciple of Vaiyāsaki, Śuka. He by whom the truth of the position of Ajita Hari was understood.
Nor is this surprising, he says. Those in whom the topics of Uttamaśloka alone [are found]—therefore, for those who constantly relish the nectar in the form of His story, there is no bewilderment.
In that king, even more, this is not surprising—so he says, “as long as.” “The son of Abhimanyu”—the sole king, the emperor, the lord, as long as [he is ruler].

“Then let there be no entry of Kali; even if he entered here, he did not prevail”—how is that? To this he says, “on that day.” “Yarhi”—in that very moment. “Earth.” “Anuvṛttaḥ”—entered. “In which there is the source of irreligion.”

“Since Kali is the cause of irreligion, why did he not kill him altogether?” To this he says, “does not hate.” “Sāraṅga” is one who takes the essence, like a bee. He states the essence: in which auspicious, meritorious acts bear fruit quickly by mere intention; the other sinful acts do not quickly succeed. Those [sinful acts] succeed only when actually done, not merely when intended.

“Since faults are abundant, hatred alone is appropriate.” No, because among the steady he does nothing; thus he says, “what indeed [would be the use]?” What would come of him? [He is] among the childish and unsteady. Being vigilant and attentive, he behaves like a wolf.
“Pārīkṣitam”—the account concerning Parīkṣit. “You asked”—you inquired.

To say no more, he states the essence of the meaning of all scriptures: “whatever [topics].” The many acts of Him that are to be spoken, concerning His qualities and deeds. By those desiring to become good, desiring true welfare.

For the purpose of speaking again at length, they praise the words of Sūta and their connection, with three [verses] beginning “O Sūta.” “Live for eternal years”—for endless years. The second case is used in the sense of complete connection. “You proclaim pure fame.” And that is nectar for us mortals, warding off death.

Moreover, in this ritual, in this sacrifice, there is no certainty, it is not reliable, because of the abundance of defects and the absence of certainty of result. “Those whose selves are smoky”—us whose bodies are discolored by smoke. The genitive case is used in relation to the ritual. “Āsava” means nectar. “Madhu” means sweet.

“Associates of Bhagavān”—devotees of Viṣṇu. “The association of them”—even its moment, a very small period of time; even with that we do not compare heaven, we do not regard it as equal. Nor liberation [apunarbhava]. The imperative is used in the sense of possibility. What need be said of the insignificant blessings of mortals, beginning with kingship—we do not compare them.

Having thus praised the association of the good, they reveal eagerness to hear: “who indeed?” “A knower of rasa”—one who knows rasa. “In the story of Him who is the ultimate refuge, exclusively, of the greatest beings.” “Without qualities”—without material qualities. The limit of His auspicious qualities even the lords of yoga—whose foremost are Bhava, Śiva, and Pādma, Brahmā—did not reach; they did not count them as having an end.
“Among us, Bhagavān is chief, whose service is to be rendered; you are that [person]. May you expand Hari’s deeds for us who desire to hear.”

This is to be narrated through the dialogue of Śuka and Parīkṣit. By the knowledge spoken by Śuka, the son of Vyāsa, by which liberation is named and which is a means to knowledge, he worshiped the feet of Hari, whose banner bears Garuḍa.

Explain that implied meaning just as it is. The narrative spoken to Parīkṣit is the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata Purāṇa. It is supremely holy and purifies the quality of sattva; its steadfastness is in an exceedingly wonderful yoga; it is endowed with the deeds of Ananta; and therefore it is beloved and pleasing to the Bhāgavatas. These characteristics especially show that it illuminates karma, knowledge, devotion and yoga.

In the explanation of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, he praises himself—the one who has obtained an opportunity and is honored by great souls—with two verses. “Aho” expresses wonder, and “ha” joy. “We” is a plural used in praise. Although born from a low lineage, we have today attained fruitful birth through following and honoring elders. Alternatively, [I am fruitful] through serving Śuka, who is advanced in knowledge. By association with great souls, even worldly contact removes low birth and the mental distress caused by it.

What more needs to be said? The recitation of Ananta’s name, which is the supreme one-pointed yoga of great souls, removes low birth. Or, what low birth could remain for a person who recites the name? This is an argument from the greater to the lesser. He has infinite powers and is Himself infinite. He whose qualities among the great are [supreme] is called “great in qualities”; they say that He is infinite even in qualities.

He expands this in three verses beginning “so much.” The knowledge that there is no equality or superiority to Him in qualities is sufficiently indicated by this; who could speak of its entire elaboration? He states the proof: Lakṣmī, although she does not desire the prosperity of anyone else, serves the dust of His feet, having abandoned Brahmā and the other gods who seek her.

Now he states another matter. The water of worship released from His toenail, offered by Brahmā, purifies the world together with its Lord. By saying that it was offered by Brahmā, even Brahmā and Śiva are shown to be His worshipers. Therefore, apart from Mukunda, who else could be the meaning of the Lord’s feet? He alone is the Lord of all.
“The steadfast” means the holy sages. “Borne” means sustained; “ultimate” means reaching the highest limit. He says that in Him nonviolence and tranquility are natural dharma.

Having praised his own good fortune, he begins to narrate the account of Parīkṣit. O Āryaman, O Suns—the three forms of the Sun—I shall speak as much knowledge of the Self as I possess. Just as birds rise into the sky only according to their own strength, not through the whole of it, so wise persons describe Viṣṇu’s course and play only in a manner proportionate to their own capacity.
He now introduces the story: “Once...”
Not seeing [the king], he saw the famous hermitage, and in it the sage Śamīka.

His senses and the other faculties had been restrained; therefore he was withdrawn. He had attained the fourth state beyond the three states marked by waking and the rest. Thus, being Brahman, he was unchanging.
He was covered by scattered matted locks and also covered with the hide of a ruru deer. His palate was especially dried. To such a sage he asked for water.
He had not obtained grass, a grass seat or another place to sit, such as the ground; nor had he received an arghya offering or pleasant words.
“Envy” means inability to tolerate another’s excellence.
“His life had departed” means he was dead. The serpent was placed with the tip of the bow, the point of the bow.

He explains the king’s intention in placing the serpent. Was this sage standing with all his senses withdrawn and his eyes closed in genuine samādhi? Or, out of contempt, was this a false samādhi, while he wondered whether the Kṣatriya relatives who had arrived had already gone? The king wished to find this out.
His son was named Śṛṅgī. He was exceedingly powerful, endowed with the strength of austerity. “Agha” means suffering; “among the children” means among the boys.

“The fat ones” means the kings; “the well-nourished” means the stout. He identifies irreligion itself: the sin of servants toward their master, like the sin of crows and dogs that eat the share belonging to others.
He shows their servitude with “by brāhmaṇas.” “Together with the vessel” means that the whole object remained situated in the vessel itself.
“Immediately thereafter” means right after that. “I punish” means I chastise.
Having said this to his companions, he whose eyes were copper-red with anger [took] the water of the Kauśikī River. The sandhi is archaic. His thunderbolt of speech was the curse.

Thus, by placing the serpent [around him], he said, “It shall bite and devour.” According to another reading, “it shall burn to ashes.” “Sma” fills the meter. “Like an ember of the family” is the meaning. “Me” means “by me”; the shortened form in “tata” is archaic.
“A serpent’s body around the neck” is a compound meaning “one who has a serpent’s body around his neck.” “With an open throat” means loudly.
Having released that serpent, [he asked:] “What benefit has been done [by this]?”
The unpraised speech begins with “Alas!”—“What a misfortune!” You have committed a great sin, an offense and betrayal. “Restraint” means punishment.
He whose fame is that he is the Supreme Person, Viṣṇu, the human king; [such a king] cannot be measured or regarded as equal by human beings.
“Not seen” means invisible, like a flock of sheep.

The world whose protector has been lost, and the sin that will arise for us because of thieves who steal wealth, will come to us because we have become the cause, though without any direct connection. He explains that sin: people quarrel with one another and speak harshly, steal animals and the like, and are full of thieves.
“The conduct of the noble” means proper conduct. [These are people] whose minds are fixed only on wealth and desire, like dogs and monkeys.

Having stated that the king alone was not fit to be cursed, he now states the specific circumstance in a half-verse. “Performer of the horse sacrifice” means one who has performed an Aśvamedha. One might ask, “If he was such a king, why did he offend him?” He answers: because of hunger and thirst. Since the sage did not ask a welcoming question, how could the king have deserved a curse?
Not seeing any other atonement for this great offense, he reports the offense and prays to Bhagavān: “Among the sinless...”

If the king had given a counter-curse, there might have been expiation, but that was impossible because he was a great devotee. “Despised” means denounced; “deceived” means cheated; “cast out” means disregarded; “struck” means beaten. Those who commit these offenses do not retaliate against the Lord’s devotees, even though they are capable.
“Afflicted” means harmed or offended. “Agha” means an offense.
He says that this is proper as well. “For the most part” refers to the dualities such as happiness and sorrow. One who has no support in the guṇas has no support for happiness, sorrow and the rest.

When the king had sat for the fast unto death on the Ganges, surrounded by yogic persons, the arrival of Śuka there is spoken of in the nineteenth [chapter]. Thinking of that act done by himself—the throwing of a serpent on the sage’s shoulder—as blameworthy and censurable, he became very distressed. He states the thought with one and a half verses: “Alas!” “Low” means sinful. In the reading amīva, the meaning is the same. “In a brāhmaṇa” means in a brāhmaṇa; “in whom splendor is hidden” means in one whose splendor is concealed.

“What was done”—the sin of disrespecting God, meaning the sin of disregarding the Lord. “From that, let calamity come to me”; but let it be soon, not after a long time; and directly to me, not through a son or another—this is the prayer. “At will” means without restriction. The purpose of the prayer is atonement for the sin, so that he may not do this again.

Having thus directly prayed for calamity to himself, before that he prays for something: “Let the fire that is the angered brāhmaṇa community burn my kingdom and so forth today itself.” The meaning is: may my understanding not again arise for afflicting brāhmaṇas and others.

Thinking thus, the king heard from the sage’s son that on the seventh day death would occur, in the form of destruction. Having heard it from the disciple sent by Śamīka, he considered Takṣaka’s poison-fire good, because it is a cause of detachment for one who is attached to worldly objects.

Then, immediately, having considered both worlds—this and the next—beforehand, even sovereignty, as things to be abandoned, he abandoned them, considering service to Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s feet alone and knowing it as the beginning of all human goals. He sat for the fast in that [place]—that is the meaning. He sat with that resolve. Or, “fast” means a supreme refuge, so that it becomes a supreme resort.

He states the result of the qualifier “on the immortal river.” The Ganges, whose shining beauty is mixed with Tulasī, is the carrier of water made most excellent by the dust from Kṛṣṇa’s feet. In both ways, inside and outside, she purifies the worlds together with Śeṣa and the guardians of the worlds. “About to die” means near death; because the time of death is uncertain, everyone is thus. Therefore who would not serve her?

Having thus definitely decided upon the fast unto death on the Ganges, the path of Viṣṇu: “Pāṇḍaveya” shows the appropriateness of his family. “One whose disposition is nowhere else.” Why? “With the vow of a sage”—peaceful. From what? “By whom all association is released”—he is released from all association.

There, at that time, sages came for the purpose of seeing him, not for bathing at a holy place, because they were fulfilled. “But pilgrimage by such persons is also seen”—to this he says, “generally”: under the pretext of pilgrimage.
Aruṇa and the others are specified separately by the special rank of kāṇḍarṣis. The various ārṣeyas are the gotras of the sages; among them, the foremost. He bowed, touching the earth with his head.

Again he bowed for the purpose of making a request. “One whose mind is secluded”—whose mind is pure. “With hands joined”—he whose two hands were joined. He informed them whether his own intended act—fasting unto death and so forth—was proper or improper.

Having perceived favor through their approval, he praises himself: “Indeed!” Those whose conduct is deserving of favor by the greatest among kings. This is very rare among kings, he says. According to the Smṛti, from the washing of brāhmaṇas’ feet, from the water used to wash their feet, remnants, stool, urine and foot-water should be cast far away; indeed they are discarded far away by them. Then “even farther”—cast away farther still, thrown away; the meaning is that it is unfit even to stand there. He speaks referring to himself, whose act is blameworthy.

“Let the favor be aside for now; even the brāhmaṇa’s curse arose solely from the Lord’s grace”—thus he says. “Of that very blameworthy act”; therefore, of me, sinful and attached in mind to household affairs, the Lord of all higher and lower beings, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Himself, became a brāhmaṇa’s curse for my attainment of Him. When that curse is present, one who is attached to household affairs becomes fearful and disillusioned. Because it has detachment as its root, it has detachment as the cause of attainment. Since detachment is the means by which he is attained, and fear is the root of that [detachment], He caused the brāhmaṇa’s curse for that purpose.

He prays to them with the two [verses] beginning “him”: “Let them recognize me, who have come to Him and taken refuge. And let the goddess Ganges, in divine form, recognize [me].” The word “vā” indicates indifference to the alternative. “Gāthās” means stories.
May there be excellent association with those who take refuge in him, in each successive creation and birth.

“Firm resolve” means certainty. “Ancient” means having the tips of the roots toward the front; he formerly sat upon those kuśa grasses. “He whose burden was placed” means one who placed the burden of the kingdom upon his own son Janamejaya.
He scattered [flowers] with joy. Drums played by hosts of gods resounded.
Those whose nature, essential quality and strength lie in the welfare of their subjects, and who are beautiful, as though adorned by the qualities of Uttamaśloka.
“Among you” means among the descendants of Pāṇḍu. “They departed” is understood according to the intention of Yudhiṣṭhira and the others.
They consulted one another—all of them. “The supreme” means the highest world. The reason is that he will go to a stainless, sorrowless destination. He states the lineage with “this one.”
“Having heard” means having listened. “Impartial” means free from partiality. “Honey-flowing” means pouring nectar. “Weighty” means profound in meaning. “Without falsehood” means truthful.

Above the three worlds, in Satya-loka, the Vedas take embodied form; the sages were equal to them. Having stated their superior knowledge, he now speaks of their compassion: you have no purpose apart from benefiting others. Is that the only meaning? No—their own nature is also [compassion].

“To be asked” means what should be asked. “Having trusted” means having placed confidence. “The state of having done” means the conviction that “this must be done” in that matter. Consider with complete attention what should be done in every condition, especially by those who are dying, and what is pure and free from contact with sin.

While those sages were disputing about sacrifice, yoga, austerity, charity and the like, the son of Vyāsa arrived there by chance while wandering over the earth. No mark of an āśrama or other station was visible on him. His appearance was like that of an avadhūta, one abandoned and disregarded by people.

“They rose” is connected with the third verse. He was sixteen years old—twice eight years. His feet, hands, thighs, arms, shoulders, cheeks and body were delicate. His eyes were beautiful and long; his nose was raised; his ears were equal, without irregularity of length or shortness; his face had beautiful eyebrows; and his well-formed neck was marked by three lines like a conch.

The two bones below the neck were his collarbones, hidden by flesh. His chest was broad and high; his navel was whorled; his belly was lovely, marked by transverse, slightly sunken folds. The directions themselves were his garment. His hair was curly and scattered; his arms were long; his complexion was like that of Hari, the foremost among the gods.

Ever youthful, with the excellent beauty and bodily luster of youth and with a lovely smile, he rose to greet him. Though his spiritual radiance was concealed, they nevertheless stood up on seeing him.
He offered respectful obeisance with his head alone, making an offering of himself. The women and others who had come with him withdrew, and he sat down.

That Bhagavān, surrounded by assemblies of Brahmarṣis and the others, shone brilliantly. “Planets” means Venus and the others; “constellations” means Aśvinī and the others; “stars” means the remaining stars.
He whose intelligence is never dull among all noble people. After bowing, he bowed again for the purpose of asking questions.

He spoke sweet words beginning with “aho” in five verses. You have become worthy of the service of the good; because of your arrival in the form of a guest, you have made the holy places worthy [of being visited].
By the proximity of Viṣṇu, they became [extraordinary], like the demons and the others [who were transformed by His presence].
He was dear to the sons of Pāṇḍu; therefore, for the sake of affection toward their maternal relatives, he accepted our lineage as his own and performed the duties of a kinsman.

Otherwise, without Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s grace, how could the unseen destination of those who are dying be attained? “Beggar” means one who asks; “the most benevolent” means the most generous; “the one to be asked” is the person whom one approaches with a request.

He from whom there is complete perfection. “Action” means what is fit to be done, whereas “duty” means what must be done. Therefore, I ask you, the teacher of yogīs, what brings the dying person complete perfection, liberation.
Tell us what should be heard, what should be recited, what should be done, what should be remembered and what should be worshiped—and also their opposites, what should not be heard and so forth.
Because seeing you again is difficult, he says that it should be spoken now. By the power of our good fortune, we have obtained your audience even for the short time required to milk a cow.
He was addressed, turned toward them and questioned with smooth, sweet words beginning with “aho” and the like. Thus ends Śrīdhara Svāmī’s commentary on the First Canto, Nineteenth Chapter.

Obeisance to Śrī Gaṇeśa.

In the Second [Canto], with ten chapters, the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata is described from the beginning. In another book there is an additional verse at the beginning: “I worship that eternal, supremely blissful Hari-Nara, whose name-chanting is the good fruit of gifts, austerity, yoga and the like.”

It is briefly described through statements of the subject and the definition. “Subject” is the naming of the object by name alone. “Definition” is that by which it is indicated and known, namely, the statement of an uncommon characteristic.

But in the First Chapter, through chanting, hearing and the like, concentration of the mind on the gross form of Bhagavān is described.

“I worship that eternal, supremely blissful Hari-Nara, whose name-chanting is the good fruit of gifts, austerity, yoga and the like.”

Now the explanation of the Second Canto. Previously the introduction, together with its context, and Śuka’s arrival were stated. “The wise know an introduction to be [that which is made] for accomplishing the intended purpose.” An introduction is, after mentally grasping the meaning to be presented, the description of another meaning for that purpose.

The sage Śuka then speaks the duty of men asked by the king.

He praises the king’s question with “glorious.” This question, asked by you among the things to be heard and so forth by men, is the supreme question concerning the highest object, and is glorious. For this is beneficial to the world, because it is a cause of liberation. It is approved by knowers of the self and by liberated persons, because of this.

The things stated at the end of the First Canto beginning with “what is to be heard and what is to be chanted” are intended.

Here, for now, while stating the capacity of natural activities to cause misfortune, he gives, in three [verses] beginning with “what is to be heard and so forth,” the answer to “Tell me what is the contrary” [Bhāgavata 1.19.30]. [He speaks] of those attached to houses, and therefore house-dwellers, devoted to the five slaughter places situated in them. The root medh is in the sense of harming.

The five slaughter places of a householder are the hearth, the grinding stone, the implements, the pounding mortar and the water-pot; and what is killed while carrying.

And through those things to be heard and so forth life is wasted in vain, he says. At night, the lifespan that is [spent] at night is taken away by sleep, sexual intercourse or pleasure. In the day, the lifespan that is [spent] in the day is [used] for exertion toward wealth, or, when wealth has been obtained, for maintaining the family. The two particles “and” indicate the collection of what is not stated.

“But why would he expend his life for the sake of an impermanent family and so forth?” To this he replies. Although the body and the rest, the armies and accessories of the self, are unreal and falsely existent, he is heedlessly attached to them; although seeing their destruction through the example of the father and the like, he does not reflect on it.

Having stated the answer to the question concerning the contrary, he gives the answer to the question concerning what is to be heard and so forth with “therefore.” O Bhārata, descendant of Bharata. By “the self of all” he states [the Lord’s] being most beloved. By “Bhagavān,” beauty. By “Īśvara,” necessity. By “Hari,” the removal of bondage. “Fearlessness” means liberation, [desired] by one who desires it.

He says that there is no other higher good than this: this alone is the fruit, the gain of birth. He states it as “remembrance of Nārāyaṇa.” By saying that it is accomplished through Sāṅkhya and the like, he prevents their being gains through their own independence. Sāṅkhya is discrimination between the self and the not-self. Yoga is the eight-limbed [Yoga]. At the end, remembrance is the supreme gain; that is the meaning, for its greatness cannot be stated.

There he establishes good conduct as authority with “mainly.” [They are] withdrawn from injunction and prohibition through injunction and prohibition, and, although situated in Brahman beyond the qualities, it is well known.

“What is this unprecedented thing you are saying?” It is indeed unprecedented, he says. This Bhāgavata, spoken by Bhagavān, having His name alone as its principal subject, is a Purāṇa equal to Brahman and equal to all the Vedas. Or, it is that by which Brahman is rightly measured.

From where did you receive it? He says: “I studied.” From Dvaipāyana, my father. When? “At the beginning of Dvāpara”—in the end of Dvāpara, that is the meaning. The incarnation of Vyāsa is famous in the time of Śantanu and the like.
“Why would there be engagement in study for you who are perfected?” To this he says: “Even though perfectly established.” “Having attracted the mind” means having an attracted mind.

He says that for practitioners and perfected persons there is no other higher good than this: “this.” For those desiring [material enjoyment], this alone is the means for the respective fruits. For those becoming dispassionate, those desiring liberation, this alone is the means of liberation. For yogins, the knowers, this alone is determined as the fruit. There is no authority that needs to be stated here; that is the meaning.

“Only a little life remains; what shall I accomplish?” “Do not grieve,” he says, in three [verses]. “By years that are unnoticed” means by unmarked years. “Years” means years. “Known” means known to pass in vain. “By which” means by that knowledge. “One should strive” means one should make effort.

Khaṭvāṅga, while stationed on the side of the gods, defeated the demons. Then, when the pleased gods said, “Choose a boon,” he said, “First, tell me the measure of my life.” Then the gods said, “That is only a moment.” Then he came very quickly by aerial vehicle to the earth and took refuge in Hari. For this heavenly-earthly realm is rich in rajas. The earth is the field of action.
But for you, even now, at this present time. “So long” means with that amount of time; accomplish the other-worldly means.

There he speaks of dispassion with “at the end of life.” “Free from fear” means free from the fear of death. “Non-attachment” means absence of attachment. With that weapon he should cut desire for pleasure, and also desire for those who follow the body—sons, wife and the like.

Having gone forth from the home, since remaining at home could again produce attachment, he teaches the eight-limbed yoga. “Steadfast” indicates the restraints beginning with celibacy; “sacred pilgrimage places” indicates the observances beginning with bathing. He describes the seat: in a clean, secluded place, properly arranged in order with kuśa grass, a deerskin and cloth. To describe breath control accompanied by recitation, he gives the mantra to be recited: one should mentally practice and repeat the threefold Brahman-syllable, Oṃ, formed from the three sounds beginning with A. To describe withdrawal of the senses, he teaches control of the mind through breath control: one should restrain the mind, having conquered the breath, without forgetting the seed of Brahman, Oṃ.
