He describes withdrawal of the senses: one should restrain the senses. He whose decisive intelligence is the charioteer. He describes concentration: the mind, again pulled away by actions and their latent tendencies, should be fixed on the auspicious form of Bhagavān.

He describes meditation with “there.” “One” means one limb at a time. “Uninterrupted” means not separated from the complete form. General stabilization of the mind upon a particular support is concentration; contemplation of the limbs one by one gives it firmness, and this is meditation. He describes samādhi: having joined and steadied the mind, making it devoid of an object, one makes it assume only the form of flashing supreme bliss; then it becomes peaceful.

When disturbance occurs again because of the guṇas, one should make concentration firm: restrain one’s mind, agitated by rajas and bewildered by tamas. “Produced by that” means produced by rajas and tamas.
When this is practiced, seeing an auspicious, happiness-filled support or object, love for that very object arises.
“As” and “where” concern the questions about the particular duties to be performed in each specific circumstance.
The answer to “as” is “having conquered the seat.” He describes the object in the following half-verse, beginning with “the gross.”
The special object is the Virāṭ body, even grosser than the gross. It is merely the effect.

Although this is an indication and an object of meditation, in reality the Virāṭ is Bhagavān Himself, the controller of the living being. Within the cosmic egg is the bowl-like enclosure; earth is its covering, followed by water, fire, air, ether, ego and the mahat-tattva—seven [coverings].

With the intention that one should worship by superimposing nondifference among the Virāṭ body, its living being and its indwelling controller, he says: “Pātāla is the base of the foot,” the underside of the foot. Pātāla and the other regions are assigned as His limbs. The seven subterranean regions, beginning below and ending with Atala, are taught by scripture. The heel and the toes are the rear and front portions of the foot.
Vitala is to be understood as the lower part of the two thighs and Atala as their upper part. The navel itself is the lake.
“The mass of light” means heaven, the collection of luminaries. The sages call Maharloka the neck, Tapoloka the forehead, and Satyaloka the highest head.

“The rays” are the gods, because their bodies are made of light; they are said to be the arms. The directions, whose presiding deities are the deities of hearing, are the ears, the support of the sense of hearing. Sound is its object, and the ear is its sense. The same is to be understood for the nose and the other organs. Nāsatya and Dasra, the two Aśvinī Kumāras, are the nostrils. “Kindled” means radiant.

The sky is the intermediate space. The two eyes are the eyeballs; sight is the sense; the sun is the bird that moves through the sky. The two days are day and night. The seat of Parameṣṭhī is Brahmā’s station. The palate is the support, and the tongue is the sense.

“The meters” are the Vedas. The head is the aperture of Brahman. The traces of affection are the slight remnants of affection for sons and the like. “Twice-born” means the teeth; the neuter form is archaic. “The endless creation” means the immeasurable creation, which is His glance.
The back of Him is the path of irreligion. Ka is Prajāpati. Mitra and Varuṇa are the two friends.
He whose power is infinite. “Age” is time, and its movement is the passage of time. The flow of the guṇas is the saṃsāra of living beings; their karma is His play.
“The All” means the all-pervading Lord. The unmanifest is primordial nature. The well-known moon is His mind. It is like a sheath, serving as the support of all transformations.
“The power of knowledge” is the mind-stuff. “Mahī” is the mahat-tattva. The inner organ is ego. Girīśa is Śrī Rudra. The animal born from a mare and a she-ass is the mule.

“Birds” means birds. His grammar is the skill of articulating names and forms, as stated in the Vedic text. As they say: “By whom swans were made white, parrots green, and peacocks variegated—he will provide your livelihood.”

Brahman, the brāhmaṇa, is His mouth; the kṣatriya is His arms; the vaiśya is His thighs; the śūdra, dark in complexion and dependent upon the feet, is His feet. The deities bearing various names, together with their hosts such as the Vasus and Rudras, are the materials for the sacrifice; the sacrificial rite, accomplished through those materials, is the action that must be performed.
This is the extent of the arrangement, the configuration of the limbs. Liberation-seekers fix their minds upon it with their own intelligence, because nothing exists outside it.

Thus meditation upon the nondifference of the Virāṭ body, its living being and the Lord was taught for steadiness of mind. He now determines that the body and living being are to be dissolved into the Lord, and that He alone is to be meditated upon: He by whom everything experienced through all mental functions is experienced, He alone is the inner Self of all. One should worship Him alone as reality and not become attached to anything else, because attachment causes the fall of the self into saṃsāra. An example of one person seeing everything through the senses of many is a dreamer seeing the people of a dream; similarly, the Lord is not bound because He is the power of knowledge.

Then, in the Second [Canto], after meditation on the gross [form], the mind having been conquered, it is said that it should be fixed on Viṣṇu, the witness of all and the Lord of all.

Thus the Vairāja meditation having a visible support has been described; here the meditation on the inner controller accomplished by it is stated.

Here, for now, he states the intermediate fruit of the previously mentioned meditation with “thus.” By that meditation, from satisfied Hari, Brahmā, having regained the remembrance of creation that had been lost before, at the time of dissolution, created this universe as it had been before the dissolution. He whose intelligence is resolute—therefore his vision is unfailing. Thus, through that meditation, the power to create the universe arises.

The meaning is that Brahmā, having obtained from pleased Hari the memory of the creation that had been lost at the time of dissolution, created this universe as it was before the dissolution.

Even one who is detached from the fruit of worship has eligibility for meditation on the pure self. Therefore, for the sake of dispassion, he censures all the fruit of action. The “sound-made Brahman” is the Veda. Its “path” is this way of understanding the fruit of action. What is it? By meaningless names alone—such as heaven—the practitioner’s intelligence meditates and makes the respective desires.

He states its meaninglessness itself: on a path made of māyā, lying as if asleep through the impression of happiness, seeing dreams and wandering, he does not obtain the objects. Even having reached that world, he does not attain blameless happiness; that is the meaning.

Then, anticipating the objection that, if the fruit of action were entirely abandoned, the body would immediately fall, he says this. “Therefore the wise person in names alone”: in names alone, whose need is only as much as is necessary for maintaining the body, he should be such a person. “Not heedless”: unattached even to that much. “Firm in understanding”: one who is certain that this is not happiness. Even then, when that need is accomplished in another way, seeing the labor involved in the effort there, he should not strive.

He explains accomplishment otherwise with two [verses], beginning with “when there is.” “Of a kaśipu” means of a bed. When the arm is naturally available, what need is there for head-rests? “In many ways” means in many kinds; “with the food-vessel” means with a vessel for eating.

“But the existence of the directions means simply nakedness; bark, food, water and a dwelling—how could these be obtained without the effort of begging?” To this he replies. “Barks” means pieces of cloth. “Those who support others” are the trees that nourish with fruits and the like. “Caves” are mountain ravines.

“But if sometimes these are unavailable, what is to be done?” To this he replies: does Ajita, Hari, not protect those who have approached and taken shelter? The word “what” is connected with the preceding [questions] as well. “By wealth”: he who is intoxicated by it; “blind”: those whose discrimination is destroyed.

“What then should he do?” Hari is to be served, he says: thus, being detached, he should worship Him. The reasons for His being worthy of worship are these: He is naturally established in one’s own mind. Because He is the self, He is therefore dear. And service of one who is dear is happiness itself. “Reality” means what is real, not false like the not-self. “Bhagavān” means endowed with qualities worthy of worship; He is also endless and eternal. Being of this nature, He should be worshiped.

“Of fixed meaning” means one whose true nature is certain. Being satisfied by the bliss of experiencing Him, his nature as happiness in itself is shown. Moreover, in that worship there is cessation, destruction, of ignorance, the cause of saṃsāra.

He strengthens this very point by censuring other thought: “who?” Neglecting that transcendental contemplation of the Supreme Hari, who, apart from materialistic animals, dull through action, would engage in thought of the nonpermanent? As the śruti says: “This one alone is an animal of the gods.” Seeing the people fallen into Vaitaraṇī, and there undergoing the afflictions born of their own actions, beginning with those pertaining to the self, who would do so? Vaitaraṇī is the river situated at the gate of Yama; saṃsāra is Vaitaraṇī because it is similar to it.

He states that same meditation, with its qualifications, in six [verses], beginning with “some.” Within one’s own body, in the heart; in the space that is there, residing. “Prādeśa” is the span between the index finger and the thumb; that alone is the measure, and therefore the measure of the heart is figuratively spoken of there. “Kañja” means lotus. “Rathāṅga” means wheel.

The śruti says: “The Person measuring a thumb, standing in the middle within the self” [Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.1.12]. In both passages, what is intended is the subtlety of the all-pervading [Lord] in relation to the lotus of the heart.

“Lotus” means a lotus; likewise, clear and wide are the eyes of Him whose eyes are so. The saffron filaments of a kadamba flower are yellow; likewise yellow are the garments of Him whose garments are so. Those golden armlets on which great jewels shine belong to Him. And those great jewels shine; His crown and earrings are made of them.

“Blooming” means opened. The whorl of the lotus of the heart is itself the abode, the place, and in that [place]. The lotus feet of Him whose feet have been placed there by the lords of yoga. “Śrī” itself is the mark, the sign; He is endowed with it. The possessive suffix na, expressing the meaning of possession, is prescribed after pāma and the like. He whose Kaustubha jewel is on the neck. He who is covered and pervaded by a forest garland, through the unfading beauty that is His.
The face that shines through a smile, on a countenance beautified by curls distinguished by smoothness and the like, is lovely.

Through that playful smile, which is not dejected but generous, and through the eyebrow movements that arise in that glance, abundant grace is indicated by Him. He is appearing through meditation, made of thought.

He states this very meditation with “one by one.” “He should experience” means he should meditate. Whatever limb—from the feet, ankles and so forth—has appeared by being conquered without effort, leaving that limb aside, he should hold and meditate on the next, the shank, knee and so forth. The intellect is purified in that [limb], or it becomes steady there.

“Purified” also means that the intellect abandons its attachment to sense objects.

He states that this meditation is an element of the previously mentioned Vairāja meditation with “as long as.” “The higher” are Brahmā and the rest; “the lower” are those from whom [the Lord is] higher. Why? Because He is the Lord of the universe, the seer, and not the seen, being a mass of consciousness. “Devotional service” is characterized by love. “At the end of action” means after performing the necessary duties. By this it is said that action too extends only up to devotional service. “Attentive” means devoted to the observance of the rule.

Thus, the duty of a person approaching death has been stated. Now he states the duty of that same person who desires to abandon the body himself, with four and a half verses beginning “steady.”

“O King,” when a renunciant of this nature desires to abandon this body, this world, then he should not attach the mind to a place, a sacred region, or to a time, such as the northern course of the sun. He should not become attached. For place and time are not causes of success for a yogin; Yoga alone is. Having become firmly certain of this, he should take up a steady and comfortable seat and control the life airs; that is the meaning.

Having restrained the mind, which has taken an object, by the decisive intelligence, and made it solely that, he should dissolve this intelligence into the field-knower, the witness of the intelligence and the rest. He should dissolve that field-knower into the pure Self, and that purified Self—thinking “I alone am the Self”—into pure Brahman, uniting it there. Having attained tranquility, he should cease from action, because there is nothing higher to attain.

He states this with “where.” In the essential nature of the Self, time has no power to do anything. Therefore even the gods are not powerful there: if time, the superior lord of the gods who do not blink, has no power, how could the gods have power? What, then, of living beings, the worlds governed by the gods? He says “of the worlds.” The reason they have no power is the absence of limiting adjuncts. Alternatively, even the causes of the world do not have power over Him at the beginning of creation. “Transformation” means ego.

He explains why there are no limiting adjuncts with “supreme.” Because they wish to abandon the false selfhood of the body and the like, saying “not this, not this,” they embrace in their hearts at every moment the feet of the worshipful Śrī Viṣṇu and have affection for no other. Therefore they declare that state of Viṣṇu to be supreme, highest in every respect.

Therefore, established in Brahman in this way, the sage should cease. The word “but” distinguishes him from the person who departs with desire. “Knowledge” is scripture, by which knowledge is born; its power destroys the desire for objects. He now describes the method of abandoning the body: pressing the root of the body with the base of the foot, he should restrain the anus and raise the vital air upward, having conquered fatigue, through the six places beginning with the navel.

He should raise it from the navel, situated in the Maṇipūraka, and place it in the heart, the Anāhata chakra; then in the chest, the Viśuddha chakra situated below the throat. “Self-controlled” means one who has conquered the mind. He should then take it to the root of his own palate, the forward part of that chakra. Because movement through that region can occur in many ways, the word “slowly” is used.

The space between the eyebrows is the Ājñā chakra. He whose seven passages—the ears, eyes, nostrils, mouth and the rest—are closed. Having no concern for anything else and having attained supreme Brahman, he should, at the crown of the head, break through the aperture of Brahman and release the body and the senses.

If he is intending to go to the station of Parameṣṭhī, Brahmā, or to the playground of the sky-traveling Siddhas, where are the eight sovereignties such as aṇimā, all within the aggregate of the guṇas, the universe, he goes everywhere. At the time of abandoning the body he should not abandon the mind and senses, but should go with them for enjoyment in that corresponding world.

Because the path of yoga is not limited like the course produced by karma, they describe the movement of the Lords of Yoga within and outside the three worlds, in Maharloka and the other regions, and outside the universe. The reason is that their subtle bodies are within the vital air. Their destination is that of those who worship knowledge, meaning meditation; austerity, meaning the dharma of Bhagavān; the eight-limbed yoga; and samādhi, meaning knowledge.

He describes that path with eight verses beginning “Vaiśvānara.” Traveling through the sky, on the path leading to Brahma-loka, he first reaches Vaiśvānara, the deity identified with fire. By what means? Through the Suṣumṇā channel, which extends even outside the body. By its fiery light he is freed from impurity, without becoming attached anywhere. He reaches the star situated above, belonging to Hari and presided over by Nārāyaṇa, then the Śiśumāra constellation described in the Fifth Canto, and proceeds through the stations beginning with the sun and ending with Dhruva.

That is Viṣṇu’s wheel, the Śiśumāra. It is the navel of the universe, the support of the sun and the other luminaries. Having crossed it, the one who has a pure subtle body alone reaches Maharloka, the station of knowers of Brahman, honored by the others, because beyond it ordinary heavenly beings have no further course. There dwell the sages, such as Bhṛgu, whose lives last for a great cosmic age.

Then, afterward, at the end of the cosmic age, seeing the three worlds being intensely burned, he proceeds to the station of Parameṣṭhī, which lasts for two parārdhas. It is filled with aerial cars enjoyed by perfected lords. “U” indicates excellence.

He explains that there is no sorrow, fear or mental pain there except for Him. What suffering arises? Through compassion, beings who do not know the meditation on Bhagavān see the endless suffering of birth. Among those who reach Brahma-loka there are three destinations: those who arrive through an abundance of merit become administrators in a later cosmic age according to the gradation of their merit; those who arrive through worship of Hiraṇyagarbha and the like are liberated with Brahmā; and those who worship Bhagavān break through the universe by their own will and ascend to the Vaikuṇṭha destination.

He now describes the method by which the devotee who is presented in this context pierces the universe. The process is as follows: from the nature presided over by the Lord arises mahat; from it ego; from ego, through the subtle element of sound, space; through touch, air; through form, fire; through taste, water; and through smell, earth. These combined elements form the Virāṭ body of fourteen worlds. Its earth covering, the cosmic shell, is fifty crore yojanas across according to one reading; other coverings, formed from the succeeding elements, are each ten times larger, and the eighth, the covering of nature, is all-pervading. Having attained each succeeding element and the identity of Earth through the subtle body, he proceeds without fear of “How shall I go?” With that self in the form of earth he enters the contiguous waters, without haste, enjoying as he wishes because he has no fear of wetness or burning. He then becomes luminous and, when enjoyment ends, reaches the great Self; alternatively, the Vedic word is its measure.

He describes crossing the subtle elements and their objects. Through the presiding sense of smell he enters smell; through the breath, touch; he enters the quality of space, sound; and through the vital air, together with each corresponding active sense, he enters intention, the respective action.

Having described crossing the gross and subtle elements, he now describes attaining mahat by reaching the ego that forms their covering. The yogī reaches the knowledge-principle after dissolving the ego. The ego is the source of diverse effects and is threefold—tāmasa, rājasa and sāttvika. From the tāmasa ego arise the inert subtle elements; from the rājasa arise the ten outward-turned senses; from the sāttvika arise the mind and the deities of the senses. These dissolve into their respective forms of ego; through that process the ego reaches the mahat-tattva, and then he reaches primordial nature, where the guṇas are restrained and dissolved.

With that self in the form of primordial nature, becoming blissful, at the end of the limiting adjuncts he reaches the peaceful, unchanging supreme Self, which is bliss. “He does not become attached” means that he does not return.

“Paths” means two routes or methods. O king, the immediate liberation described as “having broken through the crown, he releases [the body] after reaching the Supreme,” and the gradual liberation described by “if he is proceeding,” are the two paths. These paths are taught by the Veda, not invented by the author. The question asked by you concerned both routes in the matter of liberation; the southern path is also implied by the request to state the opposite. Thus these are the two paths you asked about.

There are many paths of liberation for a person wandering in saṃsāra, such as austerity and yoga, but this alone is the proper one: from the practice of devotional yoga there is no other auspicious path that is joyful and free from obstacles.

“Bhagavān” here means Brahmā. “Unchanging” means free from modification, and he was one-pointed in mind. Having examined the Veda completely three times, he determined only that in which love for Hari arises.

One might ask, “Love arises from an experienced object; how can there be love for Bhagavān, who has not been experienced?” He answers: Bhagavān is perceived through one’s own Self as the knower of the field and the indwelling controller. By what means? Through the visible objects such as the intellect. He establishes this in two ways: scriptural indications show that the perception of inert objects cannot occur without the self-luminous inner witness, and inference shows that the intellect and the other faculties, being instruments like an axe, are employed by an agent. The existence of the independent agent, Īśvara, is thereby established.
With “therefore” he concludes the answers to the questions beginning “what should be heard” and so forth.

He illustrates the fruit of hearing and the rest: the topics of the Lord, who shines as the very Self of the good, are nectar. They purify the mind, which has been polluted by sense objects, and lead one to the vicinity of His lotus feet, the feet of Śrī Viṣṇu.

In the Third [chapter], the excellence among Viṣṇu’s devotees is [described] for those hearing the sage; through an upsurge of devotion, reverent hearing of those acts is spoken.

Now, in order to state that the worship of other deities too has only a trifling fruit, like the worship of sons and the like, and is therefore to be abandoned, he repeats what was previously said with “thus.” “Me” means me. At some time, by the arrangement of fate, among living beings who have obtained human birth, among those who are thoughtful, and even among those who are dying, especially for these, this hearing of Hari’s topics and the like has been prescribed; that is the meaning.
“Brahmaṇaspati” is Brahmā, the lord of the Veda. One desiring acuity of the senses should worship Indra. One desiring progeny should worship the Prajāpatis, Dakṣa and the rest.
“Māyā” is Durgā. “Vibhāvasu” is fire. One desiring wealth is a seeker of wealth. “Power” means influence; one desiring that, being powerful, should worship the Rudras.

“Food and the like” means food that is to be eaten and chewed. “The sons of Aditi” are the twelve Ādityas. One desiring the independence of the subjects dwelling in the countries should worship the Sādhyas.
“Ilā” is the earth. “Stability” means not falling from one’s position. “Rodasī” means heaven and earth.
The Apsarās, and Urvaśī among them.

“Yajña” is Viṣṇu, qualified by sacrifice. “Treasury” is the accumulation of wealth. Here “one desiring wealth” differs in meaning by referring to wealth alone. “Conjugal relation” is mutual affection; that alone is the object of one for whom it is the purpose.

“The object of dharma” means one desiring dharma. “The Supreme Lord” is Viṣṇu, qualified by the highest praise. “Extending the thread” means seeking an increase of offspring. “Protection” is the removal of obstacles; one desiring that should worship the Puṇyajanas, the Yakṣas. “Strength” is power; one desiring that should worship the gods, the groups of Maruts.

“Kingdom” means kingship; one desiring that should worship the Manus, the gods who protect the Manvantaras. The kingdom that is the king’s activity—one desiring that should worship the Viśvadevas; this is the distinction. “Seeking victory over an enemy” means desiring the enemy’s death; one should worship Nirṛti, a demon. “Desiring desire” means desiring enjoyment. “Without desire” means desiring dispassion. “The Supreme Person” is the Lord, qualified by being distinct from Prakṛti.
“Without desire” means an exclusive devotee. Or, one who has all desires, stated and unstated, should worship the complete, unqualified Person.

By the worship of Indra and the other deities, through their respective worship, the fruit of devotional service is also stated through connection and difference. In this life, for those worshipping Indra and the others, by that respective worship, association with devotees of the Bhāgavata arises, and from that association an unwavering disposition toward Bhagavān, devotion, arises. This alone is the development, the gain, of the highest good, the supreme human aim. Everything else is trifling; that is the meaning.

“Through connection and difference” means through the distinctness of the relation. In the worship of each deity, the attainment of the particular fruit stated for that deity is “difference.” Through worship of each deity, destruction of sin gives association with the Bhāgavatas, and through that association unwavering devotion to Bhagavān arises; this is “connection”—a slight explanation. Or, connection and difference arise because one thing has both functions. Just as, in the statement “the sacrificial post is of khadira; for one desiring strength it is of khadira,” the one khadira post is both an element of the sacrifice and a means of strength, so here worship of the various deities is both a means of their respective fruits and a means of the fruit of devotion to Hari. Since it is a means for both fruits, Indra and the others should be worshipped with the desire for Hari’s devotion, not with another desire; that is the purport of the whole. Thus the cowherd maidens worshipped Kātyāyanī with the desire for Kṛṣṇa.

By “association with the Bhāgavatas” he praises the relish for Hari’s topics that is indicated: “knowledge.” In those narratives knowledge arises. What kind of knowledge? That from which the whirlpool, the mass of the waves of the qualities such as attachment, is withdrawn on every side. Moreover, immediately thereafter, self-satisfaction arises; and in those [narratives] non-attachment to the qualities, the objects, is the cause of serenity of mind. In the reading “in both,” non-attachment to the qualities exists here and in the next world. The path approved as liberation itself is devotional service. One is satisfied by the pleasure of hearing—or, alternatively, one is not satisfied elsewhere. Who would not develop relish for those narratives of Hari?

From “association with the Bhāgavatas,” the attainment of Hari’s topics is understood. The word “and the like” includes birth, death, grief, delusion, hunger and thirst. “Whirlpool” means falling again and again.
“Spoken” means said. “Ṛṣi” means one who sees the Supreme Brahman. “Kavi” means one thoroughly versed in the sound-Brahman.
The cause of the desire to hear is this: let there be, in the assembly of the devotees, those narratives in which the discussion of Hari itself is the later fruit.
He elaborates this with two [verses], beginning with “he indeed.” [He is] the one who accepted play in the form of worship of Kṛṣṇa and the like.
There are noble and expansive topics because of the qualities of Urugāya.

With the intention, “Make the life that is being wasted fruitful through Hari’s topics,” he speaks in three verses beginning “life.” The sun rises, sets and moves onward; whatever moment is spent apart from Hari’s topics, it steals away as [wasted] lifespan.

One might ask, “Is living itself not the fruit of their lifespan?” He answers: they are like trees. One might say, “They have no breath.” Then they are bellows, leather bags. One might say, “They have no food and the like.” He answers: they do not eat. “They do not urinate or engage in sexual union—is that so?” Even animals in human form are [like this].

He describes them as comparable to dogs and the rest. Their ears have never received [the Lord’s name]. Because of their contempt for sacred things they are like dogs; because of their attachment to impure objects they are like village pigs; because of their attachment to painful objects, like thorns, they are like camels; and because they carry burdens, they are like asses.

He says in five verses that their limbs too are fruitless. Alas! The ears of a person who does not hear are merely empty holes. If his tongue does not sing [the Lord’s name], it is a false and wicked tongue, like that of a frog.

If a head adorned with a cloth turban and crown does not bow, it is merely a burden. The two hands are like the hands of a corpse. The wrists on which golden bracelets shine are [also useless]. “Also” indicates the other limbs as well.
The eyes that do not behold the forms of Viṣṇu are like peacock feathers. They take birth like trees, meaning that their eyes are comparable to tree roots.
“Does not obtain” means does not approach, touch or hold. “The foot of Śrī Viṣṇu” means that which is attached to Śrī Viṣṇu’s foot. “Does not smell” means does not inhale its fragrance and rejoice.
One whose core, strength and hardness are like stone. He now describes the bodily transformation: the hair rising on the body is the manifestation of joy.
All this is futile for one without devotion. You speak what is dear and agreeable to the mind; therefore, having been properly asked, tell us what the son of Vyāsa said to the king.

In the Fourth [chapter], what was asked by Parīkṣit—the creation and the rest, the acts of Hari—is described by Śuka through the dialogue of Brahmā and his son.

To relate the king’s question, he states his former condition in four [verses]. “Of Vyāsa’s son” means of Śuka. Having understood his words, from which there is this determination of the truth of the self: “Kṛṣṇa alone is to be served, not another”—of this nature was his faithful concentration.
“Self” means the body. “Animals” means elephants and the like.
This very meaning, characterized by the pastimes of Hari.

“Death” means dissolution. “Threefold” means chiefly consisting of dharma, artha and kāma. Having renounced it, abandoned the state of identifying with the body, and having attained, through supreme love, the state of having Bhagavān as his self, he asked.
The darkness, ignorance, belonging to me is destroyed as you, being good and truthful, speak. Therefore [your speech is] correct.
I wish to know again. How He creates this inconceivable, unreasoned universe.

He protects; He maintains. He withdraws; He dissolves. “Many powers” means one who possesses many powers. “Playing, as He does,” He transforms Himself, making Himself manifold in forms beginning with Brahmā.
How the one Person takes up the qualities of Prakṛti—simultaneously, in the form of a Person, through births in incarnations beginning with Brahmā, or successively.
“Doubtful” means uncertain. You are thoroughly versed in sound-Brahman, the Veda, through investigation, and in the Supreme through experience.
“Invited” means requested. “He began” means that he performed the preliminary act in the form of obeisance to the deity and the guru, and so forth.

He states this very [obeisance] in thirteen [verses]. “To the Supreme” means to the highest of all. The reason is: to the greatly glorious One of immeasurable majesty. He displays that [majesty]. To Him by whom, through the play that is the cause of the origination and so forth of the existent universe, the triad of powers beginning with rajas is assumed in the forms beginning with Brahmā. To the inner being, the inner controller, for entering within. Therefore, because He is within all, His path is imperceptible.

“Imperceptible” means difficult to know even by yogins.

Remembering that He bestows varied fruits, he bows. Again, obeisance. To the cutter of the distress of the good, those who follow dharma, the destroyer of suffering. For the wicked, those whose conduct is adharma, [He is] the cause of their non-arising. To the form of all existence—meaning, the giver of the respective fruits in the forms of the respective deities and so forth. Or, “to the form of complete existence.” “Again” states the distinction from both previously mentioned.

The word “again,” which conveys restriction, excludes connection with another: He gives to these alone, not to others. Another reading is “again also.”

To the foremost protector of the Sātvatas, the devotees. For whom even a distant direction is far away from bad yogins, those devoid of devotion; that is the meaning, [that He is] difficult to know. Thus, even though inequality is perceived, he states His inconceivable majesty in order to establish His freedom from fault. His equality and superiority are negated; with respect to Him no other has equality or superiority. To Him who, through that majesty, enjoys Himself in His own abode, Brahman, His own nature.

“Ṛṣabha” means one who makes knowledge shine and illumines it.

Remembering the superiority of devotion over all means, he bows with the two [verses] beginning “whose glorification.” “Worship” means offering worship. To Him whose fame, heard of, is auspicious and auspicious in meaning.
The discerning and wise, by approaching and serving his feet, cast away attachment in both this world and the next, and are freed from fatigue and effort.

Showing the failure of all practices for those devoid of devotion, he bows: the thoughtful yogīs, whose conduct is auspicious, [gain nothing] without offering austerity and the other practices to Him. The repetition of “whose fame is auspicious” indicates the primacy of hearing His glories and the like.

He shows that devotion is the cause of supreme purification. Those born in sinful groups, such as Kirātas, and others who are sinful by action become purified when they take shelter of the Bhāgavatas, the devotees who have taken refuge in Him. He removes the doubt that this is impossible with “the Powerful One,” meaning one who is able to accomplish it.

Remembering that He is worshiped by all, he prays: He is the Self of those who know the Self, and is to be worshiped as the Self. The qualifications “made of the three Vedas” and the like indicate that He is to be worshiped according to the respective paths. May that Lord be pleased—He whose form is a sign to be seen with supreme wonder by sincere, guileless devotees.
Remembering that He protects all, he says: He is the protector in every danger.

Remembering that He bestows knowledge, he says in two verses beginning “whose feet.” Meditation upon His feet itself is samādhi, by which one is purified. According to one’s inclination, this may be with distinctions such as with attributes or without attributes; alternatively, “ruc” means radiance, and “according to one’s mind” is the meaning.

Formerly, at the beginning of the cosmic age, while the Unborn was extending creation in His heart, Sarasvatī, inspired by Him, arose from His mouth. She possesses her own distinctive characteristics, those taught in grammar and the other disciplines. He is the foremost of sages, the giver of knowledge.

He now prays that He adorn his own words, which delight the listeners and possess the beauty of love, compassion and the other sentiments. Suspecting that one person’s words cannot adorn another’s, he reveals that the Lord is the inner controller of all words. Having created these bodies from the great elements, He dwells within them as the indwelling controller. Scripture establishes the designation “Puruṣa” for Him. He enjoys, illuminates or protects the sixteen elements—the eleven senses and five elements. The middle voice is archaic. The reason is that He is the Self, the conscious knower, of the sixteen; he is not being described here as a finite living being, since that would contradict the prayer.
He bows to Śrī Vyāsa. “Gentle” means the devotees; he is the one whose lotus mouth is a source of nectar.
He now introduces the dialogue of Brahmā and Nārada as the answer to the questions. The Vedas were present in His womb at the time of creation. He speaks what Hari directly said.

In the Fifth [chapter], the unborn one, questioned by Nārada, speaks of creation and the rest, the pastimes of Hari, and the Virāṭ creation, through the powers beginning with time and action.

It has been said that the Veda-wombed one spoke to Nārada, who asks; there he states Nārada’s question—“O Lord of lords.” O generator of beings, therefore O beginningless first ancestor of all, know that knowledge which is a means [of knowing] because by it one knows. “Cause to know specifically” is the meaning. What kind? That by which the truth of the self is seen very clearly.

Note: The meaning of the causative affix ṇic is included.

The universe, which is in the position of an indication, is itself the means of knowledge of the self; therefore he asks its particular distinctions. “What form” means by which it is formed, manifested. “What foundation” means what support. “From which” means by which it is created. “In which established” means in which it dissolves. “What higher” means under which it is subject. “And what” means what its self is. Or, [he asks] what it is from its own existent cause—that is the meaning. Speak its truth, its reality, factually.

To say “I do not know” is not to be said; thus he says “all.” “What has been” means what has been born; “what will be” means what will be born; “what is” means what is being born. You are their lord; therefore [all] is ascertained by specific knowledge, determined.

Let this [discussion] be; first of all, he says, “tell only yourself.” “From which knowledge” means “who is the giver of knowledge to you?” “What support” means “what is your shelter?” “What higher” means “under whose control are you?” “What self” means “what is your nature?” But my understanding is that you alone are the independent Supreme Lord. Yet, because of your undertaking austerity, I ask through doubt [of one higher]; thus he says with four and a half [verses]. “One” means without assistance.

“In the self” means you manifest, protect, in yourself, yourself not causing them to be defeated [by another], without fatigue, without exertion. Just as a spider creates, relying on its own power alone, so.

Note: He caused them to be manifested so that their defeat by another would not occur. The meaning is: his desire is unfailing.

Therefore, in this universe I do not know anything superior, highest; inferior, lowest; or equal, middle. Even among these, [there are] names such as human and so on, forms, and qualities such as being two-footed and being white; by these they are to be brought about. Even there, I do not know anything whatsoever, eternal or non-eternal, gross or subtle, from another; rather, I think everything comes from you alone.
Even though you are of such a kind, you performed austerity; by that you cause us pain, bewilder us. Because you give rise to doubt of a higher [lord], doubt of another Lord.
As I, instructed, taught by you, understand, so please know and cause [me] to know it specifically.

He praises the question. “O son! O child! This question of yours, preceded by doubt, is proper”—this is the meaning. Because this question is from you who are compassionate. Here is the reason: by which I have been engaged in displaying the higher dharma and manifesting the prowess of Bhagavān. Therefore, although you are desirous of knowing, you have shown compassion only to me—that is the meaning.

Indeed, through “you alone create beings” and the like, I said that you alone are Bhagavān. It is true; your speech, in which you proclaim me to possess lordship, is not entirely false. For, because I possess this much being and power, you see in me this much greatness. But you speak without knowing the Lord who is higher than me. Thus, through resemblance, this is your delusion, not a deliberate falsehood—that is the meaning. Or, the construction is: because you do not know Him, the Lord higher than me, you say that I am this much.

Then, when it is expected [to ask], “Who is that Lord?”, while bowing to Him with devotion, he states Him in three [verses]. “By whose own radiance”: I manifest what has already been illumined, made manifest, by His own radiance, making it manifest through creation. Just as the sun and the rest illuminate only what is illumined by consciousness. And the śruti says:

“There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and stars; these lightnings do not shine—how then this fire? Him alone shining, everything else shines after Him; by His light all this shines.”

Note: Just as the sun and the rest, illumined by Him, illuminate the respective [things] only by His power—that is the meaning.

To Him [I offer] obeisance; we meditate. To Him by whose māyā, being deluded, those such as you call me the teacher of the world and the cause of the world.

Note: “We meditate obeisance” means “we perform obeisance with the mind.”

At the statement “by whose māyā,” having stated its connection with māyā and its invincibility, he says, “What saṃsāra can there be for Him? None.” “She knows my deception”: because she is ashamed to stand in whose field of vision, this māyā, not performing her own function in Him, deludes those beginning with us, whose intellects are bad, whose knowledge is covered by ignorance; they alone babble, praise themselves. By this the answer to the question “what is its form?” has been given.

Note: The meaning is: even for the Supreme Lord.

Thus, having defined the Supreme Lord other than himself, now, in order to state the answer to the nine questions beginning “what is the foundation”—He alone is all, beginning with the foundation—he states the nonexistence of another apart from Him: “the substance.” “Substance” means the great elements in their form as material cause. Action is the cause of birth. Time is that which agitates it. Nature is the cause of its transformation. The living being is the enjoyer. There is no other object apart from Vāsudeva, because an effect is not separate from its cause.

He elaborates that in two [verses]. [The Vedas are] those for which Nārāyaṇa is the supreme cause. By this very teaching that He is the source of scripture, His being Īśvara, and omniscience and the rest, is established as authoritative. The gods too are born from His limbs; therefore they are not different from Him. The worlds, beginning with heaven, are portions of His bliss. The sacrifices are means for attaining Him.

“Yoga” means breath control and the other practices. “Austerity” is the one-pointedness of mind produced by them. “Knowledge” is the result produced by them, and “destination” is their fruit. By this it has been stated that everything is dependent upon Him.
When asked, “What do you do?” he answers: Although He created me, I create what is to be created by Him. I create by His glance. The reasons are given by “of the seer” and the following words.

One might ask, “Why is there this distinction between the living being and the Lord, so that you are impelled and He is the impeller?” He gives the cause of that distinction in three verses. Even the Lord, who is without qualities, is said in the following verse to be bound by these three qualities. How are they characterized? They are taken up by māyā through His own independence for the purposes of maintenance and the rest.

Although in reality the Lord is always liberated, where and by what do the living being, the person who is the subject of māyā, become bound? By the effect, called adhibhūta; the cause, called adhyātma; and the doer, called adhidaiva—their essential relation. The substance is the great elements; “knowledge” means the deities; “action” means the senses. They bind by their respective identifications and by the supports that are their causes.

Therefore He is controlled by māyā through these guṇa-born signs, the limiting adjuncts that cover the living beings. His course and essential nature are very difficult to perceive; alternatively, His course is perceived only by His own devotees.
He describes the method of His creation. “Karma” means the unseen result belonging to the living being. Desiring to become manifold, He desired to manifest in various forms.

“Intermingling of the guṇas” means their agitation and abandonment of equilibrium. “By nature” means transformation into another form. “Puruṣa” means the Lord, and His presiding over the three is the common qualification. “Mahat” means the mahat-tattva.

From mahat-tattva, which is transforming, the threefold ego arises. Although it too is threefold, rajas and sattva are prominent in it because of the powers of action and knowledge; in ego, which covers, tamas predominates. Therefore among the effects of ego, the tamasic elements beginning with space are numerous, while the rajasic and sāttvika effects are fewer. The same predominance of tamas is found in living beings covered by those adjuncts.

As it transforms and takes another form, he describes its three divisions: vaikārika is sāttvika, and taijasa is rājasika. The characteristics of the three are stated in reverse order: the power in matter, the power in action, and the power in knowledge. O Lord, You are able to know.

“Bhūtādi” qualifies the tamasic [ego]. It is well known that sound first arises from the tamasic ego; sound, however, is the subtle form of space, and its distinctive quality is produced through sound, meaning that space arises through the subtle element of sound. The same is to be understood for touch and the other elements. Sound is a sign: if someone cries “Elephant!” from behind a wall, the sound gives knowledge both of the elephant that is seen and of the seer who sees it. The neuter form is used because the word qualifies the sign.

Because air is connected with space as its cause, it too possesses sound. Its distinctive mark is vital air, which sustains the body. “Vigor, strength and power” are the excellence of the senses, mind and body; they are the cause of those capacities.

“Arose” means came into being. Fire possesses form in itself and, because air and space are its causes, also possesses touch and sound. Water and earth similarly possess more qualities because of their greater connection with the preceding elements.
“Resonance” means sound.
“The particular” means Earth. Earth possesses more qualities because of its greater connection with the preceding elements.

By the word “mind” the moon, its presiding deity, is also to be understood. The other ten deities are the vaikārika, the effects of sāttvika ego. The five presiding deities of the ear, skin, eyes, tongue and nose are the directions, air, the sun, Varuṇa and the Aśvinī Kumāras. The five presiding deities of speech, hands, feet, the anus and the generative organ are Fire, Indra, Upendra, Mitra and Prajāpati.

Because intellect, the power of knowledge, and vital air, the power of action, are effects of the taijasa ego, the senses, whose special forms are knowledge and action, also arise from taijasa ego. He lists them: ear, skin, eyes, tongue and nose; speech, hands, feet, anus and generative organ. Their order is not intended here.
Having described the creation of causes, he now describes the creation of effects. When these elements were unconnected and unmixed, they were unable to construct the body, the abode.
Then, taking on the principal and subordinate states of primordial nature and its qualities, they formed both the collective and the individual body—the universe.
The living one, the Supreme Self, stood presiding over time, karma and nature, and made the inert conscious, causing it to live.
Having pierced and separated them, he remained distinct. This is the meaning of “having emerged from the root and remained.”

He describes the arrangement of the worlds through His limbs. The waist is the rear portion at the roots of the thighs; the hips are the front and lower portion. Below are the seven worlds beginning with Atala, and above are the seven beginning with Bhūḥ.

He now shows the origin of the social orders. “Brahman” means the brāhmaṇa and is called His mouth, with the intended nondifference of cause and effect; the same applies to “arms.” “Kṣatra” means the kṣatriya.

For the purpose of meditation, he now shows the different arrangements of the worlds and presents the view of seven worlds in two verses. Bhūrloka extends from Pātāla up to the waist, from the feet to the waist.

Because this is for meditation, the reversal of the upper and lower parts in the phrase “from the two breasts” is not a fault. Alternatively, “from the breasts” means from the two lips that produce sound. Brahma-loka, called Vaikuṇṭha, is eternal; it is not within the created universe. A traditional note clarifies that this is Satya-loka, the seventh world above the others.

He now presents the view of the fourteen worlds. There, the seven beginning with Bhūḥ and the others, already mentioned, are [shown] by the hips and the rest; by the waist and the rest he speaks of the seven lower worlds—“in that waist,” in two verses. They are pure because they are residences of devotees of Hari.
He speaks of the view of the three worlds. Bhū-loka is together with Pātāla and the other [lower worlds].

In the Sixth [chapter], the glory of the Virāṭ is spoken according to distinctions beginning with the ādhyātmika and the rest. And everything previously said is strengthened from the Puruṣa-sūkta.

Now the glory of the Vairāja is described in detail. His mouth is the field, the place of origin, of speech—of our speech organs and the rest—and of Fire, its presiding deity. His seven bodily constituents beginning with skin are the field of the seven [metres] beginning with Gāyatrī. Havya is food for the gods. Kavya is food for the fathers. Amṛta is the remainder of both, for human beings. His tongue is the field, the place of origin, of those foods, of all tastes, sixfold beginning with sweet, and, by the word “and,” of our taste organ and Varuṇa, its presiding deity. Thus, everywhere, what has not been stated should be inferred.

Note: “Beginning with” includes Uṣṇih, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, Paṅkti and Bṛhatī.

Note: By “and the rest,” skin, flesh, blood, fat, marrow and bone are included.

Note: By “beginning with,” pungent, bitter, astringent, sour and salty are included.

His two nostrils, the nasal openings, are the supreme place, the excellent field, of all life-breaths beginning with ours. The smelling organ is the supreme abode of common and particular fragrances, moda and pramoda.

The eye organ is [the field] of forms, of lights and of the manifestations of forms. The two eyes are the eye-balls. Everywhere, where [the words] end in the genitive, the nominative [word] should be understood as “field.” The two ears are the seats of the presiding [deities] of hearing. Hearing is the organ.
His limb, his body, is the receptacle and place of the essential parts of things. “Of this” means of His skin, touch and air. [It is] of every sacrifice.

Of the plant-born classes, all trees. Or, only those trees by which sacrifice is properly accomplished. The hair is the field of the clouds, because this was said earlier. The beard is [the field] of lightning. The nails of the feet and hands are [the field] of stones and metals; this is to be inferred from similarity.

Of the acts of protection, [and] of those who perform protection. “Vikrama” is the placing of the foot; it is the āspada, the support, of the worlds beginning with Bhū. Because the words beginning with Bhū are indeclinable, the genitive ending is elided. “Kṣema” is the protection of what has been obtained.

Note: The word “āspada” should be supplied by carrying it over from the next verse.
“Śaraṇa” means protection from fear. Hari’s foot is the support of all desires, of the boon, and also of the choosing of the boon.

“Vīrya” means semen. The penis is its seat. But the upastha is the organ. “The pleasure of procreation” means [pleasure] for the sake of offspring. Sexual union is the cause of the satisfaction, the removal of distress, that comes from it.
The organ of evacuation, of the giving up of feces, is the anus. The rectum is the place of Nirṛti, of misfortune.
The back portion is [the seat] of darkness, of ignorance. The accumulation of bones is [the seat] of the mountains.

“Avyakta” is the Pradhāna. “Rasa” is the essence of food and the like. “Sindhus” are the oceans; [the belly is] of them. [It is also the seat] of dissolution, of laya. The belly is the place, the abode, known by the wise. The heart is the place of the mind, of the subtle body beginning with ours.

Note: “Of dissolution” is a slight explanatory gloss, because at that time everything dissolves there.
“To you” means yours. “Of the Kumāras” means of Sanaka and the others. “Of Bhava” means of Śrī Rudra. The self, the mind, is the supreme abode.

Thus, for the present, the universe born from the Supreme Lord is not different from Him, just as an ornament is not separate from gold. But He is the controller of all and the illuminator of all, and is eternally spoken of; this is the meaning of what was said. He strengthens this very meaning by explaining the meaning of the Puruṣa-sūkta. There, the meaning of the three ṛks beginning “He has a thousand heads” and [the ṛk beginning] “The brāhmaṇa was His mouth” (12) was shown in the previous chapter. He shows the meaning of “the Puruṣa alone is all this” (2) with three and a half [verses], beginning “I am you.” “Those are your elder-born [ones]”—these Sanaka and the others, and Marīci and the others (13). “Those whose abodes are water, land and sky” [are meant]. “Nabhaukas” is an archaic sandhi (14). “All this is indeed the Puruṣa; it is not separate from Him”—this is the meaning (15).

Note: “The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet. Enveloping the earth on every side, He stood beyond it by ten fingers” (1).

“The Puruṣa alone is all this, whatever has been and whatever will be. And He is the Lord of immortality, which grows beyond through food” (2).

“Such is His greatness, and the Puruṣa is greater than this. All beings are one foot of Him; the three-foot [portion] of Him is immortal in heaven” (3).

“Three-footed, the Puruṣa rose above; one foot of Him again became here. From there He spread out over all, over what eats and what does not eat” (4).

“From Him Virāṭ was born; from Virāṭ, the Puruṣa [was born] above. Having been born, He spread beyond, behind and in front of the earth” (5).

“When the gods extended the sacrifice with the Puruṣa as oblation, spring was its ghee, summer the fuel, autumn the offering” (6).

“They sprinkled that sacrifice on the sacred grass, the Puruṣa born at the beginning. With Him the gods, the Sādhyas and the ṛṣis who [were there] sacrificed” (7).

“From that all-offered sacrifice the curdled ghee was gathered; He made those animals, those that are of air, forest and village” (8).

“From that all-offered sacrifice the ṛcs and sāmans were born; the metres were born from it; from it the yajus was born” (9).

“From it horses were born, and whatever animals have [two rows of teeth]. Cows were indeed born from it; from it goats and sheep were born” (10).

“When they divided the Puruṣa, into how many did they arrange Him? What was His mouth? What were His arms? What were called His thighs and feet?” (11).

“The brāhmaṇa was His mouth; the rājanya was made His arms; that which was the vaiśya was His thighs; from His feet the śūdra was born” (12).

“The moon was born from His mind; from His eye the sun arose; from His mouth Indra and Agni [were born]; from His breath Vāyu was born” (13).

“From His navel was the midspace; from His head heaven came to be; from His feet earth; from His hearing the directions; thus they arranged the worlds” (14).

“Seven were the enclosing sticks; thrice seven were made the kindling sticks. Extending the sacrifice for the gods, they bound the Puruṣa as the sacrificial animal” (15).

“With sacrifice the gods sacrificed the sacrifice; those were the first dharmas. Those great ones attained the heaven where the former Sādhyas, the gods, are” (16).

To state His immeasurability in detail, he explains the meaning of “the earth” (1) with “by that Puruṣa.” “World” is the meaning of the word “earth.” “A span” is the meaning of “ten fingers”; “beyond” is the meaning of ati; “covered” is the meaning of vṛt, “having enveloped.” Since He stands pervading more than a span, only excess is intended, not a measurement, because it is inapplicable and because He is unbounded (16).

Note: “Ten fingers” is an indicative expression. It means that He pervades and stands outside the Brahmāṇḍa on every side. “A span” is exactly the object of the words “ten fingers.”

He gives this with an illustrative example. The śruti says: “This breath is the sun,” and “this sun is the breath.” Just as the sun, illuminating its own seat, the disk, also illuminates outside, so Virāṭ, illuminating the body, illuminates the Brahmāṇḍa both within and without.

To show that He is spoken of eternally, he explains the meaning of “of immortality”—“He,” and so on. “Of fearlessness” explains the word “immortality” occurring in the mantra. He explains the word “by food” with a reversal of case-ending. “Mortal” means subject to death; “food” means the fruit of action, because He has crossed beyond it. Therefore He is not only the self of everything, but also the Lord of immortality, of His own bliss—this is the meaning.

Having wondered, “How can the one whose nature is the phenomenal world be spoken of as eternal?” he removes that doubt by explaining “Such is His greatness.” Even the greatness of this Lord, whose nature is the phenomenal world, namely His lordship over immortality, is difficult to cross and boundless, because He is not overcome by the phenomenal world. “Such is His greatness” means “His glory”; by saying “He is greater,” the very meaning is stated.

Thus it has been said that the Lord is eternally liberated. He now shows that bondage and liberation are arranged according to the condition of the beings dependent on Him, explaining “All beings are one foot of Him.” “In His feet”: the Bhū and other worlds are called abodes because beings stand there; they are like feet, or portions, of Him who is the support of existence. In those feet, in those worlds that are His portions, they know all living beings. In the mantra “All beings are one foot of Him,” the common grammatical case is intended to express the non-difference of support and what is supported. The singular “foot” is explained as referring to the generality.

Showing the variety of results among beings, he explains “His three feet are hidden in heaven.” The three feet belonging to this Lord are immortal, everlasting happiness, in the higher worlds, not in the three-world system. Showing the threefold division expressed by the word “three-footed,” he says: Maharloka is the head of the three worlds; the worlds above it are its heads. In those worlds, immortality and the rest are placed in order.

In the three-world system there is only perishable happiness. Although Maharloka is a place of gradual liberation, its happiness is not imperishable because its residents leave their station at the end of the kalpa. In Jana-loka there is immortal, imperishable happiness because its residents do not leave their own station for as long as they live. But the residents of Maharloka, tormented at the end of the kalpa by the heat of the burning three worlds, go then to Jana-loka; therefore there is an appearance of insecurity there. In Tapoloka there is no such condition, but only security. He will indeed say: “When the three worlds are being burned by the fire of Saṅkarṣaṇa, the sages beginning with Bhṛgu, tormented by the heat, go from Maharloka to Jana-loka.” In Satya-loka there is fearlessness, liberation, because of its proximity to that [liberation].

He explains the meaning of “three feet above,” establishing this distinction according to differences in eligibility. “Those without offspring” means the āśramas of lifelong brahmacārins, vānaprasthas and yatis; they are outside the three worlds. The householder, however, is within them, because one without the great vow is without the vow of celibacy.

He shows that this difference of eligibility is due to differences in the stages of one person, not to subjects that are utterly different, by explaining “thence he moves in every direction.” “Viṣvaṅ” means one who goes variously and well. The person, the knower of the field, moves along the two paths, the southern and the northern. What are these two paths like? They are accompanied by eating and non-eating, and are the means of attaining enjoyment and liberation. Here this second qualification is given as the cause: one of them is ignorance in the form of action, and the other is knowledge in the form of worship, which is its means.

“Accompanied by eating” means conscious beings endowed with the activities of eating and the like; “without eating” means the unconscious, such as mountains and rivers, which lack these activities.

Because the egg was born from Him, and within it Virāṭ—composed of the elements, senses and qualities—was also born, that Lord transcended the universe, the Virāṭ body and the material egg. “Like the sun” is the very example mentioned earlier.

If the Puruṣa alone is everything, then worship of the Puruṣa by sacrifices, and of the means of sacrifice, would not be established, because the sacrifice and its means would be non-different from Him. Anticipating this objection and removing it, he gathers and presents the meaning of the mantra beginning “When the gods extended the sacrifice with the Puruṣa as oblation.” “Of this” means of the indwelling Lord within Virāṭ, since He is the subject under discussion. “Born in the navel” means born from that [navel]. “I did not see the implements of sacrifice.”

Then, when those implements had to be prepared, the statement “these implements were assembled through the limbs of the Puruṣa” is connected with the fourth [ṛk]. The plants are the sacrificial posts. “The place of offering” is the sacrificial ground. Since the text says “this,” it is understood that He, seated in a place suitable for sacrifice, speaks. The time beginning with spring is endowed with many qualities. “The place of offering” means that in which the gods are worshiped.

The objects are vessels and the like. The plants are rice and the like. The oils are ghee and the like. The juices are the sweet taste and the rest. The metals are gold and the rest. Earth and water [are also included]. The fourfold priestly function is the rite beginning with the Hotṛ and the other priests.

The names are Jyotiṣṭoma and the like. Since the ṛk and the rest have already been mentioned, “mantras” means the utterances beginning with svāhā and the like. The sequence of the deities is their designation in order. Kalpa is a ritual manual beginning with Baudhāyana. “With this I shall sacrifice” is the resolve. Tantra is the method of performance.
The paths are the strides of Viṣṇu and the like. The thoughts are meditations on the deities. [It is] the dedication of what has been performed to Bhagavān.
I am the one by whom the requisites were collected and prepared. By that very sacrifice. The meaning of the mantra “with that sacrifice they sacrificed the sacrifice” is indicated.

He elaborates the meaning of “then the gods sacrificed” in the two [verses] beginning “from that.” [The sacrifice is] manifest in the form of Indra and the rest, and unmanifest in itself. In this way the meaning of “from that Puruṣa born at the beginning” is shown.
In time, at their respective occasions.

He concludes the answer to the question “What is the foundation?” with “Nārāyaṇa.” “Placed” means established or presided over. The reason for His being Bhagavān is that He is inherently without qualities. At the beginning of creation He is the one in whom the powerful qualities were taken up through māyā.

He concludes the answer to “You are beyond,” which was stated earlier: “This same Bhagavān is the Lord of the minds of all.” “I create” is the meaning. He Himself performs maintenance, as he says “the universe.” “In the form of the Puruṣa” means in the form of Viṣṇu. He is called the bearer of the three powers because He bears māyā, which consists of those powers.

He concludes the general answer to all the questions of this Fifth Chapter—“What is this universe, and of what nature are You?” What was stated was: “There is no other object beyond Vāsudeva in truth,” and it was strengthened by the śruti, “the Puruṣa alone is all this.” All this, consisting of effect and cause, something to be brought into being, is stated to arise from Bhagavān and not to be separate from Him.

Having established and concluded the statement “You are that, from whom I came; not knowing Me, the Lord, you speak,” he concludes with “not [mere] speech.” Because I have eagerness, an increase of devotion, and because Hari has been held and meditated upon in a heart endowed with that devotion, O Nārada, the activities of my speech, mind and senses are meaningful and true; this is not merely due to my own power.

Here he proves the point by his own experience, through agreement and difference, in two [verses]. Although I am the highest even according to the Veda and the other [means of knowledge], and although I have resorted to yoga, I did not know the arising or birth of myself from the Self; what then could I say about another? This will be explained in the Third Canto concerning the lotus-born one.

Then I bow to that foot of the Lord, which is easy to serve, most auspicious, and cuts off worldly existence, for those who have approached Him for shelter. “Those who have come” means those who have surrendered. Then, by the maxim that if even He is of inconceivable greatness, how much more so others, he says “for He.” He Himself has not crossed the expansion of His own māyā; the word “pari” expresses negation. The meaning is: He has not known its limit. How could others know it? “I bow to His foot” is connected with what came before.

One may object: If He is omniscient, how does He not know its end? He answers with an example: just as the sky does not reach the end of itself, so [it is with Him]. The non-perception of a sky-flower does not destroy omniscience. Thus it will be said: “The lords of heaven did not reach Your end because of Your endlessness; what of You, within the hosts of universes, each with its coverings?” The śruti also says: “He who is the overseer of this in the highest heaven—He alone knows, or perhaps He does not know.”

He elaborates this in the two [verses] beginning “I do not.” Vāmadeva is Rudra. “He whose movement of truth” means He whose ultimate nature is reality. Rather, we see and know this phenomenal form, made by His māyā. Even that is only equal to the self, according to the measure of our own knowledge, and not the whole [of Him]. “Those whose minds are deluded” is the reason both for not knowing Him and for knowing the phenomenal world.
It may be seen that everyone describes Him. To this he replies: “whose.”

He shows the acts of the incarnations in brief. He is that first Bhagavān who, becoming the Puruṣa incarnation, performs creation and the rest. “The self in the self, by the self” means that the agent, the locus, the instrument and the object are all Himself. “The Puruṣa incarnation” and “creation and the rest” are a concise statement.

It was said, “They do not know Him in truth.” What is that truth? He answers: knowledge alone, true, is the reality. The qualifications exclude knowledge that takes the form of an object such as a pot. “Pure” means free from the form of an object; “inward” means within all; therefore it is right knowledge, free from doubt and the like; “established” means steady; and “without qualities” means free from the guṇas. The effect of the guṇas is unsteady because of their mixture. Although knowledge occurring as a mental modification is also knowledge of the self, and is not inherently subject to the defect of instability, it is distinguished here because it becomes so through the defects of the internal organ. These same qualifications establish its truth. Moreover, whatever has modification is seen to be unreal; therefore he says that it is without beginning and end, free from birth and destruction. Consequently it has no change consisting in existence after birth, nor growth, transformation or decline. It is full. The reason throughout is that it is eternal and nondual: eternal at all times, and ultimately nondual even when duality is perceived.

Note: Just as water in a pond exits through openings, enters fields as channels, and takes on their four-cornered form, so the luminous internal organ goes through the eye and the other gateways to the place of an object and takes on the form of that object; that transformation is called a mental modification.

Here he makes the experience of the learned the proof. O seer Nārada, they know when the self, senses and inner disposition are tranquil—when the body, senses and mind are clear. At other times he gives the cause of their not knowing: when that very self-luminous reality is covered over by the arguments of those who assert non-being, it becomes concealed.

He explains the incarnations in detail, beginning with “the first” and continuing to the end of the chapter. “Of the Supreme, the great” means the Puruṣa who sets prakṛti in motion. The līlā-body described as “having a thousand heads” is the first incarnation. He will indeed say: “When, having fashioned the city of Virāṭ from the five elements created by Himself, Nārāyaṇa, the first god, entered it with His own portion and obtained the designation Puruṣa.” As it is said: “They know Viṣṇu’s three forms called Puruṣa: the first, the creator of the Great Principle; the second, situated in the egg; the third, situated in all beings. Knowing these, one is liberated.”

Although all are generally called incarnations without distinction, the distinction should be understood: time, nature, and the existent and non-existent—the material nature consisting of cause and effect—are powers; mind and the rest are effects; Brahmā and the others are incarnations of the guṇas; Dakṣa and the others are manifestations of power. “Mind” means the Mahat-tattva. “Matter” means the great elements. No sequence is intended here. “Modification” means ego. “Quality” means sattva and the rest. “Virāṭ” means the collective body. “Svarāṭ” means the Vairāja. “Standing still” means the immovable, and “moving” means the mobile, including individual bodies.

“I” means Brahmā. “Bhava” means Rudra. “Yajña” means Viṣṇu. “Dakṣa and the others” means these lords of progeny. “And those beginning with you” means the steadfast ones [such as Nārada]. “Protectors of the worlds below” means the rulers of Pātāla.

The lords of the Gandharvas and the others; the lords of the Yakṣas and the others. The sandhi in “Rākṣoraga” is an archaic form. The foremost of the ṛṣis and the fathers; the rulers of the pretas and the others.

To say no more, whatever is headed by Bhagavān—all that is the supreme reality; this is the syntactical connection. “Bhagavat” means endowed with lordly opulence; “mahasvat” means endowed with splendor. “Ojas” and “sahas” are the powers of the senses and mind; [He is] endowed with them. “Bala” means skill. “Śrī” means beauty; “hrī” means aversion to evil action; “vibhūti” means prosperity; “ātman” means intellect; [He is] endowed with these. “Arṇa” means color. “Adbhutārṇa” means wondrous color, that is, an astonishing color. Form itself is the essential nature, and whatever is formless as well—all that is the supreme reality and its manifestation.

To speak of the incarnations in pure sattva, he says “chiefly.” They dry up the impurities in the ears—the dirt produced by listening to tales of the unreal—and therefore are so called. “Supeśas” means beautiful; the loss of the s in that word is archaic. O seer, I shall enumerate them for you; let them be drunk by you as they are enumerated. Or “let them be drunk” is a present participle: let them drink the impurities of the ears away.

In the Seventh [chapter], the avatāras of the Lord’s līlā are spoken by Brahmā, along with their acts, purposes and qualities.

“When,” for the purpose of lifting the earth, the Unlimited, having assumed a boar body, was engaged, then He pierced the very famous Hiraṇyākṣa with His tusk.

Note: “Being engaged” means having plunged into the ocean, lifting the earth that had gone to Rasātala, placing it on the tip of His tusk and going upward.

He states the Yajña avatāra. A son named Suyajña was born from Prajāpati Ruci, in his wife Ākūti. He begot the gods headed by Suyama in his own wife Dakṣiṇā. When, becoming Indra, he removed the distress, then, although previously called Suyajña, afterwards he was called Hari by Manu, his maternal grandfather. By this the production of the gods and the removal of the distress of the three worlds are shown as his acts. Thus everywhere the avatāra and his act should be known.

He states the Kapila avatāra. He was born in the house of Prajāpati Kardama, in his wife Devahūti, together with nine female sisters. He spoke to his own mother the path of the self, Brahma-knowledge. By that path of the self, she, in this very birth, having shaken off the impurity of the self—the mud in the form of association with the qualities—attained the path of Kapila, liberation.

He states the Dattātreya avatāra. Because he said, “I myself am given to you by me,” he was born with the name Datta. He shows as his act the giving of the powers of yoga to his own devotees. Those whose bodies are purified by the dust of whose two lotus feet [are meant]. [They obtained] both, worldly and otherworldly, in the form of enjoyment and liberation, respectively.

Note: In the expression “I myself am given by me,” one and the same person cannot have the state of both agent and object of giving, except the Lord. In the Dharmaśāstra it is established that the eldest son, wife, one’s own self, all one’s possessions and the excellent guru are not to be given. Therefore he says, “the Blessed Lord.”

Note: “Enjoyment” is enjoyment of powers beginning with aṇimā.

He states the Kumāra avatāra. The austerity that I performed at first—because of my own austerity, because of my penance—Hari became the four-Sana, He whose name has the four words beginning with Sana: Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sanandana and Sanātana. What kind of was his own austerity? Unbroken. Or, “from his own austerity” means from the giving, the offering, of his austerity; the root ṣaṇu is in the sense of giving. He spoke properly, in this kalpa, the truth of the self that had been destroyed in the dissolution of the previous kalpa, its succession having been cut off. He shows its correctness: merely when it was spoken, the sages saw it directly, by the self, in the self, in the mind.

Note: Here “sanāt” is an indeclinable. The long vowel is archaic. Its meaning is “named Sanan.” Or, from sanāt, “most eternal,” according to the Sahasranāma hymn, its meaning is “named Sanan.”

Note: In this alternative, “tapas” has the genitive ending.

He states the Nara-Nārāyaṇa avatāra. He was born in two forms, Nārāyaṇa and Nara, in the wife of Dharma, the daughter of Dakṣa, named Mūrti. What kind? He whose own, extraordinary power of austerity [is great]. This itself he states: the armies of Ananga, the goddesses who are Apsarases, seeing women beginning with Urvaśī, their own counterparts, from Bhagavān, were unable to cause the violation of His rule, the breaking of His vow.

Or, seeing there the violation of His own rule, whose form is the destruction of austerity, they were unable to make that happen in Bhagavān. This narrative will occur in the Eleventh [chapter].

Note: “Of the self” should be understood as an accusative, the object of the act of seeing.

Where even anger is afraid, where desire does not prevail—what need be said? Thus he says “desire.” The accomplished ones, beginning with Śrī Rudra, burn desire with a glance joined with anger. But they do not burn anger itself, although it burns [them] too; that is, they are overcome by anger. Ah! This anger greatly fears when entering the interior of Him. Or, [it fears] the interior of Him whose mind is [so] pure. What kind? Entering the stainless one.

Note: In “although burning,” the word uta in the original has the sense “also.”

By the deed alone he indicates some avatāra. The words uttered by the co-wife of his mother themselves became arrows; pierced by them, Dhruva, the son of King Uttānapāda, went near [the king] to perform austerity. “The path of Dhruva” means the position of Dhruva. The seven divine ṛṣis, situated below, praise that [position] which is situated above in heaven. Or, Bhṛgu and the others are above, and the seven ṛṣis are below.

Note: “Some” means the avatāra who, being pleased with Dhruva, gave him the position of Dhruva.

He states the Pṛthu avatāra. When requested by the ṛṣis, then, having protected Vena, he obtained the name “son,” appropriately, according to its components.

Note: “Requested” means requested to descend; then, having descended from Vena’s body, this is the meaning.

Note: “Appropriately” means having a meaning that follows its components, that is, an etymological meaning. The kṛt suffix in “having protected” is stated as though future were past, because the necessity of protection is intended.

“Because a son protects his father from the hell named Puṃ, therefore he is declared to be a son”—thus the Self-born himself has declared. This indeed is the derivation of the word “son.”

What kind? He whose virility and lordly fortune were burnt by the thunderbolt that was the curse-word of the twice-born. He states another deed: by whom, in the world, for the purpose of the world, the riches, substances beginning with food, were milked from the earth.

He states the Ṛṣabha avatāra. This Hari was the son of Sudevī, from Nābhi, the son of Āgnīdhra. Sudevī is also a name of Merudevī, the wife of Nābhi. [He performed] conduct like an inert person through yoga, through constant samādhi. “Which” means which [conduct]. The reason for that is “equal-seeing.” The reason even for that is “self-established,” situated in his own nature. Because his senses were pacified. From what? Because he was entirely free from attachment.

Note: “Sudevī” means Merudevī, who in the First [Canto] is said to be the one from whom Urukrama was born, from Nābhi and Merudevī.
