“Adevān” should be divided as “a-devān,” “non-gods,” because the Śruti says, “He created the Asuras from his loins.” “Ati-lolupān” means exceedingly greedy and lustful toward women. “Abhipedire” means they approached.
“Parāpatat” means “she fled.”
He manifests himself in a form corresponding to the devotee’s desire; having approached him in that way…
With the words “pahi” (“protect us”) and the following two verses, they prayed. “Yabhitum” means to unite sexually, to assault through intercourse.
“Lokānām” means “of the people.” It refers to those whose feet are not near you, that is, those who have not taken shelter at your feet.

Hari is one whose inner vision is clear and free from doubt, whose knowledge of the self includes knowledge of others’ minds. “Give up your dreadful body, polluted by desire”—this is understood as what he told Brahmā. Having been told this, Brahmā gave up that body. In every such case, giving up a body means giving up the corresponding mental disposition; taking on a body means entering that corresponding state.

According to the Śruti, “the junction of day and night came to be.” The body he cast off became the evening twilight, the time when desire intensifies. Since the Asuras are rajasic and lustful toward women, they imagined that twilight itself was a woman and became bewildered; this is stated in three verses beginning “tām.” Her lotus feet rang with her anklets; her eyes were bewildered by intoxication; her hips, adorned with a girdle and shining silk, were covered.
Her breasts were lofty and close together, pressed against each other in an embrace. She was beautiful of teeth; her smile was gentle, and her glance playful and sidelong.
“Gūhantīm” means concealing, covering with the movement of her garment. She had a mass, a cluster, of dark curls. O Vidura, O upholder of dharma, they saw and supposed her to be a woman.
He explains the sequence of thought of those who were bewildered, beginning with “aho.”
“Abhisambhāvya” means honoring and showing respect. “Viśrambhāt” means from confidence and intimacy. Those foolish men then questioned her.

The explanation beginning with “kāsi” spans three verses. “Kāsi” means “of what birth are you?” or “whose daughter?” “Bhāmini” means an angry or passionate woman. Her beauty itself is priceless wealth, an incomparable thing; it alone is the merchandise fit to be bought. By withholding it, you distress us.
“What is the use of asking about birth, family, and the like? Whoever you may be, fortunately at least this has happened: we have seen you. Yet you alone agitate and churn our minds.”

Because the words of their agitated minds do not stay on one subject: “O graceful woman, O praiseworthy one, your [playful movement] does not remain in one place”—or, in its many varied graceful motions, it excels everywhere. “A falling ball” means a ball bouncing upward. Your slender waist, burdened by your large breasts, droops and grows weary. Your calm, slow gait spreads like a churning motion. Your hair is a beautiful mass of locks. In another reading, “suśikhāḥ” means beautiful locks; “samūha” is taken with “badhāna,” “bind them as they are being loosened.” Here one should infer the imagery: the setting sun is the bouncing ball; the break in the clouds is the waist drooping; the star-like gaze is the eyes; and darkness is the hair, and so on.
Thinking her to be a woman acting like a lover, they seized her.
“Laughing, smelling herself with herself.” “Kāntyā” means by beauty. Laughter and smelling herself are transformations arising from the skill of experiencing her own beauty.
“Jyotsnām” means moonlight. They were those very groups of Gandharvas and others. Viśvāvasu was the foremost, the leader among them.
“By his own drowsiness” means through his own languor. Seeing them with their hair loosened, he closed his eyes.

That condition in which there is a discharge from the senses is called sleep. Through that discharge of the senses, as its cause, they assail those who are impure and make them deluded. That group of Bhūtas and related beings is called madness. The fourfold character of their forms is stated because they cause drowsiness, yawning, hiccuping, and madness.
“Ūrjasvantam” means powerful. “Parokṣeṇa” means in an unseen, invisible form.

“From whom the creation of the self [arose]”—this is the reading of the text. “Yat” means “for which purpose,” with the recipient relation as its cause. “Kavayaḥ” means the wise, those skilled in ritual action. To the Sādhyas and to the Fathers, who are forms of their own fathers, they extend and give the oblation and ancestral offering through rites such as śrāddha.
“By concealment” means by the power of becoming invisible, even though one may otherwise be visible.

“Pratyātmyena” means by reflection. “Ātmābhāsam” means a reflection. “Mānayann ātmanā ātmānam” describes the reflected one’s self-admiration: seeing his reflection, the handsome one makes gestures such as nodding his head. Therefore those created by him, mutually admiring one another, are continually paired as couples.
“That” means that reflected form. “By their deeds” means by describing his prowess.

“Bhoga” means a coil or expansion, the extension of the feet and so forth; “bhogavat” means possessing such a body. “Anupacite” means not yet grown or increased. That body was endowed with a coil, anger, and the like.

“From this body” means from that body: the hairs that fell away became snakes. “Crawling” means moving by contracting the feet and the like; the snakes came from that moving body. Because they do not walk, they are called nāgas; that is, they are exceedingly swift. Since they arose from the body possessing coils, they have broad necks, with coils in the form of hoods. All of them are fierce because of their connection with his anger. The subdivisions of their species are well known in the treatise on snakes.
When he came to regard himself as having accomplished his task, then he created the Manus.
“Unto them”—that is, unto the Manus—he created and gave his own “puruṣa,” a body shaped like a city and like a man.

“What you did is meritorious”; they call it meritorious. “In which” means in that creation of Manu. “Kriyā” means rites such as the Agnihotra. Therefore in that creation we all partake together of food, including the shares of oblation. “O Brahmā”—this is the address.

Having spoken of bodily creation, he now describes the creation of the sages: “tapasā” and the following words. “Vidyā” means worship. Here “yoga” means postures and the like. “Well-concentrated” means concentration joined with renunciation, powers, and so forth, and [Brahmā] was also endowed with that. “Hṛṣīkeśa” means master of his own senses. Being thus, the seer Brahmā created the sages as his offspring.

“What is that body of which he gave a portion?” To this he answers with “yat.” That is the body in which concentration, yoga, prosperity—that is, supernatural power—austerity, knowledge, and detachment are present.

In the twenty-first chapter the marriage of Kardama to the daughter of Manu, arranged by Viṣṇu who was pleased by austerity and knowledge, is described. “Edhire” and “edhāñcakrire” mean that they grew and flourished.
“How they protected dharma and the earth”—this is to be connected with the third verse: “Tell me that.”
“Of that Manu.”
“Endowed with the characteristics of yoga, beginning with restraint.” How many kinds of potency did he create? How many sons did he produce? This is the meaning.
“Having obtained Manu’s human daughter, Ākūti and Prasūti as wives, how he created beings”—and the word “ca” means “tell that too.”
“Ten thousand years” means ten thousands of years.
Then, in that austerity, “by kriyā-yoga” means by the method of worship. “He approached” means he served the giver of boons to those who have taken refuge in him, the devotees.
Assuming a body composed of that Brahman which is known only through sound, he showed himself to him.

“That Kardama, seeing him standing in his own place, fell to the earth with his head and praised him with words”—the syntactic connection extends across these four verses. “Padma” and “utpala” are [lotuses and water-lilies] which open by day and night. He wears a garland of white lotuses and water-lilies; a mass of soft, dark curls is on his lotus face.
He has a white water-lily as a plaything. His smile and glance touch the mind, that is, bring joy to the mind.
Lakṣmī is on his chest; the Kaustubha jewel is on his neck.
Love itself is his nature, an innate and self-established quality; his mind is of that kind.

“Without you, O supreme bliss, fie on the one who desires another boon! Yet, kindly grant a boon to this poor one.” “Bata” expresses joy. “O praiseworthy one!” Today, through seeing you, the treasure of all existence, our eyes have attained fulfillment and success. He establishes that seeing you is itself the great fruit: even those whose yoga has grown through increasingly excellent births, attained by the good, [find its fulfillment in seeing you].

He criticizes devotees who worship with desires, saying “yaḥ.” “O Lord, those whose understanding has been destroyed by Your māyā worship You for even a particle of the desires they would have in hell. But You grant them those very desires.”

“I who criticize those with desires am myself just like that,” he says with “tathā.” “Gṛhamedha” means household life. Wishing to marry a wife who, like a cow, yields the three aims of life, I have come to the root—Your feet—of the wish-fulfilling tree that grants every desire. One might ask, “Why not worship something else for desires and the like?” No: You alone are the root of every human aim.

“Then why do you not worship solely for liberation?”—because you are not qualified, he says. “O Lord of lords, You are Prajāpati; by Your command this world, struck by desire, is bound like an animal. O Śukla, embodiment of pure dharma, I follow the people; therefore I offer tribute to You and obey Your command, which takes the form of prescribed action. ‘For the Unblinking One,’ the personification of time. ‘And’ means that for this purpose I also desire a wife. The word ‘indeed’ indicates that I offer tribute not only because I follow worldly custom but also to discharge the three debts.”

By saying “for the Unblinking One,” he has said, “I act out of fear of You, who are time personified.” He says in two verses that this fear does not exist for Your devotees. The people overwhelmed by desire, their followers, and animals; even those who possess discernment but, like me, are dull in action—having abandoned them, those who have taken shelter of the umbrella that is Your feet are described. The discourse on Your qualities is a story; it is wine because it makes one forget worldly existence, and nectar because it is delightful. Those who have been made to cast off bodily conditions such as hunger and thirst by that [story] are the people referred to next.

Your three-naved wheel of time, while running, cuts through and draws along the universe, but it does not cut off the lifespan of these devotees. How is it constituted? Brahman is undecaying; the rotation is on its axle. “Bhrami” is used figuratively for “revolving,” by an identity of expression that conveys exceptionally rapid rotation. It has thirteen spokes, with the intercalary month; its joints are the three hundred and sixty days and nights; its rims are the six seasons; its leaves, or leaf-shaped blades, are the endless moments and instants; its three hubs are the supporting circles of the three four-month seasons. It has a terrible, swift current. These descriptions are to be understood as specifying the wheel that is the year.

“Why do you ask me, who am without limiting adjuncts and detached?” Even so, since by māyā You perform the creation of the universe and the rest, You alone are to be asked. He says: although You alone exist, the powers such as sattva, which You have assumed within Yourself through yogamāyā acting as their cause, bring about this universe. “As” gives an example of not needing an instrument separate from oneself.

“Although, because it is māyic, You may not wish to give sense-pleasure to Your devotees, nevertheless fulfill it in accordance with our intention,” he says with “naitad.” “O Lord, You do not expand for us, Your worshipers, through māyā the subtle-element state that is the basis of sense pleasures such as sound.” Although this may not be what You desire, let it be for Your favor to us; after the three debts have been discharged, may it lead to liberation. Since You are seen, joined with Tulasī, shining as though bounded by māyā, this vision of You grants both enjoyment and liberation.

I bow to You, who bestow both enjoyment and liberation. As the giver of liberation, You are the one in whom action directed toward its fruit is brought to rest through knowledge born of experience. As the giver of enjoyment, by Your own māyā You set in motion the order of the world, the instrument of the universe. Therefore Your lotus feet are to be bowed to by those with desires and by those without them. For a person with only a small desire, or in a modest act of worship, You are one who rains down the desired objects.
“Amṛtena” means by that which gives happiness, nectar. His eyebrow is moving playfully through his loving smiles and glances.
“Caittyam” means the heart, the inner feeling. “By me it was joined together with me”—that very thing for whose sake I was worshiped.
For those whose minds have been gathered and made one-pointed upon Me, whatever worship of Me they perform will not be entirely false or fruitless in people like you.
“Vikhyātam” means auspiciousness and prosperity; it is characterized by good conduct and the like.
“O Brāhmaṇa, together with your wife.”
“O Lord! O one whose disposition is devoted to worshiping Me!”
“Yatra” means “in whom,” that is, in which wife. “Samāhitam” means placed with intention. “Nṛpa-vadhū” means a king’s daughter.
“Your potency, retained and held within yourself, will be received by the one who gives birth. From the daughters born of that potency, they will readily beget sons for themselves.”
“Nideśam” means an order. “Uśattamaḥ” means pure sattva. “Tīrtha” means a recipient or worthy vessel; by it, giving is indicated—meaning, one who has surrendered all the fruits of action to Me.
By showing compassion through household life, and by giving fearlessness through renunciation, you will see yourself and the world united as one in Me.
It is understood that [Kapila] descended in Devahūti together with your potency.
“Pratyag-akṣajaḥ” means that which is born or manifests in the inward senses. “Pariśritāt” means surrounded by the river Sarasvatī.

His path is praised by all accomplished masters of austerity, mantra, and the rest: the perfected path is the road to Vaikuṇṭha. Or, he himself is praised by all accomplished lords, and he went along the perfected path sought by the siddhas. While listening to the Sāman song made manifest by the wings of Garuḍa, king of birds—since the Śruti says that the Bṛhat and Rathantara Sāmans are his wings—and hearing the pronounced stoma, the collection of Ṛks that form the basis of the Sāmans. The Śruti says, “the stoma is the self.” In the compound recitation, “pronounced stoma” means the collection of stotṛ verses belonging to the Sāman.
“Awaiting that time,” means waiting for the day called “the day after tomorrow.”

Having mounted the chariot furnished with golden ornaments and seated his daughter in it, he traveled about in search of a bridegroom. “O Sudhanvan” is an address to Vidura. “Yad ahaḥ” means “on that day.”

To show that he attained supreme bliss simply upon entering, the hermitage is described in seven verses beginning with “yasmin,” when Kardama received him. “Śivam” means health; the water there is tasty like nectar.
It is furnished with clusters of auspicious trees and vines, and with sacred deer and birds that call out.
“Ghuṣṭam” means resounding. There the intoxicated bees sport; the intoxicated peacocks are dancers, their movement a display of dancing; and the excited cuckoos call to one another.
It is adorned with trees such as the kadamba.
The birds called kāraṇḍava and the others coo sweetly.

The place is surrounded by deer and other animals. Here “kroḍa” means boar, “śvāvid” means porcupine, “marka” means monkey, and a particular kind is the gopuccha. “Hari” means either monkey or lion; “nābhi” means musk deer.
In it the sacred fire was offered, suitable for a celibate student and for ascetics.

He was shining with a body whose discipline was intense. The speech of the Lord Himself was a drop of nectar, a digit of the nectar-filled moon; by hearing it he was not excessively emaciated—though wasted by austerity, he was not wasted.

“Prāṃśum” means tall, elevated. “Having approached” means having gone near. “He saw the soiled one” is connected with the preceding action. “Arhaṇa” is a great jewel used for worship; unworked and unpolished, it appears dirty.
“Uṭajam” means a leaf hut; he had arrived there. Having welcomed him with blessings while he bowed at his feet, Kardama received and honored him with worship.
“Te” means his pacing about, his wandering. “Hi” means “because.”
He bows to Viṣṇu situated in Manu, saying “yaḥ.” “Sthāne” means at the proper place, at the occasion for each particular task; [he bows] to Śukla, Viṣṇu.

This is the meaning of the five verses beginning “na yadet”: “Although Your coming may be occasioned by Your roaming everywhere to protect dharma, nevertheless, if there is a special task, please state it.” “Jaitra” means victory-giving; the chariot is adorned with a row of gems. The syntax of three verses is: “When You do not travel around the circle of the earth mounted on that chariot, the bridges would break.” He whose bow makes a fierce, resounding sound; “those by whom the social and spiritual orders are established”; “bata” means “ah!”
“By unrestrained men” means by men who act as the instrument or cause. “When he is lying down” means when he is resting without concern.
“Nirvyalīkena” means sincerely and joyfully. “Pratipadyāmahe” means “we accept.”

In the twenty-second chapter Manu gives his daughter Devahūti in marriage to Kardama, as Viṣṇu had ordained. Manu, whose excellence is made manifest through praise—the impetus and eminence of all qualities and deeds—is the emperor. As though embarrassed to hear his own fame, or fearing a refusal, he spoke to the sage. “Upāratam” means one who has withdrawn, intent on renunciation.

Intending to propose, “My daughter is to be married by you,” he explains that the relationship between you and me had already been arranged by the Lord. “Ātmanaḥ parīpsayā” means by the desire to protect Himself; “paryāptum” means to sustain. The Vedic form of the Lord is sustained by the propagation of the Veda, according to His desire. “You” means the brāhmaṇas; “for their protection” means for the protection of the brāhmaṇas. “Brahma” means the brāhmaṇa class; “kṣatram” means the kṣatriya class.
Thus that very Lord protected him. Who is He? He is constituted of both being and nonbeing, the Self of all; nevertheless, He is imperishable and without change.
He praises the sight of the Lord and the rest in order to make his request, beginning with “tava” in three verses.
“Akṛtātmanām” means those whose minds have not been brought under control.
Grace takes the form of instruction and the like. “Uśatīḥ” means desired [boons].
He makes his request in seven verses beginning with “sa bhavān.” His mind was distressed by affection for his daughter. “Śrāvitam” means the proposal that was communicated.
The doubt that she was the sister of Priyavrata and Uttānapāda is removed. The words “my daughter” show that she is a kṣatriya maiden suited to you.
“This is Devahūti.”
“Pratīccha” means “accept.”
“Udyatasya” means an object already arisen and obtained of its own accord. “Prativādaḥ” means a counterargument or refusal.
“Kīnāśam” means wretched or miserly. “Avajñayā” means through contempt, through an insult.
“Upakurvāṇaḥ” is one who observes celibacy until a prescribed point. “Me prattām” means “given by me.”

“If she had not been given [to you]”—the meaning is that, being firmly resolved upon me alone, she has not been promised to anyone else. “Ādyaḥ” means first or primary, since there was no marriage before this; or it means the chief one.

“Bhūyāt” means “may it be.” “Pratīta” refers to the well-known Vedic mantra, “I take your hand for good fortune,” and the rest. “Svayaṅga-kāntyā” means by her own bodily beauty. “Śriyam” means the splendor of ornaments and the like.
Seeing her, he fell down. His mind was bewildered and agitated by delusion. Her feet were beautiful with their tinkling anklets.

She was the crest-jewel of women, an ornament among them. Those who had never served her feet—Lakṣmī’s own feet—had not seen her and were not even fit to see her. “Uccapadaḥ” means “of Uttānapāda.” “Abhiyātām” means one who had arrived of her own accord.

“I will accept her.” The agreement is expressed as follows: “Householder life continues until offspring are born; after that, renunciation.” He explains this very point: she will carry my potency in her womb until it develops. Or, she will carry the semen that has left my body. After that I regard as primary the knowledge of the paramahaṃsa, and the nonviolent disciplines such as tranquility and the rest—taught directly and with excellence by Viṣṇu, the pure one—as practices to be performed abundantly.

One might object: your father, the Prajāpati, ordered creation, not renunciation. He answers with “yataḥ.” “Saṃsthāsyate” means “will come to an end, will be dissolved.” “Vā” is used emphatically. The Lord has taught that for people like me, renunciation is appropriate only after discharging the three debts.
Manu was enticed by the sage’s face; or, he himself enticed the sage by his own face.
“Saḥ” means Manu. “Anu” means immediately afterward. He knew the queen’s determination as well.
“Pāribarhān” means gifts to be presented at the time of marriage; “bhūṣāḥ” means ornaments, garments, and household furnishings.
“Prattām” means given. “Sadṛkṣāya” means to one who is equal. “Gatavyathā” means one whose anxiety has gone; whose heart was shaken by intense longing.
Speaking, “O mother! O daughter!” in order to bear her separation. The construction is an archaic sandhi. “Śikhāḥ” means the hair; he sprinkled them.
“For the welfare of the family of sages,” on the two beautiful banks of the river.
“Abhipretya” means having understood. From the land of Brahmāvarta, the people came forth to welcome the lord of progeny.
If one asks, “What is Brahmāvarta?” he says, “where the city named Barhiṣmatī is.” And where is that? “Where the hairs of Yajña, the Boar, fell.” The word “yatra” is connected everywhere.

In explaining the name Barhiṣmatī, he also praises the excellence of the region in two verses. Kuśa and kāśa grasses grew there, their green color ever fresh. The sages defeated demons and other destroyers of sacrifice and worshipped Yajña, Viṣṇu, the Lord of sacrifice.

“Where he sacrificed to Viṣṇu, the Person of sacrifice”—“yatas” means “where.” “Bhuvam” means place. “Labdha” is formed with the tṛn suffix; it means “having obtained.” Or, the sense is “having obtained that Person of sacrifice.” Thus it is stated that the earth is superior even to heaven, and that among places this one is the best.
He returns to the subject: “the city named Barhiṣmatī, which he inhabited.” The connection is: having entered that city where he had formerly lived, he enjoyed its pleasures.
Without conflict with the other duties beginning with dharma. Every morning his good fame was sung; yet he enjoyed his pleasures while listening only to the stories of Hari.
“Yogamāyāsu” means in the arrangements of desired enjoyments. “Yat yataḥ” is explained as “to cause to fall, even slightly,” that is, to overcome.

The time of cooked food passes, and it loses its essence; hence anything whose essence has passed is called yātayāma. The time divisions were ayāta-yāmāḥ, fresh and without loss of essence. These yāmās—divisions of time—carry forward his own period, the Manvantara. This describes one who listens to and meditates on Viṣṇu, and who composes and speaks His narratives.
“Paribhūtam” means surpassed the three conditions—waking and the rest, or the modes beginning with sattva.
The divine afflictions are those arising in the atmosphere; the human afflictions arise from enemies; the material afflictions arise from cold, heat, and the like. “O son of Vyāsa!” means “O Vidura!”
He speaks of the extent of his superior knowledge: “the ordinary duties of human beings.”
“His offspring”—Devahūti; this means her arising and influence.
In the twenty-third chapter, then, enjoyment in the wondrous, wish-moving aerial palace created by yoga and endowed with every prosperity is described, once departure and travel had taken place.
“Dambham” means deceit or pretence. “Agham” means prohibited conduct. “Tejīyāṃsam” means one exceedingly powerful and radiant.
“Greater than fate” means capable of changing even fate. Worn down by observance of vows, and there—over a very long time—exceedingly emaciated.
“Suhṛt” means beloved. She was not considered or reckoned as something to be expended for my sake. Although suitable and praiseworthy, she was neglected because she was devoted to serving me.

Austerity, concentration, knowledge, and worship; among these, “self-yoga” means one-pointedness of mind; through them divine enjoyments are attained by the Lord’s grace, so behold those very enjoyments, mastered by you. I grant you divine sight, by which you will see. “What of other enjoyments?” “Nothing at all.” That is, they are exceedingly insignificant. The reason is this: the eyebrow of the Lord Urukrama, by its expansion or curve, shatters the plans and desires of those seeking material aims. They are consumed by their own dharma, their chastity. “Hard to attain” means difficult to obtain. Their changes as kings are transformations produced by each respective enjoyment.

All the yogic powers and sciences, and the practices associated with each of them, her anxiety left her and she became free of worry on seeing her husband, proficient in all of them, speaking in this way. Overwhelmed by humility and love, her voice faltered; with a glance slightly touched by bashfulness, her face shone with a blossoming smile; she spoke.

“Bata” expresses joy. “Dvija-vṛṣa” means “O best of brāhmaṇas”; “O husband!” “All this has indeed been accomplished by you.” “I know this.” “But may the agreement you made with me be fulfilled.” “Once” means only until conception has taken place. Because, when the husband is excellent, childbirth is a great benefit and virtue for women. Or, in the compound reading, when an excellent husband is present, the virtues of chaste women expand; therefore, once my virtues have been increased by the birth of a son, let everything you said afterward come to pass.

First he says that the arrangements for bodily union must be made. “O Lord, teach me and explain what should be done for union, the means, according to instruction and in keeping with the treatise on love; that is, prepare it.” By those means—massage, food, drink, and the like—may this body of mine, emaciated and weak from intense longing for pleasure, become fit for union. “Of what sort am I?” I am tormented by the desire for love that you yourself aroused; therefore consider and decide upon a suitable dwelling.
At that very moment he caused it to appear.

He specifies that very thing in nine [verses], beginning “sarva-kāma-dugham” (“fulfilling every desire”). It was furnished with every kind of jewel and the like. It contained the progressive increase of every prosperity and abundance. “Upaskṛtam” means adorned.
“Upakaraṇam” means equipment or furnishings. “Paṭṭikā” are narrow special cloths; “patākā” are broad banners, with which it was hung.
They had garlands of various flowers. The bees hummed sweetly among those garlands.
The houses were arranged one above another. “Kaśipu” means beds; they were lovely and pleasing. Couches and the like were also lovely.
It was adorned here and there with diverse works of art. It was furnished with coral platforms and a great emerald floor. “Not explained by any [of them]” [is the source’s note on this expression].
At the doors, the thresholds were made of coral and shone beautifully. The doors were set with diamonds. The palace-tops and upper roofs were made of sapphire.
The finest rubies were like seeing eyes—or, alternatively, were like eyes. What were they? The finest rubies. The canopies were varied. They formed a multitude of ornamental awnings.
Artificial swans and other birds, taking the real swans to be their own kind, repeatedly alighted here and there and cooed.

A “vihāra” is a place for recreation; “viśrāma” is a bedroom; “saṃviśa” is a place for enjoyment; a courtyard is outside the house; an outer yard is beyond the enclosure; “as one pleases” means as is comfortable for oneself; even the magical airplane seemed astonishing.
She was not greatly pleased because her body was dirty and she had no attendants.

“In this lake” means in Lake Bindu. “Āruha” means “climb up.” It was made by the white Lord Viṣṇu, by the descent of drops of bliss. “Yāpaka” means that which carries one across or brings one to the goal.
“Samādāya” means “taking” or “bringing.” “Sarajam” means soiled. “Veṇī-bhūtān” means formed into matted braids.
“Śabalau” describes breasts that are mottled and discolored. Or, it is a place where the auspicious waters of Sarasvatī dwell; alternatively, a place inhabited by auspicious aquatic beings.
While submerged there, she saw something wondrous. He explains it in ten verses, beginning “sāntaḥ-sarasi.” “Utpalagandhayaḥ” means fragrant with the scent of lotuses.
The women said, “We are your servants and attendants; please give us your orders.”

Then, by bathing and by oils suitable for bathing, and the like. “Parardhyāni” means most excellent. “Varīyāṃsi” means superior and dear to him. “Dyumanti” means radiant. “Pānam” means a drink. “Amṛtam” is sweet; “āsavam” is intoxicating.

The words “she saw herself in the mirror” are understood. He describes her in four verses. “Kṛta-svāsty-ayanam” means that auspicious rites had been performed for her. The masculine form is used because “ātman” is grammatically masculine.
This elaborates “virajam.” “Snātam” means bathed, scrubbed, and washed. Her body was anointed, and her head was bathed. “Bhūṣitatvam” means adorned. She wore a necklace-pendant at her neck.

She wore an ornament containing many jewels. “Rucaka” is an auspicious substance such as kuṅkuma. As the lexicon Viśva-prakāśa says: “rucaka” denotes an auspicious substance, a neck ornament, or a tooth.

“Having beautiful teeth,” “beautiful brows,” and “eyes” are singular forms used collectively. Her face shone and was lovely because of these features. What sort of eyes? Their outer corners were gentle, charming, and lustrous. They rivaled the lotus bud.
When she saw her husband and remembered him, she herself remained there, in that very place.
“Seeing herself” means beholding herself. She also saw his yogic power. She wondered, “What is this?”
The sage now bore the very form he had possessed before marriage. Her beautiful breasts were covered with fine garments. Another reading gives a different form.
She wore beautiful garments. Love had arisen in her. “O slayer of enemies! O conqueror of desire!”

The sage shone in that airplane. His majesty and independence had not diminished. His body had been well attended. He was exceedingly beautiful, like the full moon among blooming water-lilies. The airplane was like the sky, the women like stars, and their eyes like lilies.

By that airplane he travelled. In the ravines of Meru, the king of mountains, where the eight guardians of the worlds sport, breezes—cool, fragrant, and friends of Kāma—made them beautiful. Praised by the Siddhas, he enjoyed himself in those caves where the falling stream of the heavenly Gaṅgā made a sound. He was surrounded by a company of the finest women.
In the celestial gardens, such as Vaiśrambhaka, and at Lake Mānasa, he enjoyed himself.
He stood surpassing [all others].
“Those of exalted minds” means the steadfast sages. From him comes the end of the distress of worldly existence.
“Having shown” means having made visible. “Gola” means a sphere or globe. By its own arrangement of islands, lands, and regions, it had a corresponding extent. It contained many wonders.
Having divided himself into nine forms, making himself ninefold.
The expression means: having reached the sixteenth year, he is conventionally called “āvīcya.”
“Śaradaḥ” means years. They passed almost imperceptibly.

He lovingly contemplated her, becoming the form of half her body. In that way, good offspring would be born. “Navadhā” means ninefold. “Knower of every resolve” means that he knew her desire for many children. The all-powerful Lord was able to act accordingly. “Knower of the self” indicates his lack of attachment to her. Tradition says: when the man’s semen predominates a male is born; when the woman’s predominates, a female.
Immediately thereafter. At once, on a single day. They were all beautiful in every limb.
Seeing and conjecturing that he was about to depart, she smiled outwardly; inwardly, however, her heart was agitated, distressed, and burning, and she spoke [as described next].
The splendour of her feet, whose nails were jewels, as she traced the ground with them, showed the mark of her unending anxiety.
“Upovāha” means “brought about” or “provided.” “Fearlessness” means: remove the future fear of destitution and the fear of worldly existence.

Here she states her distress. She felt humbled because suitable husbands equal to your daughters must be sought by you yourself. Accepting the fear of worldly existence, she says, “someone…” “For freedom from sorrow” means for instruction in knowledge. Since offspring discharge one’s debts, might there be some son, a knower of Brahman, who would remain with you for a time?
If you ask, “Why enjoy sense objects? What need is there for knowledge of Brahman?” she answers: “That much is enough; let it be fulfilled.” “I am one by whom the Supreme Self has been abandoned.”
She laments what she herself has done, in four verses beginning “indriyārtheṣu.” “Me” means “by me.” “Your supreme nature” means: you, the knower of Brahman.
One may ask, “How can attachment lead to fearlessness?” He answers: through knowledge of the Lord of sacrifice.

For one whose action proceeds merely from material nature, it is not directed toward dharma. Nor does it lead through desireless dharma to detachment, and then to service of Hari, the Lord of the sacred place.
“I did not even desire liberation”: I did not form even the wish to leave.

In the twenty-fourth chapter, then, the father’s narration of Kapila’s birth after granting him permission to renounce, upon release from the three debts. “Śālinīm” means praiseworthy. “Spoken by Śukla” refers to “I shall descend with my own portion” and the following words [3.21.32].
Do not grieve in this way or be distressed; do not think of yourself, “I am unfortunate.” “Adūrāt” means soon.
“By self-control” means by restraint of the senses. “By observance” means by one’s own duty. Through austerities and gifts of wealth.
He will cut the heart-knot: bondage characterized by ego and composed of consciousness and inert matter. “A son born from your womb.” He teaches or imparts Brahman.
“Śraddhā” means faith or trust.
When a long time—many days—had passed. “Kārdamam” means related to Kardama.
“Ghanāghanā” is one compound word. Clouds pouring rain. They sang and danced.
“Apavargitāḥ” means liberated.
“Pariśritam” means surrounded.

What did he do after arriving? He explains in the two verses beginning “bhagavantam.” To communicate Sāṃkhya, the system in which the principles are enumerated, Brahmā—the unborn, self-luminous one, whose knowledge is innate—honored the Lord’s intention; his senses rejoiced, and he addressed Kardama. This construction connects both verses. The word “ca” also includes Devahūti.
There, in five verses beginning “tvayā,” he speaks to Kardama. “Apaciti” means worship or honor. “Yat” means “because”; “nirvyalīkataḥ” means sincerely, without deceit, having properly received.
“Anumanyeta” means “one might approve”—only to this extent.
“They will increase” means they will enlarge and multiply through many kinds of powers and lineages.
“The foremost sages” means Marīci and the others.
He says that the son is the Lord Himself, beginning “vedāham.” “Śevadhim” means a treasure that grants every desired thing.

He addresses Devahūti in three verses. “Knowledge” is what scripture teaches; “realization” is direct perception. These two are the means of yoga; by them he will uproot the tangle of actions—the latent impressions. He whose lotus feet bear the mark of a lotus. “O daughter of Manu”: ignorance is not knowing one’s true nature; doubts and false cognitions—these form the knot in your heart.
“Susammataḥ” means being highly honored. “Gantā” means he will go or attain.

“Together with the Kumāras” is understood. “With Nārada” means accompanied by Nārada. Having arranged marriages for Marīci and the others, Brahmā, called Haṃsa, went with these five lifelong celibates. The third of the three realms is heaven; its highest limit is Satyaloka.
“Śatadhṛti” means Brahmā.
The source explicitly says “not explained”; no gloss is supplied.
“Yuktām” means suitable. “Ayacchat” means he gave.
“Vitan'yate” means it is extended, enriched, or made abundant. It means the deity presiding over peace. “Samalālayat” means he pleased or satisfied.
“Nimantrya” means inviting and asking. Having attained joy.
“He” means that sage. “The three-age one” means Viṣṇu. “In a secluded place” means privately.
“Being cooked” means being intensely burned by suffering. “In hell” means in worldly existence. By one’s own inauspicious deeds, one’s sins.

Why? Knowing that all the deities were pleased, and that he had gained what is hard to obtain, he explains in two verses. Ripened and brought to perfection through many births. “Yoga” means bhakti-yoga; “samādhi” in it means concentration, and by that [he attained]. “In empty houses” means in secluded places. “Whose feet are yours.” “Not counting” means not regarding contempt, disrespect, or slight as significant. He says, “This is indeed fitting for you,” because you support the side of your own devotees.
He elaborates this in two verses. You yourself descended to make true your own statement, “I shall become your son.” Wishing to teach knowledge and the Sāṃkhya that is the means to knowledge.
Those extraordinary forms of yours, such as the four-armed form, are fitting for you. The human-like forms pleasing to your own people are pleasing to you as well. You are without a material form.
He whose footstool is worthy of worship. Complete with sovereignty and the other divine attributes.

Explaining sovereignty and the rest, he says: “Supreme” means the Supreme Lord. The reason is: whose powers are independent and under His own control. These are the powers: pradhāna is material nature; puruṣa is its controller; mahat is the great principle; time agitates them; the threefold form is ego, comprising the worlds and their protectors. Having stated that through māyā He assumes the forms of pradhāna and the rest, he states His freedom from manifestation through the conscious potency. The universe is absorbed in Him through the conscious power of self-realization. “The seer” means the omniscient witness of the manifestation and dissolution of pradhāna and the other principles.

He requests permission to renounce. “I ask” means “I ask whatever there is to ask.” Since the debts associated with the gods and others have been ended by Your descent as my son, I, now fulfilled in my desires, shall follow the path of renunciants, remembering and worshiping You as I wander.

I descended into your house solely to teach knowledge; therefore liberation is readily available even while you remain at home. If you insist that you must depart, go remembering Me alone. He says this in six verses beginning “mayi.” In worldly and Vedic duties. He shows the authority of His own statement. Because I said, “I shall become your son,” I took birth so that this may indeed be true.

“Know,” to be connected with what follows: for the self-realization of sages seeking liberation from false identifications, and for the enumeration of principles. One may object that this path of self-knowledge was already established and need not now be newly introduced; he answers, “This…” “Avyakta” means subtle, unmanifest.

“At will” means as you wish. “Having been asked” means having been given permission. Or: just as you asked Me whether you might go, I too have asked you to remain here. By dedicating actions to Me and crossing death, which is ignorance, through knowledge, one attains immortality—the śruti says so.
Then, seeing Me—the Supreme Self—in your own self by your own self, you will attain fearlessness, liberation.

“To his mother” means to Devahūti. “Śamanīm” means that which pacifies and uproots. “He will cross” means he will cross completely beyond fear. The word “ca” also conveys that she will attain supreme bliss.
Having been fully instructed. Having circumambulated Him.
This is the sages’ vow of silence, characterized by nonviolence.
“That which is beyond the manifest and unmanifest” means Brahman. “In the quality-illuminating, quality-free [Lord].” Through unwavering devotion, He is experienced and made directly manifest.

Therefore, free of ego regarding the body and the rest. Therefore free of dualities, undisturbed by heat and cold. Even-seeing, not grasping difference, but seeing only the self. Whose steady understanding is inward-turned, peaceful, and free of distraction.

Having described the cessation of these imagined limiting adjuncts, he now speaks in three verses of attaining the Supreme Lord, beginning “vāsudeva.” The individual self has been realized within the mind, and its bondage—ignorance—has been released.
He explains the attainment of the self with “ātmānam.”
Thus he attained that divine destination. In another reading: “He alone attained that destination.”

In the twenty-fifth chapter, when Kapila is asked by his mother about release from bondage, her son Kapila first explains the highest devotion and its defining marks. The jewel-box of yoga, given by Kapila to his mother and governed by a hidden meaning, is now clearly opened. Having restated the question, she asks about Kapila’s teaching of yoga in three verses beginning “kapila.” “The enumerator of principles” means the reckoner, the originator of Sāṃkhya. Therefore he is self-born. “For explaining the self” means for teaching the truth of the self.

Among men, “great in stature” means foremost. Among all yogīs, “the most excellent”: “varimā” is the state of being best; the wording emphasizes the agent, meaning the highest. Or, it means “because he is superior.” “In fame” means in renown. “The senses are not satisfied by much.” “Śruta-deva” shines through what he has heard and through hearing. Or, “the god heard much” by him; the phrase “my senses too” is connected in that way.
He whose body is for the pleasure and will of his own devotees. Whatever action he performs, recount those deeds worthy of praise.
As you prompt me, having been prompted in this way. In accordance with that question. In philosophical inquiry—in the knowledge of the self.
“In Bindu-sara” means in Lake Bindu.
He who shows the farthest limit of the path of truth. “This enemy of Kaiṭabha has entered your womb, O Manu,” and the following words are cited from scripture [Bhāgavata 3.24.18].
I am weary from thirsting for sense objects, which are the unsatisfactory senses of the unwise. By Him who is contemplated and fulfilled.
You alone are the excellent eye that carries me across; I have obtained [that sight] through you. When the end of births is to be reached by your favor.
He explains that: the Lord Himself, Bhagavān, has arisen as the sun in the form of the eye.

“Apākraṣṭum” means to draw away or remove. “What is that delusion?” He explains it. The insistence, “I” and “mine,” which You Yourself have placed in this body and the like. The second use of “iti” includes its effects, such as attachment.
I have taken refuge in You, wishing to know Prakṛti and Puruṣa; this is the syntactic connection of “I bow.” “Kuṭhāram” means an axe, one who cuts.
“Increasing liberation” means producing delight in liberation. He whose face is beautified by a slight smile.
“Ādhyātmika” means fixed in the self. “Yatra” means “where.”
The source explicitly says “not explained”; no explanatory gloss is supplied.

To show that mastery of every limb depends on control of the mind, he says “cetaḥ.” “Of this self” means of the living being. “Among the qualities” means among the objects of the senses. “In the person” means in the Supreme Lord. The word “vā” has the force of “indeed.”

He shows in three verses beginning “aham” how attainment of life’s purpose follows from control of the mind. When the mind, freed from impurities, becomes pure. He gives “aduḥkham” as the sign by which purity of mind is known.
“Nirantaram” means uninterrupted, without division. “Aṇimānam” means minuteness or subtlety. “Akhaṇḍitam” means unbroken, unlimited.
“Hataujasam” means one whose strength has been diminished.
He says that, when the mind is pure, devotion alone is the inner means.
He says that association with the good is the root of all this, beginning “prasaṅgam.” “Apāvṛtam” means uncovered, without obstruction.

He describes the characteristics of saints in four verses beginning “titikṣavaḥ.” “Saints” means those who follow scripture. “Sādhu” means virtuous and well-behaved; that alone is their ornament. These devotees of the described character are not afflicted by the troubles beginning with those of the body. Why? Their minds are fixed on Me. Those who are not overcome by afflictions are saints—this is the meaning.

He establishes that association with the good is a limb of devotion, beginning “satām.” They are those in whom knowledge of the Lord’s power is complete. Their words are a tonic for the heart and ears, bringing delight. By savoring and serving those words, one reaches Hari, in whom the path of liberation—the ending of ignorance—abides. First comes faith, then attachment, then devotion; it will arise in sequence.

“What follows?” He answers: “through devotion.” Through devotion born of contemplation on My acts of creation and the rest. Becoming dispassionate toward sensory pleasure, both seen and heard, in this world and the next. Then, being intent, one strives to restrain the mind. By straightforward, effortless means, since devotion is primary.
Thus, through knowledge and the like, without serving the qualities of material nature, this living being attains and holds only Me, even here in this body.

“Kācit” means “some” or “any.” “Ucita” means suitable. Even then, what sort of woman is suitable for Me? One within My sphere, fit for Me. “Nirvāṇa” means liberation; “Your state” is Your own nature; I shall attain You completely and immediately. In the reading “añjasā tu,” the sense is connected with “I alone.”
“Bhagavad-bāṇa” means that which makes Bhagavān its target. “Yataḥ” means “because of which yoga.”
“Vijānīhi” means explain distinctly, teach. “Sukham” means without effort.

Knowing in this way His mother’s purpose. The reason for His affection: He had appeared in that body, in that womb. In it the principles are taught and set out in order. What is that? He taught the Sāṃkhya they proclaim, the unfolding of devotion, and yoga.

Asked, “What devotion is suitable for me?” [Bhāgavata 3.25.28], He defines the highest devotion. “By which the qualities are perceived and known.” The activity directed only toward Hari, the embodiment of pure goodness, who presides over the senses and their illuminating deities, is devotion; it is greater even than perfection and liberation. What is it like? Causeless and free of desire. Natural, perfected without effort. He states the reason for their having this kind of disposition. “That which is heard from the teacher” is the Veda; what it prescribes is Vedic action; therefore the mind of the pure person is one and undivided.

He establishes devotion’s supreme excellence in five verses beginning “naikātmatām.” “Oneness of self” means liberation by merging. Those whose actions are performed for Me. “Prasajya” means becoming attached. “Pauruṣāṇi” means powers or energies.
Along with those forms of Mine, in which the eyes are serene and radiant. The meaning is that the joy of constant experience of the Supreme Lord is greater in devotion.

He says that the bliss of the self is surely attained through them. They have beautiful, captivating features—face, eyes, and the like. Their minds have been captured. Their life-breaths and senses have been captured. Serving those devotees, even without wishing to do so, He grants and brings them to the subtle state of liberation. By what means? Their minds are captivated. By noble pastimes and the like: “vilāsa” means divine play; “vāma” means lovely; it also means charming words and sweet speech.

He says that divine opulence is also greater there. After ignorance has ceased, the enjoyments of Satyaloka and the eight mystic powers—such as aṇimā—may arise naturally along with devotion. Although they do not desire the prosperity of Vaikuṇṭha, they nevertheless attain it in both realms.

One may object: if this is a realm like heaven, might its enjoyers and objects of enjoyment eventually perish? He answers, “O tranquil One!” Or, “tranquil” means pure goodness; in Vaikuṇṭha, whose nature is pure goodness, My devotees never perish and are never deprived of what is enjoyed. My unblinking weapon—the wheel of time—does not lick or devour them. Here is the reason. To them I am loved like a son, trusted like a friend, a teacher like a guru, a benefactor like a well-wisher, and worshipful like their chosen deity.

He says in two verses beginning “imam” that He grants this kind of liberation only to exclusive devotees. Along with the conditioned self, which travels between the two worlds, are sons, wives, and the like, as well as cattle and other animals. “Rāyaḥ” means wealth. And other possessions. “I carry them beyond death” means beyond worldly existence.

He says that for nondevotees liberation is not possible by any means, beginning “na.” “Other than Me” means apart from Bhagavān. “Without Bhagavān”—without Me. “Of all beings” means of the self; the three epithets of Bhagavān state His power, independence, and benevolence.

He explains sovereignty, beginning “mad-bhayāt.” And the śruti says: “From fear of Him the wind blows; from fear of Him the sun rises.” “From fear of Him Agni and the moon [shine], and Death, fifth, runs”—so says the Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8.1.
He establishes through the conduct of the good that liberation comes only through worship of Me, beginning “jñānena.”
He concludes, beginning with “etāvān”—“this much.” “The mind, when offered to Me, becomes steady”: that alone is the whole meaning.

In the twenty-sixth chapter, the distinction between Puruṣa and Prakṛti is described. Through Sāṅkhya, the differences among all entities are set out according to their origin and defining characteristics. That which the Creator spoke to his son, and which Maitreya, son of Mitra, spoke to the kṣatriya, the knower of truth now chiefly speaks to his mother as Sāṅkhya concerning the self. Here, in the expression “that tradition of truth which people call Sāṅkhya,” the triad of Sāṅkhya, devotion, and yoga is introduced under the word Sāṅkhya. Having spoken of devotion there, he now speaks of Sāṅkhya with “now” (atha).

The word “knowledge” is explained: it is knowledge in the form of realization of the Self. Therefore it cuts the knot of the heart and removes ego. “I shall describe to you that which they call [knowledge] for the sake of the highest good.” The purport is that knowledge of the defining characteristics of the principles alone gives rise to knowledge of the distinct Self.

Here he defines the Puruṣa with the word “beginningless” (anādi). The Self alone is the Puruṣa. What is that Self? He whose luminous abode is inward, turned back from external objects. He rejects the momentariness thesis [100] with “beginningless”; he rejects the view that the Self is subject to transmigration with “beyond Prakṛti”—distinct and unattached. He rules out knowledge and the like as qualities [101] with “without qualities.” He rules out the Mīmāṃsakas’ view that the Self is an object of knowledge with “self-luminous.” By this same statement, the Prābhākaras’ view that the Self shines as the support of cognition is refuted as well. The reason for self-luminosity is “by whom the universe is pervaded”; supply “it shines.” By these same reasons, the Puruṣa’s transcendence of Prakṛti is also established.

[100] The momentariness thesis is the view of Buddhist idealists that a continuum of momentary cognitions is the Self. Since such momentary cognition arises, it is not beginningless; this is the point of the refutation.

[101] According to the logicians, selves are inert in themselves and become conscious through conjunction with consciousness. To refute this view, he explains “knowledge and the like as qualities.”

Here Prakṛti is twofold, distinguished by the covering and projecting powers. Through the covering power, that same [Prakṛti] is avidyā, the limiting adjunct of the jīva. Through the projecting power, that same [Prakṛti] is Māyā, the power of the Lord. The Puruṣa, too, is twofold, as the jīva and the Lord. Among these, the one who transmigrates through failure to distinguish himself from Prakṛti is the jīva; the one who brings Prakṛti under control and performs the creation of the universe and the rest is Īśvara. He now describes, in five verses beginning “this one,” how the jīva transmigrates through failure to distinguish himself from Prakṛti. The syntax is: “He approached at will that subtle, unmanifest, divine power of Lord Viṣṇu, which had been approached through play.”

He describes the play of that [Prakṛti] with “by the guṇas.” She is called the concealer of knowledge because she hides and covers knowledge. The Śruti likewise says: “One unborn [Prakṛti], red, white, and black, producing many offspring of the same form; one unborn [puruṣa] lies beside her, enjoying her; another unborn [puruṣa], having enjoyed her, abandons her” (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5). He became bewildered: he forgot his own self.
“Contemplation upon another” means superimposition of Prakṛti. Through that, while actions are being performed by Prakṛti’s guṇas, he considers agency to belong to himself.

“That” means the thought that one is the agent. “Of this Puruṣa”: although he is merely the witness and is not an agent, he imagines bondage through actions. Dependence in experience caused by bondage to action, even for the independent Lord, and transmigration—the stream of birth and death—even for the blissful Self, are caused by failure to distinguish oneself from Prakṛti. That is the meaning.

An objection is raised: since agency and the like are perceived through their shared locus with consciousness, let them be accepted as belonging to the self itself. He answers: No. The body is the effect; the senses are the causes; the class of deities is the agent. When the Puruṣa assumes that condition, they know Prakṛti to be the cause. Since the immutable self has no change in itself, agency and the rest are produced only by egoism connected with the body and other products of Prakṛti; that is the meaning. The meaning of “in the case of experience, they know the Puruṣa to be the cause” is this: although agency and experience both belong to egoism, agency is chiefly associated with the limiting adjunct because its modification ends in insentience, whereas experience is chiefly associated with the conditioned self because experience culminates in consciousness.

Having thus understood the transmigrating Puruṣa and Prakṛti, its cause, he now asks about Īśvara, the cause of the universe, and His Prakṛti, beginning with “from Prakṛti.” “Of this universe”: that whose nature is both manifest and unmanifest, gross and subtle, as effect, belongs to those two: Prakṛti and Puruṣa.

There he defines Prakṛti. They call that which is the pradhāna itself “Prakṛti.” What is that pradhāna? In itself it is undifferentiated, yet it possesses differentiations; it is the support of differentiated entities. Then is it Brahman? No, it is constituted of the three guṇas. Is it the mahat-tattva and the rest? No, it is unmanifest and not an effect. Is it time and the rest? No, those have the nature of manifest and unmanifest, and the form of effect and cause. Is the jīva Prakṛti? No; the jīva is eternal.

To state the characteristics of the other principles, he enumerates them, beginning with “in five.” By their numerical distinction this group has twenty-four. Know that group, consisting of Pradhāna and its effects, as the primary form of Brahman.
He explains this in three verses beginning “the great elements.” They are indeed five.
“Constituted within” means the inner instrument. “By its defining form” means by a distinguishing characteristic.

Whatever I have described is exactly that much, counted by knowers of the principles. With regard to Time, he states two views: Time is the twenty-fifth principle. The suffix ka has a diminutive sense. The meaning is that [Time] is only a particular state of Prakṛti.

But some call the power, might, or potency of Puruṣa—the Lord—Time. He defines that same Time in two ways as that from which fear arises. Fear for whom? For one who has entered, who has reached, Prakṛti; and therefore for the embodied jīva, the agent deluded by ego. Here Time is characterized by its power of dissolution.
He defines Time as the cause of creation with “from Prakṛti.”

Who is that Lord? He answers with “within.” Within all living beings, He remains fully pervading as the Puruṣa, uniformly and free from change; outside, this Lord exists in the form of Time. Alternatively, the well-known Puruṣa is Time, the twenty-fifth principle. Some, however, call the power of Puruṣa Time; “from which” defines that very power. “From Prakṛti” is the reason for Puruṣa himself being Time. “Within” is the reason when both meanings are intended; the rest is the same. Thus Prakṛti has twenty-four divisions. When the jīva and Lord are intended as one, there are twenty-five principles; when their distinction is intended, there are twenty-six.

Now he states the characteristics of the principles along with their origin, beginning with “by the divine.” This is explained by the preceding passage, before “these remaining uncombined.” There he states in four verses the characteristic of citta following its origin. “Agitated by the divine” means that whose qualities are disturbed by the unseen karma of the jīva. “Womb” is Prakṛti, the place of manifestation; “potency” means the power of consciousness. That Prakṛti gave birth to the mahat-tattva. He states the nature of mahat with “golden”: abundant in luminosity.

“The universe” means the manifested array beginning with ego. The great principle manifests what was within itself, present there in subtle form, and drank the intense darkness belonging to the time of dissolution. “Immovable” means free from dissolution and projection. What sort of darkness? That which puts the self to sleep and conceals it. The meaning is that earlier, at dissolution, the Lord had caused the great principle to merge into Prakṛti.

By way of incidental reference, he teaches worship of the fourfold emanation with “that which.” He states its fame in all scriptures with “clear,” meaning pure; “peaceful” means free from passion and the like. “The Lord’s abode” is the place of realization; therefore it is called Vāsudeva. As the presiding principle over material objects He is called Mahat; as the inner principle, citta; as the object of worship, Vāsudeva; the presiding deity is the knower of the field. Likewise, Saṅkarṣaṇa is worshiped in ego and Rudra presides over it; Aniruddha is worshiped in mind and the Moon presides; Pradyumna is worshiped in intellect and Brahmā presides.

“Clarity” means the capacity to reflect the image of Bhagavān; “immutability” means freedom from dissolution and projection. The natural state of water is its condition free from foam, waves, and the like. Before contact with earth, it is sweet, clear, and peaceful; that is the intended comparison.

Thus he indicates that this [favor] is due solely to compassion, showing the Lord’s compassion even toward those who harmed Him, and says: “Ah, what a wonder of compassion!” Although she intended to kill Him, she fed Him the deadly Kālakūṭa poison gathered in her breasts. Though wicked, the demoness Pūtanā obtained the fitting destination of a nurse, like Yaśodā. The meaning is that He granted her a good destination merely because of the appearance of devotion. Whom other than Him should we worship?

One may object that it is well known that the Lord favors only devotees. True; I consider even the demons devotees, because, like devotees, they too behold Him directly, their minds absorbed in Bhagavān through anger. Therefore, during the battle they saw their enemy, wielder of the discus, seated upon the shoulder of Garuḍa, the son of Kaśyapa, called Tārkṣya. Thus the Lord’s favor toward them too is fitting. He will also say: “Therefore, by any means, one should fix the mind on Kṛṣṇa” (Bhāgavata 7.1.28).

Now, to explain how He disappeared, he briefly recounts His story beginning from the start. He was born to Vasudeva’s wife, in the prison of Kaṃsa, lord of the Bhojas. Desiring personally to bring happiness to this earth, He came when requested by Brahmā, who was born from the Unborn Lord.

He states the characteristic with “agency.” Agency is in the form of the deities and the like; instrumentality is in the form of the senses; being an effect is in the form of the elements. Peacefulness and the rest are in the form of the three qualities in their respective causal conditions.

In two verses beginning “from the vaikārika [ego],” he states the mind’s characteristic after its origin. Saṅkalpa is thought; vikalpa is particularized thought. Since desire arises from the mind’s saṅkalpa and vikalpa, its function in the form of desire is stated as its characteristic. This is not the origin of the Pradyumna emanation, since that is not an effect of saṅkalpa and the like, and Aniruddha has already been stated as the emanation to be worshiped.
[It is] dark blue like an autumnal blue lotus. Because it is difficult to grasp, it should be worshiped gradually and is fit to be brought under control.

In two verses beginning “from the taijasa [ego],” he describes the intellect’s characteristic after stating its origin. “O virtuous one, cognition in the form of an object’s manifestation” is stated to distinguish it from citta. “The favor of the senses” refers to determinate cognition. But the phrase “lord of the senses” refers to indeterminate cognition.

Doubt and the rest are developments of the manifestation of an object itself. Error is false cognition; ascertainment is valid cognition; “sleep” means slumber. This follows Patañjali’s statement: “Valid cognition, error, conceptualization, sleep, and memory” (Yoga Sūtra 1.6).

He describes the origin of the senses: the taijasa senses are born from the fiery ego. The emphatic particle eva removes the doubt that the organs of knowledge are vaikārika. The construction is: both kinds of senses are indeed taijasa. The reason is “because of prāṇa”: prāṇa has the power of activity, and intellect has the power of cognition. Therefore, because prāṇa is taijasa, the senses endowed with its activity-power are taijasa; and because intellect is taijasa, the senses endowed with its power of knowledge are taijasa as well. That is the meaning.

In fifteen verses beginning “from the tāmasa [ego],” he describes the origin and characteristics of the great elements, ether and the rest, following the origin of the subtle elements. Phrases such as “the ear goes to sound” describe only their relation after the objects arise, not their production, since they were produced earlier. “Goes to sound” means “reaches sound.”

He states sound’s characteristic: “support of an object” means expressing an object. Being a sign of the seer means indicating a speaker concealed behind a wall, as it is said: “A sign is that which [connects] seer and seen.” The construction is: the subtle-element nature of ether is the subtlety that is sound’s characteristic.

He states the characteristic of ether with “of the elements.” “Giving openings” means providing space; “being the basis for transactions” means serving as the locus for external and internal dealings. “Self” means mind. Being the seat of prāṇa and the rest means serving as their support through openings such as channels. Function is the effect itself: its characteristic is its function. The same pattern should be understood below: one verse gives the origin of subtle and great elements, a second the characteristics of the subtle elements, and a third the characteristics of the great elements.

What is that skin? It is that by which touch is fully apprehended. The word is masculine because its grammatical gender is fixed. Alternatively, supply: the apprehension of touch arises from it. The phrase “from sound and the subtle elements” is stated to show their successive relation.
He states the characteristic of touch with “softness.” The meaning is that being touch is its essential characteristic. And air’s subtle-element nature is touch.

“Movement” is the motion of tree branches and the like; “gathering” means the joining of grass and the like. “Reaching” is the contact of a fragrant substance with the nose, and likewise the contact of something cold and the like with touch. Sound leads toward the ear. “Being the self of all the senses” means supporting them. It is characterized by action, the effect; the suffix lyuṭ is used in the sense of a state. Alternatively, parse it as “action itself is the characteristic,” with the suffix in an instrumental sense.

“Giving the form of a substance” means imparting shape to the substance. “Quality” means being perceived as subordinate to a substance, whereas sound is perceived independently. Even an imperceptible substance is independently perceived through touch and the like, but not through form; this is the distinction stated for form. “Having an arrangement of an individual” means that the arrangement or configuration of a manifested substance is itself perceived as its transformation. Fire’s being fire means its distinctive, exclusive nature.
“Illumining” means shining; “cooking” is the cooking of rice and the like. Hunger, thirst, eating, and the desire to drink—through these [functions come] drinking and eating.
The tongue is the organ of taste. “Grasping taste” means that by which taste is apprehended. Alternatively, supply: the apprehension of taste arises from it.

Salt too should be included among the astringent and other tastes. [These are] substances composed of elements and combined with one another. The meaning is that one taste, though sweet, is differentiated in this way into many forms; that is taste.

Moistening means making wet; forming a lump means shaping clay and the like into a mass. Satisfaction means the capacity to satisfy; “giving life” means sustaining life. As the Smṛti says, “prāṇa is constituted of water”; replenishing means removing the distress of thirst. “Undana” means softening; the reading “ondana” has the same meaning. “Abundance” means repeated emergence, as with water that repeatedly wells up after being drawn from a well.
“Going to smell” means reaching the odor.

Karambha is a mixed smell, as in condiments prepared with asafoetida and the like. “Putrid” means foul-smelling; fragrance is that of camphor and the like; “mild” is the scent of lotus and the like; “pungent” is the scent of garlic and the like; “sour” is the scent of tamarind and the like. Smell is differentiated in this way by differences in the combined constituents of substances.

“Making manifest” means giving Brahman a form, such as an image. “Being situated” means existing without dependence on another support, unlike water and the like; “holding” means serving as a support for water and the rest. The differentiating characteristic of existing things such as ether is that which delimits them. The manifestation of all beings, living creatures, and their qualities such as masculinity means making them evident through their transformations.

The capacity of hearing and the other senses to receive sound and the rest has been stated. He says in five half-verses that their characteristics are those very qualities. The special quality of ether is sound, which is its object.

He shows what the term “special quality” excludes with “of the prior.” The property of a prior cause, such as sound, is seen in a later effect, such as air, because the cause continues in the effect. Therefore every distinctive quality of entities such as ether—sound and the rest—is found in earth, because the four [elements] are present there. In water and the rest, only the qualities present there occur, not all; in ether there is only one, since the others are absent.

Having explained the origin of the cause, he explains the origin of the effect in three and a half verses. When these remained separate and uncombined, the Lord, source of the universe, entered them. “Seven” is stated with reference to the principal categories, but entry into all of them is intended.
“Interpenetrated” means agitated. From this egg the Virāṭ Puruṣa arose.
“The form of Bhagavān” is stated with reference to His non-difference from the Puruṣa.

In nine verses beginning “from the golden [Virāṭ],” he describes the divisions of the individual elements and the rest. “Rising” means giving up indifference, entering it, and presiding over it. “He is great and divine”; “kha” means an opening.

Fire came into being and entered along with speech. The two nostrils were pierced. The construction is: pervaded and threaded through by prāṇa, the sense of smell became present in these two nostrils.

After the organ of smell comes air. The qualifier “pervaded by prāṇa” should be understood of all the senses. The two readings “nyabhidyetām” and “anvabhidyetām” have the same meaning. Then the directions entered.
The word “and the rest” includes the hair.
Svarāṭ is Indra; Hari is Viṣṇu.
It was brought forth and came into being.
The heart alone is the seat of intellect and the rest. Brahmā is the lord of speech. The inner ruler is the knower of the field.
To distinguish the knower of the field through agreement and difference, he describes the re-entry of all, in nine verses beginning “these.”
Showing the individual body as an illustration of the universal Virāṭ body, he explains the purpose of narrating Sāṅkhya with two verses beginning “as.”

First, devotion to the Supreme Lord; then dispassion toward other things; then an intellect inclined to yoga. Then, with the mind one-pointed, there arises knowledge by which one should distinguish and contemplate the inward Self, the knower of the field, within this aggregate of effects and causes.
